Furthermore, there are those who say that those heterodox teachers do not actually establish these one hundred and twenty faculties.
Question: If it is not so, then how is it? Answer:
Those heterodox teachers posit one hundred and twenty Indras, as it has been said:
the lord of nāgas, the lord of garuḍas, the lord of asuras, the lord of devas, the lord of humans, and the lord of brahmās.
"Such a most supreme and most wondrous body ought to receive one hundred and twenty masters each.
Upon hearing this, that brahmin again gave rise to doubt, not knowing which was the primary designation: was it the single faculty?
"Does it reach one hundred and twenty faculties?

Having heard that a young man born into the Śākya clan possesses a body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, a golden halo, and a Brahma-voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird—such that one never tires of beholding him—[he asked this].
When he was born, he took seven steps, and two dragons bathed him.
A brahmin diviner prophesied that there were only two possibilities for him and no other:
if he remains at home, he will become a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous Dharma-king; [if he goes forth, he will become a Buddha].
"If one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saṃghāṭī robe, and with faith and joy leaves the home life to study the Path, they shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

This shall be heard by all the world: that he has already left the home life to study the Path and subdued the host of Māra; that he has attained unsurpassed, supreme, perfect enlightenment; that he has acquired all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*); and that he has manifested the severance of all doubts, bestowed all meditative concentrations, and resolved all treatises."
"I shall go and ask:
'Which is the ultimate truth—[the teaching] that establishes one faculty up to one hundred and twenty faculties?

He then went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arrival, exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having concluded the exchange of courtesies, he sat down to one side and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"O Gautama! I wish to ask you something.
Grant me leave to ask, and you shall explain it to me."
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin, ask whatever you wish."
The brahmin said:
"Gautama! 'Roots' refers to roots."
Gautama! How many sense bases (āyatana) are there?
What, Gautama, is their nature?
It is established by means of the designation of what is comprised within each faculty.
This does not state who establishes it or how many faculties there are. Question:
Why is it not mentioned?
The answer is: He thinks thus:
"If I were to speak, that victor, having heard it, would refute me.
The World-Honored One said: "O Brahmin!"
"There are twenty-two faculties, from the eye faculty up to the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown.
Brahmin! There are just so many faculties; it is in this way that the Tathāgata designates them by means of the designation of the inclusion of faculty within faculty."
"O Brahmin! If one were to say:
'These faculties are not as they have been designated by the ascetic Gautama; I shall abandon these faculties and designate other faculties instead';"
He possesses nothing but mere words; having been questioned, he does not know and thus increases his delusion.
Why is this? Because it is not within his sphere of experience.
Question: For what reason is it said that this brahmin possesses such faculties, and that he is designated by the designation of being encompassed by the faculties of a Tathāgata? Answer:
He merely adheres to what he has previously heard—that is, the designation of one faculty up to one hundred and twenty faculties.

This is not as he claims; even I, who am all-knowing and all-seeing, cannot increase or decrease the twenty-two faculties, let alone those of other teachers who, with their views having corrupted their minds, possess only ordinary knowledge.

For this reason, that brahmin asked about the faculties (*indriya*), but did not ask about the elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), aggregates (*skandha*), truths (*satya*), fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), or dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The twenty-two faculties range from the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) to the faculty of one who has nothing further to know (*ajñātāvīndriya*).
Question: There are twenty-two faculties (indriya) by name; how many are there by way of seed?
The Abhidharmikas say:
The Master says that while there are twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) by name, there are seventeen by way of category (*prakāra*).

According to the Abhidharma, five faculties are not considered to be of this category: the male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Question: Why are the male faculty and the female faculty not intended to be of this [seed] nature? Answer:
He explains it as stated in the Abhidharma:
"What is the female faculty (strī-indriya) and a portion of the body faculty (kāya-indriya)?
What is the male faculty (puruṣa-indriya) and a portion of the body faculty?"
Since he is devoid of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), he does not wish for the male and female faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*) to have separate seeds. Question:

Why does he not wish for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) to be seeds?
The answer is:

That [text] explains that the collection of these nine faculties constitutes the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), the collection of nine faculties constitutes the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the collection of nine faculties constitutes the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
Regarding the combination of nine faculties: the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*), the three feeling faculties (*vedanā-indriya*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

These nine faculties are sometimes the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), sometimes the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and sometimes the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Specifically, they are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the faculty of "knowing" during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the faculty of "one who has known" during the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) exists within the mental continuum of those with firm faith and firm Dharma; the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) exists within the mental continuum of those liberated through faith, those who have attained vision, and those who have realized through the body; and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya) exists within the mental continuum of those liberated through wisdom and those liberated in both ways.

Thus, these nine faculties—namely, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," or the faculty of "one who has known"—constitute twenty-two faculties in total; however, there are seventeen distinct types.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta says:
"There are twenty-two faculties by name, but fourteen by way of their essential nature (*jāti*).
The Venerable Dharmatrāta does not intend for these five faculties to be of that nature; there are three others:"
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the protection-faculty (anurakṣaṇendriya), and the concentration-faculty (samādhīndriya). Question:
For what reason does he not wish for these to be the seeds?

Answer: This life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha); however, for that Venerable Dharmatrāta, the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind is not a seed.
Question: For what reason does he guard his faculties and not wish for this seed to be produced? Answer:
The Venerable Dharmatrāta said:

"There are only these two kinds of sensation—namely, pleasure and pain. As for that sensation which is neither painful nor pleasant, it can neither cause suffering nor cause joy; how, then, can this be considered a sensation?"
Question: How is that sutra of the Buddha to be reconciled?
For the Buddha taught three types of sensation:
Pleasurable feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The answer is:

they speak of there being pleasurable feelings and painful feelings that are either weak or intense, or dull or sharp; that is to say, when those pleasurable and painful feelings are weak, or when those pleasurable and painful feelings are dull, or when those pleasurable and painful feelings have ceased—that is their "neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
It is simply because those who have transcended suffering and pleasure do not wish for further sensation;
that is why it is so. Question:
For what reason does he certainly not desire these seeds?
Answer: It arises from the sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
What is the faculty of concentration?
The answer is:
a well-directed mind in one-pointedness.

For that *dharmāyatana*, apart from mind (*citta*), there is no separate category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); for this reason, it is called the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), though its categories (*prakāra*) number fourteen.
The Venerable Buddhadeva says:

"There are twenty-two faculties by name, but their categories are either two or five; that is to say, they are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) consisting of the two divisions [of form and mind], the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and mind."

They state that those which are material faculties (*rūpindriya*) are variations of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), while those which are non-material faculties (*arūpindriya*) are variations of the mind (*citta*).
For this reason, they are said to have twenty-two faculties; as for their types, there are either two or five.
Speaking in this manner, there are twenty-two faculties (indriya) by name and seventeen by substance (dravya).

Just as it is with names and substances, so too should one understand the enumeration of names and the enumeration of substances; the characteristics of names and the characteristics of substances; the distinctness of names and the distinctness of substances; the differentiation of names and the differentiation of substances; and the cognition of names and the cognition of substances—all of these should be understood in their entirety.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"One should speak of a single faculty; it is the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) in its ultimate sense.
He was asked:
Why is this? The answer is:
because this is internal, universal, and a common object-condition (*sādhāraṇālambana*).
"Internal" means that which is subsumed under the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*).
"Universal" means it can be found from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
"Commonly conditioned" means taking all phenomena as its object.
This means that among the remaining faculties within this collection—
namely the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, male, and female faculties— although they are internal, they are neither universal nor common objects of perception.

Among the five faculties, with the exception of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the remaining four sensations (*vedanā*), although they share a common object, are neither internal nor universal.
The faculty of equanimity and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), although universal and sharing a common object, are not internal.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya) do not have distinct seeds; this was already explained previously as a collection of faculties.
Question: For what reason do the other faculties receive the name "faculty" (indriya)?
Answer: Because of dependence, because of reliance, because of attachment, because of purification, and because of having already been purified.
"Dependence" refers to the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
"Repose" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
"Attachment" refers to the five sufferings.
"Purity" refers to the fivefold faith (*pañcaśraddhā*)."
The "already purified" refers to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known. Question:
If that is so, for what reason do the male faculty and the female faculty receive the designation of "faculty"?
The answer is:

Within this desire realm, there are the seeds of sexual misconduct and the species of sexual misconduct; these seeds of sexual misconduct and species of sexual misconduct depend upon the male organ and the female organ.
Or it is said:

Due to five reasons: first, the production of birth; second, the arising of desire for pleasure; third, the ability to cease the fetters; fourth, the basis for the arising of defiled body-consciousness; and fifth, those who engage in sexual intercourse with fixed intent.
"Born from birth" refers to those born from a womb.
"Those who experience sensual pleasure" means that when such lustful persons give rise to sensual pleasure at this location, pleasure arises throughout their entire bodies.

Just as a noble one gives rise to the noble pleasure from between the eyebrows and pleasure arises throughout their entire body, so too does that lustful person give rise to sensual pleasure at this location and pleasure arises throughout their entire body.
That which can stop the fetters (saṃyojana) stops them for a brief moment.
Regarding the body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna) based on defiled [roots]: based on the other three types [of roots], consciousness arises as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Based on the male organ or female organ, unwholesome body-consciousness necessarily arises; it is neither wholesome nor indeterminate.
Regarding those who definitely engage in sexual intercourse: it is the habitual mind of lust, not a mind that is not habitual to lust.

For five reasons, the male and female organs receive their names: first, they produce successive births; second, they give rise to sensual pleasure; third, they can arrest the fetters; fourth, they serve as the basis for the arising of defiled bodily consciousness; and fifth, they belong to those who definitely engage in sexual intercourse. It is for these reasons that the male and female organs are so named.
Furthermore, there are those who say that among these, the six life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*) should be explained as the primary faculties in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
These six life-faculties are: the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, and the life-faculty.
Question: For what reason? Answer:
This refers to the fundamental category of sentient beings. Question:
If this is the fundamental category of sentient beings, by what cause are those other faculties named?
The answer is:
by reason of the seed, by reason of defilement, by reason of purity, and by reason of having become pure.
"By reason of the seed" refers to the faculty of mind (manas-indriya).
That which is caused by defilement refers to the five types of suffering.
That which is caused by purity refers to the five faculties of faith and so forth.
That which is caused by that which is already purified refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
For this reason, the other faculties receive their names.
Question: By what cause do the male faculty and the female faculty receive the name "faculty"?
Answer: This refers to those who undergo rebirth and those who have emerged from the cycle of existence.
Those who undergo rebirth are, for example, the six heretical teachers.
Those who give rise to essential persons are the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
For this reason, the male organ and female organ receive their names. Some say:
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is to be explained as the first of the ultimate faculties (paramārthendriya).
Regarding the eight [faculties] beginning with the life-faculty: they are the eye-faculty, the ear, nose, tongue, body, male, female, and life-faculties. Question:
Why is this? The answer is:
it refers to these fundamental seeds of sentient beings.
Question: If this is the fundamental seed, by what cause are the other faculties so named? Answer:
They receive the designation of "faculties" (indriya) due to their nature as seeds, due to defilement, due to purification, and due to having attained purification.
That which is due to being a seed is the faculty of mind (manas-indriya).
That which is due to defilement refers to the five feelings of pain (vedanā).
The "purity of cause" refers to the five faculties of faith and so forth.
The "purity of the cause already attained" refers to the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*).
It is for this reason that the other faculties receive their names.
This is the natural character of the body consisting of the individual natures of each faculty.
Having explained their nature, one should now explain their activity.
For what reason are they called "faculties" (*indriya*)?

What is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)? The answer is: the meaning of sovereignty (*adhipatya*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of clarity (*vidyā*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of gathering (*saṃgraha*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of being primary (*mūla*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of being supreme (*agra*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of being excellent (*praṇīta*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of being sublime (*viśiṣṭa*) is the meaning of faculty; the meaning of arising (*janman*) is the meaning of faculty.

Question: If "predominance" (*adhipati*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*), then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) would each be predominant over one another, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) would also be predominant over conditioned phenomena.
For what reason are twenty-two faculties established?
The answer is:
these are predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which may be predominant or weak, and either superior or inferior.
It should be understood that the dominant conditions which are dominant and sublime are the twenty-two faculties;
it should be understood that the remaining phenomena are the dominant conditions which are weak and inferior.

Some say: Although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) mutually increase one another, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) increase conditioned phenomena, there is nothing else that possesses a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) such as these—such increase, such clarity, such inclusion, such thesis, such supremacy, such excellence, and such subtlety—as do the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
Just as individuals mutually increase one another, yet there is nothing else that serves as a sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*),

so it is with the village headman, the king of a country, the wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) of the four continents, the Brahmā of a great thousandfold world system, and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, of a trichiliocosm.

Thus, although all conditioned phenomena mutually augment one another, and unconditioned phenomena augment conditioned phenomena, there is nothing else that possesses such dominance (*adhipati*), such clarity, such inclusion, such thesis, such supremacy, such excellence, or such subtlety as do the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, it is said that the meaning of predominance, clarity, inclusion, thesis, supremacy, excellence, subtlety, and production is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya).
Question: If the meaning of "predominance" (adhipati) is the meaning of "faculty" (indriya), for what purpose does this faculty serve as a predominant condition (adhipatipratyaya)? Answer:

The eye faculty serves as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for four matters: first, the physical beauty of one's own body; second, the maintenance of one's own body; third, the arising of consciousness based upon it; and fourth, its unique function.
Regarding one who is upright and dignified in person: they cause the body to be exceedingly exquisite, fully endowed with all its limbs and joints.
If the faculty of the eye is incomplete, that person is not upright; it increases much that is unwholesome.
If the eyes are complete and one’s countenance is upright and handsome such that the multitude does not harbor ill-will toward them, this is called the physical majesty of one's own body.

As for maintaining one's body: when the eyes perceive the good and the evil, one eliminates the evil and follows the good so that the body may endure for a long time; this is called maintaining one's body.
Regarding "arising in dependence on [the sense organ]": it means that visual consciousness arises in dependence upon this eye; this is what is meant by "arising in dependence on [the sense organ].
Regarding "unshared function": the eye-faculty sees visible forms, a function which no other faculty possesses.

The ear faculty also has four functions as its predominant conditions: first, the physical beauty of one's own body; second, the maintenance of one's own body; third, serving as the basis for the arising of consciousness; and fourth, its unique function.
Regarding "one's own body being upright and majestic": this means making the body exceedingly sublime and complete in all its limbs and joints.
If the faculty of hearing is incomplete, one is not upright and handsome; it greatly increases what is unwholesome.
If the faculty of the ear is complete and one’s countenance is upright and handsome, such that the multitude does not harbor ill-will toward them, this is called having a dignified and majestic self.

As for "maintaining the self," when the ears hear what is good or evil, one eliminates the evil and follows the good so as to cause the body to endure for a long time; this is called maintaining the self.
Regarding "arising in dependence on [the sense organ]": it means that the ear-consciousness arises in dependence on this ear; this is what is meant by "arising in dependence on [the sense organ].
Regarding "its unique function": the ear-faculty's hearing of sounds is a function that no other faculty possesses.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the eye-faculty serves as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for maintaining the body of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
As it is said in a verse:
"The eye sees all evils;..."
"One should seek it according to reality; through wisdom one abides in the world, removing all evils.
The faculty of hearing maintains the Dharma-body as its dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
As it is said in the verse:
"By hearing the Dharma one can understand; by hearing, one refrains from evil; by hearing, one abandons what is unwholesome;
by hearing, one attains cessation."
Furthermore, there are those who say that both the eye faculty and the ear faculty serve as dominant conditions for upholding both the body of birth-and-death and the Dharma-body.
Upholding the body of birth-and-death is as previously explained.
One who upholds the Dharma-body does so by means of the faculty of the eye drawing near to spiritual friends for recitation and study, and the faculty of the ear hearing the Dharma.
Having drawn near to spiritual friends and heard the Dharma, one contemplates and directs the mind toward the successive stages of the Dharma.
For this reason, that sūtra states:
"At that time, the two faculties of the brahmin Brahmā were unimpaired—the eye faculty and the ear faculty.
It is asked:
Why is this? Because among all the faculties, two faculties are said to be indestructible: the eye faculty and the ear faculty.
The answer is:
these two faculties are the gate, the crossing, and the path for entering into the Buddha-dharma.
For this reason, among all the faculties, it is said that two faculties are indestructible: the eye faculty and the ear faculty.

The nose, tongue, and body faculties also have four matters as their predominant conditions: first, the physical beauty of one's own body; second, the maintenance of one's own body; third, serving as the basis for the arising of consciousness; and fourth, their unique functions.
Regarding one’s own physical excellence: it means making the body supremely sublime and fully endowed with all its limbs and joints.
If the three sense organs are incomplete, one is not upright or handsome, and this increases many forms of unwholesomeness.
One who possesses the three faculties has a handsome countenance, and the multitude does not harbor ill-will toward them;
this is called the physical excellence of one's own body.

To sustain one’s body is to rely on these three faculties for the consumption of edible food (*kavaḷīkārāhāra*); that is to say, edible food consists of the three sense-bases of odor, flavor, and tangibility—this is called sustaining one’s body.

Regarding "arising in dependence on consciousness": based on these three faculties, the three types of consciousness arise; this is what is meant by "arising in dependence on consciousness. Regarding "unique functions":
these refer to the nose smelling odors, the tongue knowing tastes, and the body knowing tactile sensations; such functions do not exist for the other faculties.
The mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for two things: first, the subsequent production of future existence; second, sovereignty.
Regarding the subsequent production of future existence, it is as stated:
"Ānanda!..."
"If consciousness did not enter the mother's womb, would the layers of name-and-form gradually thicken?
Ānanda replied, "No,
World-Honored One."
World-Honored One!
This is called the existence of the next birth to come.
As for "sovereignty," it is as has been said:
"Monks! The mind drags one toward the world; the mind is afflicted, yet the mind can attain mastery.
Furthermore, it is said that the faculty of mind has two further predominant conditions: first, defilement and attachment; second, purification."
Regarding "attachment," it is as said:
"The mind is attached; sentient beings are attached.
Regarding "purity," it is as said:
When the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
This refers to the two matters that serve as the predominant conditions for the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).

The female faculty (*strīndriya*) and male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) likewise have two matters as their predominant conditions: first, the establishment of the faculties (*prajñapti-indriya*), and second, the severance of the faculties (*chedana-indriya*).
Regarding the establishment of the faculties (*indriya-prajñapti*): originally there was a single person who knew neither "male" nor "female.

When a small amount of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) arises, because of that small amount of derived matter, there arise differences in female form, differences in location, differences in the wearing of clothing, differences in speech, differences in food and drink, and differences in coming and going;
the male form likewise differs.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these male and female organs also serve as two types of dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*): first, defilement and attachment; second, purification.
Regarding defilement and attachment, they are called the "dominant masters" because they are not [merely] sexual; of this there is no doubt.
Question: If it is not sexual misconduct, what is it? Answer:

If one possesses these two faculties, they will engage in conduct that is contrary to dignified decorum; they will be able to commit the five heinous crimes and sever their roots of goodness, extinguishing all seeds of virtue and destroying every root of goodness.
These do not constitute masculinity; they are neither male nor female, being either sexless or possessing both sexual organs, and thus cannot commit such evil deeds.

As for those who are pure—if they possess these two faculties, they may receive the full ordination and, through their majestic deportment, be able to give rise to the majestic deportment of meditative concentration and the majestic deportment of the outflow-free state. They can eliminate the fetters of the desire realm and the form realm, and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, or the fruit of a Buddha.
Those who do not achieve masculinity, who are not male, who are sexless, or who possess both sexual organs, cannot produce such merit.
Thus, it is said that the male and female faculties serve as the dominant conditions for these two matters.
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) serves as the dominant condition for two matters: first, the establishment of the faculties; second, the severance of the faculties.
Regarding the establishment of the faculties: as long as life exists, one speaks of the existence of the faculties. Once death has occurred, what faculties remain?

Furthermore, there are those who say that the four factors of the life-faculty serve as its predominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*): the continuity of the species, the succession of the species, the maintenance of the species, and the non-interruption of the activity of the species; these are called the four factors of the life-faculty serving as predominant conditions.
The five faculties of pain (duḥkhendriya) are exclusively characterized by defiled attachment and serve as the predominant condition.

It is because of these five pains that sentient beings are driven toward the east, west, south, and north; they must traverse paths of planks, paths of thorns, paths of caltrops, and paths of mountain precipices; they must cross the island of rākṣasīs, enter the great ocean with its swirling eddies and surging waves, lose sight of Mount Sāgaramata which has become the color of water, encounter violent black winds, and pass through the realm of evil nāgas—all for the sake of the wealth and goods they seek, which are entirely due to these five pains.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) also have two things as their predominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*): first, defiled attachment; second, purification.
Regarding defiled attachment, it is as stated:
"The sensation of pleasure is driven by the underlying tendency of craving."
Regarding purification, it is as stated:
"One delights in one's own mental concentration.
The faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief also have two matters as their predominant conditions: first, defilement and attachment; second, purification.
Regarding "defiled attachment," it is as stated:
"one who is driven by the underlying tendencies of suffering, pain, and aversion.
Regarding "purity," it is as stated:

With regard to the cause of suffering and its origin, the faculty of faith and the faculty of conscientiousness also serve as two predominant conditions: first, defilement and attachment; second, purification.
Regarding defilement and attachment, it is as stated:
One who is neither in pain nor in pleasure is driven by the underlying tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). Regarding "purity," it is as stated:
namely, by relying on the six means of deliverance, guarding them, practicing them, and establishing oneself upon them.

This means that based on these six desires, one abandons protection; thus, one attains cessation. In this way, the five faculties of pain (duḥkhendriya) serve as the predominant conditions for these two matters.
Furthermore, the five faculties of faith (śraddhendriya), being exclusively pure, serve as the predominant condition.
As it is said in a verse:
"Faith can cross the stream; heedfulness [crosses] the ocean; through truth one abandons suffering;
and by means of wisdom, one attains purity."
As it has been said:
"Śāriputra is accomplished in faith; if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī removes what is unwholesome and practices what is wholesome.
Furthermore, as it has been said:
Ānanda’s diligence can indeed lead to the transformation into the Path.
As it has been said:
"The noble disciple Śāriputra has perfected the power of diligence; he eliminates what is unwholesome and practices what is wholesome."
As it has been said:
"I declare mindfulness to be the foremost among all things.
As it has been said:
Śāriputra, the noble disciple achieves mindfulness, acting like a gatekeeper who removes what is unwholesome and cultivates what is wholesome.
As it is said in a verse:
"Concentration is the path; that which is not concentrated is not the path. Having attained concentration, one knows for oneself."
"The rise and fall of the five aggregates.
As it has been said:
"Śāriputra, when a noble disciple accomplishes the three samādhis, he must eliminate what is unwholesome and cultivate what is wholesome."
As it is said in the verse:
"Wisdom is the excellence of the world; It can bring about that which is to be reached, And through the use of right and perfect knowledge, It brings an end to birth, old age, sickness, and death."
As it is said: "Wisdom transcends all dharmas.
As it is further said:

Sisters! With the sword of wisdom, the noble disciple cuts off all fetters, bonds, underlying tendencies, afflictions, and entanglements; he cuts them deeply, strikes them repeatedly, and strips them away.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) serves as the predominant condition for that which has not yet been seen to become a state to be seen.
The faculty of one who has already known and already seen serves as the predominant condition for the removal of all evils.
The faculty of one who has not yet known serves as the predominant condition for experiencing happiness in the present life once all evils have been removed.
This is called the "matter.
Within this, these twenty-two faculties serve as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Having explained their common functioning, their distinct functioning shall now be explained.
What is the eye-faculty?
The answer is:
it refers to the eye that has seen, will see, or is currently seeing visible forms, as well as all other things belonging to this category.
That which has already been seen is the past.
That which is yet to be seen is the future.
That which is being seen now is the present.
And as for whatever else exists therein, it refers to that eye-consciousness being either empty or non-empty.
As it is with the eye-faculty, so it is likewise with the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Question: What is the faculty of mind? Answer:
This refers to that which has been cognized, will be cognized, and is currently being cognized by the mind with respect to mental phenomena (dharmas), as well as all other such things.
That which has been cognized belongs to the past;
that which will be cognized belongs to the future.
The consciousness of the present is "now.
Furthermore, whatever else exists therein refers to that which is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Question:
What is the female faculty?
The answer is:
a portion of the body faculty.
What is the male faculty?
It is a portion of the body faculty. Question:

If the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the body are fully present from the feet to the crown of the head, why is it that the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) are said to exist only in a small portion of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*)?
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
"These two faculties cause sentient beings to be designated as 'male' or 'female.'"
Question: Regarding the designation "possessing both sexual organs" (*ubhayavyañjana*), is it intended that those two organs themselves receive this designation?
The Venerable Dharmatrāta said:
"O Venerable Ones!
Within these two faculties, Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, Ṛṣis, and Māṇavas are born, well-pleased and well-guided. He asked:
What is the life-faculty?
The answer is:
it is the lifespan of the three realms.

Question: For what reason is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) established as a faculty within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*), while the genus (*nikāyasabhāga*) is not? Answer:
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a fruition-result (*vipākaphala*), because it is the result of all retributive causes and formations.
Its category is indeterminate; it may be either a fruition-result or a dependent-result (*niśrayaphala*).
For this reason, while the life-faculty is established among the faculties, its [specific] category is not so established.
Question: What is the faculty of pleasure? Answer:

Pleasurable sensation arises from contact; that is, wholesome pleasure produced within the body and mind, which is capable of being cognized as a sensation—this is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?
Answer: It is the contact of painful sensation.
If an unwholesome bodily pain arises and is experienced as such, this is called the faculty of pain (duḥkhendriya).
Question: What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)? Answer:
The contact of pleasant feeling associated with joy.
If wholesome pleasure arises within the mind and one perceives it as a sensation, this is called the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*). Question:
What is the faculty of grief?
The answer is:
it is contact associated with the experience of grief.
If unwholesome suffering arises within the mind and one perceives it as painful, this is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
Answer: It is the contact with the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
If, within the mind, there arises that which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and one perceives this as feeling, this is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of faith? Answer:

When practicing without desire for the sake of wholesome dharmas, if one possesses faith—being able to believe, possessing profound trust, and being reverently cautious; having understood, will understand, and now understands; with a mind that is subdued and pure—this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of diligence? Answer:

When practicing without desire for the sake of wholesome dharmas, if one exerts oneself with the power of skillful means and diligence—having been able, being able, and now being able to maintain right mindfulness of the mind—this is called the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya)? Answer:

When practicing without desire for the sake of wholesome dharmas, if one contemplates, contemplates again, and contemplates repeatedly—having remembered, about to remember, and currently remembering—with mindfulness that does not forget and with right recollection, this is called the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)? Answer:

When practicing without desire for the sake of wholesome qualities, if the mind abides, abides evenly, and abides supremely—undisturbed, undistracted, and concentrated in right samādhi—this is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*).
Question: What is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya)? Answer:

When practicing without desire for the sake of wholesome dharmas, if one discriminates and selects dharmas, discriminates views, equal views, superior views, understands, equally understands, and thoroughly understands, and if there is the eye of the mountain-like earth, awakening, discernment, wisdom, practice, and contemplation—this is called the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
Question: What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"? Answer:

If a person has not yet seen or contemplated, it refers to those training in wisdom—the faculty of wisdom and the other faculties—who, having firm faith and firm dharma, are able to contemplate the Four Truths though they have not yet contemplated them.
"If a person has not yet seen" means that they have not yet perceived them.
"Those who have not yet contemplated the truths" refers to those who have not yet contemplated the [Four] Truths.
"The faculty of wisdom belonging to those in training" is precisely the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, "the various faculties of those with firm faith and firm Dharma who have not yet contemplated the Four Truths but are able to contemplate them" refers to the eight faculties.
The aggregation of these nine faculties is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya). Question:
For what reason is wisdom (prajñā) designated by two names, while the other factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are not?
Answer: Because it is a sublime exposition and a sublime meaning.
Among all those categories, which one is the most sublime?
Wisdom is as it has been said:
"The king and his retinue proceed."

Some say: Wisdom (*prajñā*) is capable of three types of contemplation—first, the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*); second, the contemplation of views (*dṛṣṭi-vipaśyanā*); and third, the contemplation of conditions (*ālambana-vipaśyanā*).

They maintain that although the associated mental factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) possess two types of contemplation—the contemplation of phenomena and the contemplation of conditions—they do not possess the contemplation of views, because their intrinsic nature is wisdom but they are not themselves wisdom.
This means that although those co-existent factors possess a single contemplation of things, it is not a contemplation by way of seeing, because their nature is not wisdom;
nor is it a contemplation by way of an object, because they do not take dharmas as their objects.
This wisdom is able to perform the three contemplations; for this reason it is so.
Or it is said:
because wisdom perceives the fetters, they cannot remain long.
Just as a subterranean insect that sees an object returns to its hole, so too, when wisdom perceives the fetters (*saṃyojana*), they cannot remain for long.
Others say: it means that when wisdom illuminates the mind, the thieves of the fetters cannot cause disturbance.
Just as thieves do not dare to harass a room where there is a lamp, so too the thieves of mental fetters do not harass one whose mind is illuminated by wisdom.
It is said: "Lacking wisdom, one is bound; possessing wisdom, one is liberated."
Some say: Within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is called bliss; to be able to awaken is sublime.
It is like a blind person entering an island of precious jewels—such is the state of one who enters the Buddha-dharma without wisdom.
Just as one with eyes enters an island of precious jewels, so does one with wisdom enter the Buddha-dharma.
This speaks of the joy of wisdom within the Buddha-dharma; to be able to awaken to it is sublime.
Some say: Wisdom is that which is able to observe, while the other factors of the path are blind.
It is like a group of blind people who have one person with sight to serve as their guide.
In this way, those who are blind regarding the other factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) can be observed by the wise, who act as guides to lead them into the precious True Reality.
Some say: it is like a person speaking of the eye; [the Buddha] is the primary awakening, the seed of awakening, the path, and the seed of the path.
Some say: Wisdom is that which can illuminate all phenomena.
These are external matters, such as the sun, moon, stars, mani jewels, medicinal herbs, necklaces, and palaces.
It is able to illuminate one realm, one base, one aggregate, and a small portion of one time.
"One realm" refers to the realm of form; "one base" refers to the base of form; "one aggregate" refers to the aggregate of form; and "one time" refers to the present.
This wisdom is able to illuminate the eighteen realms (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), the five aggregates (skandhas), and the three periods of time.
Some say: it means that wisdom is able to sever the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all phenomena.

The establishment of the specific and general characteristics of phenomena eliminates delusion regarding seeds and delusion regarding conditions, such that one acts without inversion with respect to phenomena.
Some say: this is like what is called a lecture hall.
As it has been said:
"Venerable friends!
I rely upon the precepts to establish the precepts; having ascended the precepts, I have entered the lecture hall of unsurpassed wisdom and, with little effort, observe a thousand worlds."
Some say: When referring to the severing of fetters, it is said to be like a sharp blade.
As it has been stated:

Sisters! Noble sisters and noble disciples, with the sword of wisdom, sever the fetters, bonds, underlying tendencies, and entanglements of affliction; they cut them repeatedly, strike them repeatedly, and hack them apart.
Some say: This teaching is like a precious jewel.
As it has been said:
Śāriputra! The noble disciple accomplishes the precious jewel of wisdom, eliminating what is unwholesome and practicing what is wholesome.
It is said:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, delights in wisdom.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not delight in physical beauty, nor in lineage, nor in strength, nor in wealth, nor in noble status, nor in retinues; he delights only in wisdom.
By means of these two names for wisdom (*prajñā*), the remaining factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are one.
Question: What is the faculty of "already-known" (*ājñātendriya*)?

Answer: It refers to a person who, having already seen and contemplated the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) cultivated through training, as well as the other faculties, has—through faith-liberation (*śraddhādhimukta*), vision-attainment (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*)—already contemplated the truths and is now able to ascend to further contemplation.
"Those who have already seen" refers to those who have already seen the truths (*satya*).
"Those who have already contemplated" refers to those who have already contemplated the truths.
"The faculty of wisdom of one training in wisdom" is precisely the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

Furthermore, for those who have attained the faculties of faith-liberation (śraddhā-vimukti), vision-attainment (dṛṣṭi-prāpta), and bodily realization (kāya-sākṣin), and who, having already contemplated the truths, are capable of further higher contemplation, these consist of eight faculties.
When these nine faculties are combined and gathered together, they are called the faculty of "already-known" (ājñātendriya).
Question: Just as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are also able to progress upward—

such as one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) reaching the nature of non-falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), one of the nature of non-falling away reaching the nature of mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), one of the nature of mindfulness reaching the nature of protection (*sthitākampyadharman*), one of the nature of protection reaching the nature of advancement (*prativedhanādharman*), and one of the nature of advancement reaching the nature of being unshakable (*akopyadharman*)— [is it not the same for those in training?]
Why is it said that one speaks of the "learner's superior contemplation" (śaikṣa-adhiprajñā) but not of the "non-learner's" (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: It should indeed be spoken of.

If it were not so stated, this would be a statement of the Blessed One with further meaning (*savyavaccheda-vacana*); one should understand the meaning through these gateways to the meaning, these summaries of the meaning, and these transitions of the meaning.
Or it is said:
that which refers to the further severing of fetters and the further experiencing of results is called the higher contemplation (*uttara-vipaśyanā*).
That one beyond training (aśaikṣa) neither further severs fetters nor further undergoes fruition; for this reason, "higher observation" is not mentioned.
Alternatively, it is said:

that which refers to the acquisition of the acquisition of dharmas through the further severing of bonds, and the further undergoing of the acquisition of liberation—that is what is called "higher observation."

That one beyond training (aśaikṣa) no longer further severs the acquisition of fetters (bandhana-prāpti), nor does he further undergo the acquisition of liberation (vimukti-prāpti); for this reason, "higher contemplation" (ūrdhva-darśana) is not mentioned.
Alternatively, it is said:
when one further severs ignorance and further attains knowledge, that is called "higher contemplation."

Although that one beyond training (aśaikṣa) further attains knowledge, he does not further sever ignorance or the defilement of ignorance; therefore, it is said that this refers to the higher contemplation of the learner (śaikṣa), and not to the one beyond training.
Question: What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"? Answer:

This refers to a person who, having seen and having contemplated the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), and all the faculties [of those] liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), has contemplated the truths and experiences happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Regarding the phrase "a person who has seen": it means that such a person has already seen the truths (*satya*).
"Those who have already contemplated" refers to those who have contemplated the Truths.
"The wisdom of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the faculty of wisdom" refers precisely to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

Furthermore, regarding "the various faculties, those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*), those doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), those who have already contemplated the Truths, and those who experience happiness in the present life," this refers to the eight faculties.
The aggregation of these nine faculties is called the faculty of "one who has no more to learn" (aśaikṣa-indriya). Question:

Since those in training (śaikṣa) also experience happiness in the present life, why is it said that only those beyond training experience happiness in the present life, while it is not so stated for those in training?
Answer: It should be explained.

If it were not explained, this would be a statement by the World-Honored One that is incomplete; one should understand the meaning through these presented gateways to the meaning, these presented summaries of the meaning, and these presented transitions of the meaning.
Some say: It is because it is a wondrous teaching and a wondrous meaning.
If one speaks of the wondrous Dharma, it is the learning of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that is superior, not that of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
If one speaks of the excellence of persons, the person beyond training (aśaikṣa) is superior, not the person in training (śaikṣa).
Or it is said:
this refers to the pleasant feeling of pliancy and bliss.
That learner’s mind is tormented by the fetters; therefore, the pleasure of tranquility is not experienced with satisfaction.
In this one beyond training, the heat of the mental fetters has ceased; therefore, the pleasure of tranquility is experienced with satisfaction.
Some say: This refers to the feeling of extreme vastness associated with that pliancy and bliss.
Whether those practitioners exhaust their enmities or do not exhaust them, for this reason, the feeling of pliancy and bliss is not one of extreme vastness.
Just as a king may have either subdued his enemies or not yet subdued them, and therefore does not experience the full extent of a king’s vast dominion;
so too, that practitioner may have either exhausted all fetters of enmity or not yet exhausted them, and therefore does not experience the full extent of the bliss of tranquility.
This one who is beyond training has exhausted all fetters and enemies; he experiences an exceedingly vast and sublime bliss.
Just as when a king has subdued all his enemies, he experiences an exceedingly vast and sublime sovereignty over his realm.
Thus, for this one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all fetters and enmities are exhausted; therefore, he experiences an exceedingly vast and sublime bliss of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).
Some say: "This refers to happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha*), not happiness in future lives."

That learner experiences happiness in the present life and will also experience happiness in the future; this one beyond training (aśaikṣa) experiences happiness in the present life but not in the future.
For this reason, it is said that the one beyond training experiences happiness in the present life, whereas the learner is not so described.

Question: Regarding this teaching that those with the liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) and those with the twofold liberation (*ubhaya-to-bhāga-vimukti*) both contemplate the truths and experience happiness in the present life—
do these three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) exist in such Arhats, or not?
If it exists, why is it not mentioned here?
If it does not exist, how is that sutra to be reconciled?
That sutra states:
The Venerable Śāriputra approached the World-Honored One and asked:
"World-Honored One,
among these five hundred bhikṣus, how many possess the three types of clear knowledge?"
"How many bhikṣus are liberated both ways?
How many bhikṣus are liberated by wisdom?
The World-Honored One replied:

Śāriputra! Of these five hundred bhikṣus, ninety bhikṣus possess the three types of higher knowledge (traividya), ninety bhikṣus are liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), and the remaining bhikṣus are liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta).
"Śāriputra! This assembly is without branches or leaves, and is also without knots; it is pure and firmly established. He asked:
Does the Venerable Śāriputra know or not? If he knows, why does he ask?
If he does not know, how can he be called a śrāvaka who has attained the pāramitās?
Having composed this treatise, he said:
"It is known.
He was asked:
If one already knows, for what reason does one ask?
The answer is:
there are cases where one asks despite already knowing.
As it is said:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, asks knowing [the answer].
Or it is said:
He asks for the sake of others;
although the Venerable Śāriputra knows [the answer], there are those among that assembly who do not know.
Those who do not know have not attained the quality of fearlessness, and thus they are unable to question the World-Honored One.
The Venerable Śāriputra knew that he too had accomplished the dharma of fearlessness, yet he questioned the World-Honored One for the sake of others.
Alternatively, it is said that he questioned because, although they have entered into the state of equality, there appear to be differences in their progress.
The Buddha taught the Dharma for those five hundred bhikṣus, and they all attained the fruit of arhatship, no longer subject to future existence.
Because the World-Honored One’s mind was filled with joy, he spoke these identical words.
"Who is able to [attain] the ultimate truth?
The World-Honored One’s heart was filled with joy, for he had severed future existence.
The Venerable Śāriputra then thought to himself:

Although all have attained the fruit of arhatship and severed future existence, and the World-Honored One’s mind rejoices in the ultimate sense, he does not yet know who is diligent in effort and who is not.
For this reason, he asks because although they enter into the same nature, differences in their levels manifest.
Alternatively, it is said:
the Buddha spoke of them as equal based on the fruit of that path; the Venerable Śāriputra asks because there are differences in their paths.

Some say: Because the Buddha’s liberation through the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is identical [to others], the Venerable Śāriputra asked because there are distinctions and gradations within liberation through the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Others say:
This question arises from the donor’s intention and aspiration.

If a donor receives offerings during the four months of the summer retreat, his intention and aspiration are such that he regards [the recipient] as an exceptionally sublime field of merit; let him not think, "I am sowing seeds in a bad field."
Some say: "The storehouse of merit is covered by the ashes of few desires, yet it is displayed for the sake of the world.
It is like a person who covers a treasure with ashes, only to reveal it."
Thus, because he wished to reveal to the world the treasury of merit covered by the ashes of fewness of desires,
he asked. Alternatively,
it is said that he asked in order to manifest the virtues of his disciples.
This should be so, like a disciple questioning and a teacher answering; it is asked in order to manifest the disciple's merit.
Or it is said:
because of unreal arrogance, parched wisdom, and increased intellectual pride, it is asked in order to sever such arrogance and conceit.
This refers to those who have achieved an inflated pride of knowledge (*jñāna-māna*) and take no pleasure in inquiry.
The Blessed One said:
"The wisdom of the bhikṣu Śāriputra cannot match even a sixteenth part of that of [the Buddha], let alone the mere intellectual vision achieved by you ordinary people."
This refers to the arrogance of unreal wisdom, the increase of wisdom through parchedness, and pride; it is asked for the purpose of severing such arrogance and pride.
Alternatively, it is said:
it is asked for the purpose of severing slander.
Regarding the heterodox teachers' slander against the World-Honored One’s teaching:

they claim that the śramaṇa Gautama receives the Dharma from Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and then teaches it; that he receives it at night and teaches it by day, just as when the Venerable Śāriputra joined his palms and questioned [the Buddha], and the World-Honored One answered.
This is called "for the sake of severing slander.
Alternatively, it is said:
he asks for the sake of severing envy regarding the Dharma.
If one is envious, they do not even take pleasure in hearing others speak of their own virtues, let alone when it is spoken of by themselves.
The Venerable Śāriputra was free from this fault; therefore, he asked because he had severed all envy regarding the Dharma.
Some say: He asks because he currently lacks arrogance and seeks the sublime Dharma. Others say:
He asks because he has seen that the World-Honored One has well explained and authorized [this teaching].
It is like the king’s sealed decree on a legal edict: if it lacks the king’s seal of authorization, all gatekeepers will create obstacles to its passage.
In this way, if a well-spoken teaching were not authenticated by the seal of the Tathāgata, the fourfold assembly would encounter obstacles regarding the Buddha-dharma of the past.
It is like the royal decree inscribed on a scroll: if the king authenticates it with his seal, none of the gatekeepers may create obstacles.
Thus, if what has been well-spoken is confirmed by the Tathāgata, there shall be no obstacles for the fourfold assembly within the Buddha-dharma of the past.
This is called "the present World-Honored One’s confirmation of what is well-spoken," as asked by the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having composed this treatise, he said:
"There are Arhats who possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā).
He was then asked:
If that is so, it is consistent with that sūtra;
why then is it not stated in this sūtra?
The answer is:
It should be stated.
If it were not stated, the Blessed One’s words would be incomplete.
Or, it is said:
This has already been explained herein.

If there is such an Arhat possessing these three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā), they are either one liberated by wisdom by nature (prajñāvimukta) or one liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).

Since the one liberated by wisdom has already been explained, it should be understood that the Arhat liberated by wisdom by nature who possesses the three supernormal knowledges has also been explained.
Having already explained the one liberated both ways, it should be understood that this also explains the Arhat of natural liberation and the Arhat possessing the three knowledges (*traividya*).
Regarding those who explain this, there are two other masters: the Venerable Visākha and the Venerable Ghoṣaka.
The Venerable Revata spoke in praise of the excellence of wisdom.
The Venerable Kuṣṭhila spoke in praise of the excellence of the attainment of cessation.
The Venerable Revata said:
Wisdom is superior, not the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Wisdom has equal objects of focus (*samālambana*), whereas the attainment of cessation lacks equal objects of focus.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is superior, not wisdom (prajñā).
For while ordinary persons may possess wisdom, they do not possess the attainment of cessation.
If one speaks of wisdom but not of the attainment of cessation, that refers to those who possess the three knowledges (trividyā) but lack the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa).

This refers to the Arhat of the Threefold Knowledge (tevijja), meaning that one who possesses the three knowledges and the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) is also said to possess the threefold knowledge.
Why is this? Because their excellence lies in wisdom rather than the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); those who possess one or two knowledges are liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta).

If one claims that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is not wisdom (*prajñā*), they say that if there are the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) but no three knowledges (*trividyā*), this is called "liberation through both" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
If there are both the eight liberations and the three knowledges, this is also called "liberation through both."

Why is this? It is because that attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is superior to wisdom (*prajñā*), whereas the "one who possesses clear knowledge" (*ekavidya*) and the "one who possesses twofold clear knowledge" (*dvividya*) are those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*).
Those who say this are merely engaging in empty debate; it neither benefits the sūtras nor benefits the meaning.
It is so, as previously stated. Among these Arhats of the Threefold Knowledge (*traividyā*), some have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and some have not.
Those who have attained the absorption of cessation are said to be "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*); those who have not are said to be "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*).

Furthermore, regarding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya), there is another distinct explanation of their activities.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
The answer is:

That which is not yet known shall be known, that which is not yet contemplated shall be contemplated, and that which is not yet abandoned shall be abandoned; for this reason, it is called the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya). Question:

If the faculty of "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" refers to that which is not yet known being made known, that which is not yet contemplated being contemplated, and that which is not yet abandoned being abandoned, then once the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) has arisen and one contemplates the five aggregates of the desire realm, and subsequently the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) arises regarding the higher realms, the five aggregates of the desire realm have already been contemplated and are now being contemplated again. How can this be?

Having thus already observed what is to be observed, why is it said that there is the faculty of "I-have-not-yet-known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and not the faculty of "having known" (ājñendriya)? Answer:

When the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) arises, one first observes the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) of the desire realm; this is "not yet having observed. Subsequently, when the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) arises in the higher realms, one has already observed the five aggregates of the desire realm.

Some say: Although the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* arises with respect to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the desire realm and contemplates these five aggregates of the desire realm, it has not yet known the subsequent *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*.
Because it knows the cause of the five aggregates of the desire realm through wisdom, it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) rather than "patience" (*kṣānti*).

Some say: When one is about to give rise to the Path in the higher realms, the mental aggregate (manaskāya) that has never before been observed may fall back into the lower realms; for this reason, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), and not the faculty of "one who already knows" (ājñendriya).
Question: What is the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*)? Answer:

That which has already been known should be known, that which has already been observed should be observed, and that which has not yet been abandoned should be abandoned; for this reason, it is called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*). Question:

If the faculty of "having known" refers to what has already been known and should be known, what has already been observed and should be observed, and what has not yet been abandoned and should be abandoned, then when the patience regarding the knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) arises—excluding its co-existent and associated factors—all other dharmas, as well as the wisdom and observation therein; and when the subsequent path-knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) arises along with its co-existent and associated factors of wisdom and observation—in these cases, there is still "the unknown to be known" (*ajñātamājñāsyamāna*) and "the unobserved to be observed" (*adṛṣṭamadraṣṭavya*). How can these be included?
Why is the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) mentioned, but not the faculty of "not yet known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)?
The answer is:
the latter pertains to the sixteen moments of mind during the path of vision (darśanamārga).

When that initial path of the knowledge of the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-jñāna*) arises, within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there is the wisdom and contemplation associated with its concomitants; therefore, one knows what has already been known and does not know what is unknown, and contemplates what has already been contemplated and does not contemplate what is un-contemplated.
Question: In this context, we do not inquire about nor answer regarding the external [factors].
If it is said that the path of insight (darśanamārga) consists of fifteen moments of thought, how is this to be explained?
The Venerable Saṅghasavhaya said:
"When the present momentary acceptance of the unknown regarding the Path (mārga-anājñāta-akṣānti) manifests, one cultivates the future immeasurable acceptance of the unknown regarding the Path.
If that future immeasurable acceptance of the unknown regarding the Path is cultivated, it is the associated dharma co-arising with that contemplation."
The [author] says:
This is not discussed.
[The opponent] asks:
Why is this not discussed here?
The answer is:
it is not the future path that is capable of observation.
Question: If it is not so, then how is this? Answer:

Because it is much. That which has been largely observed and that which remains to be largely observed should be observed; that which has been little observed and that which remains to be little observed should be observed.
Just as the earth is immeasurable and boundless, one knows what has been observed and what remains to be observed.
As a single clod of earth [compared to the whole earth], so should one contemplate what has not yet been contemplated.
As space is immeasurable and boundless, so should one contemplate what has already been contemplated.
As space occupied by a single mosquito or gadfly, so should one contemplate what has not yet been contemplated.
As the ocean is immeasurable and boundless, so should one contemplate that which has already been contemplated;
as a single drop from the ocean, so should one contemplate that which has not yet been contemplated.
As Sumeru, the king of mountains, is immeasurable and boundless, so should one contemplate that which has already been contemplated.
"As numerous as the mustard seeds on Mount Sumeru—these are yet to be observed and should be observed.
This is called 'because they are many. Or it is said:"

Regarding that which has already been contemplated as the path to be produced in the higher [realms], the aggregate of mind (manaskāya) that was previously contemplated falls back into the lower [realms]; for this reason, it is called the faculty of "having known" (ājñātendriya) and not the faculty of "not yet known" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Question: What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"? Answer:

That which has already been known is to be known; that which has already been observed is to be observed; there is nothing remaining to be abandoned that could be abandoned—this is called the faculty of one who has completed their knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Question:

If that which has already been known is to be known, that which has already been observed is to be observed, and there is nothing remaining to be abandoned that could be abandoned, then the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas have likewise already known what was to be known, already observed what was to be observed, and have no further abandonment to be made. How then do they differ?
Why is it that the Buddha alone is spoken of as the "Threefold Equality" and not others?
The answer is:
it refers to initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*), which awakens to all phenomena without destroying right wisdom.

Some say: It refers to the initial attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), which eliminates two kinds of hindrances: the hindrance of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the hindrance to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*). Others say:
This refers to removing from the mind two kinds of ignorance—the darkness and delusion of both defiled and non-defiled attachment—as well as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Alternatively, it is said:
it refers to removing from the mind two kinds of doubt—hesitation regarding various points and hesitation regarding the points of bondage (*saṃyojana*).
Some say: it means being insatiable in hearing the Dharma. Others say:
This means that one has reached the very bottom of the profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), unlike all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
To provide an analogy:
three animals cross a river—a rabbit, a horse, and a fragrant elephant.
The hare crosses the river by floating; the horse crosses by touching the sand slightly; the fragrant elephant crosses by treading upon the very bottom of the sand.
In this way, those of the three vehicles—Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—cross the river of dependent origination.
Just as a rabbit crosses a river by floating on the surface, so should one contemplate the wisdom of dependent origination of the śrāvaka;
just as a horse crosses by touching the sand with its hooves only slightly, so should one contemplate the wisdom of dependent origination of the pratyekabuddha;
just as a fragrant elephant crosses by treading upon the sand all the way to the bottom, so should one contemplate the wisdom of dependent origination of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Therefore, it is said that he has reached the very bottom of profound dependent origination, unlike all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Or it is said:
his arrow of wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths has penetrated to the utmost depth, unlike that of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
To provide an analogy:
it is like three men shooting together—one being Mahānagna, the second Bṛhatkṣatra, and the third Nārāyaṇa.
As for Mahānagna, although he can pierce through armor, he cannot enter it; how much less can he pass through it?
As for Patañjali, although he can pierce through armor, he can enter it but cannot cause himself to pass through it;
as for Nārāyaṇa, he shoots and pierces the target, passing right through until he enters the earth.
The target itself does not manifest as hard or soft; rather, according to whether one’s strength is weak, middling, or superior, the piercing of the target is likewise weak, middling, or superior.
In this way, the three vehicles—Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—shoot at the target of the Four Noble Truths.
Just as a mahānagna, though he may pierce a target, cannot pass through it, so should one contemplate the wisdom of the four noble truths of the śrāvaka;
just as a pattrin, though he can pierce a target, cannot cause it to pass through, so should one contemplate the wisdom of the four noble truths of the pratyekabuddha;
and just as Nārāyaṇa shoots an arrow that pierces the target, passes through it, and enters the earth, so should one contemplate the wisdom of the four noble truths of the Buddha.

These Four Noble Truths likewise do not manifest as soft or hard; rather, according to whether one's faculty of wisdom is weak, middling, or superior, the Four Noble Truths appear as weak, middling, or superior.
Therefore, it is said that the arrow of wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths penetrates extremely deeply, such that it is not shared by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Alternatively, it is said:
"It is known through self-awakening, exhaustion, and possession."
As for the Pratyekabuddha, although he has awakened by himself and possesses [realization], it is not yet exhaustive;
as for the Śrāvaka, he cannot awaken by himself, let alone possess or exhaust it.
This is what is meant by knowing self-awakening, possession, and exhaustion.
Some say: It refers to self-awakening and the exhaustion of all practices.
Although a pratyekabuddha possesses self-awakening, they are unable to exhaustively practice [all paths].
The śrāvakas are unable to awaken by themselves, let alone practice it exhaustively.
Someone may say:
"It is said that there are two kinds of eloquence; if one does not exhaust what is to be spoken, there is no difference [between them]."
Some say: "The perfection of the body and the perfection of the knowledge and conduct that support the body constitute [the path].
Although a Wheel-Turning Sage King possesses the perfection of the body, he lacks the perfection of the knowledge and conduct that support the body."
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas achieve a body, that which serves as its basis is not the body;
the Buddha likewise achieves both the body and the basis of the body, perfected through knowledge and conduct (vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna). Some say:
This refers to the three accomplishments of form, touch, and sublime speech, as well as the three accomplishments of vows, fruits, and instructions.
Alternatively, it is said to be the three types of non-protection and the three unique applications of mindfulness (*manasikāra*).
Some say: it refers to the four kinds of non-protection and the four kinds of non-admonition. Others say:
That is to say, one accomplishes four knowledges: knowledge of causes, knowledge of time, knowledge of perceptions, and knowledge of what others have said.
Furthermore, there are four other knowledges:
unimpeded knowledge, non-abiding knowledge, non-erroneous knowledge, and unhindered knowledge.
Some say: it refers to awakening to various causes, awakening to various effects, awakening to various remedies, and awakening to various intentions.
Others say:
There is no one else; he alone, through the power of his merit, subdues Māra, unlike all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The commentator says:
This refers to when the Bodhisattva, having eaten the milk-rice offered by Nanda and Nandabalā, formed this thought:
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, he took a firm vow not to break his cross-legged posture until all outflows were exhausted.
At that time, the palace of Māra Pāpīyān shook six times; he thought to himself:
"I do not know whose power this is?"
Seeing the Bodhisattva seated beneath the tree of enlightenment, he formed this thought:
"I shall not break my cross-legged posture until all outflows are exhausted.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas rained down flowers and approached the place where the Bodhisattva was; having arrived, he addressed the Bodhisattva with pleasant words:
"Siddhārtha! In this age of turbidity, the minds of sentient beings are stubborn and fierce; in such times as these, it is difficult to attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
Arise now! I shall provide you with the seven treasures and a thousand sons, and you shall rule over the four continents as a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
The Bodhisattva said:
"Pāpīyān! Your exhaustion is in vain."

"Quickly cause this land, its springs, ponds, and waters, as well as the villages, cities, houses, and their inhabitants, to fly into the air; and quickly cause the sky, the sun, the moon, and the stars to fall to the ground! We shall not rise for you until all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted."
Māra Pāpīyān said: "I have spoken these words of loving-kindness to you; if you do not arise, you shall witness the ultimate evil.
Having spoken these words, he returned to the heavens and addressed the gods of the six desire realms:
"Virtuous ones!
You must take up spears, halberds, swords, hooks, golden mallets, battle-axes, nooses, and long pikes.
I have an enemy who is now sitting beneath the Tree of Enlightenment."
At that time, not long after Māra Pāpīyān had departed, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"Ordinary people constantly engage in disputes; they must maintain their defenses and should not remain silent. How much more so, then, for one who is noble and powerful within the realm of desire?"

The Bodhisattva has already fully practiced the traces of departing from the fetters of desire; having swiftly eliminated desire, he manifests various transformations through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
