That is to say: when taking the form of a rat, he transforms into a cat; when taking the form of a cat, he transforms into a dog; when taking the form of a dog, he transforms into a leopard; when taking the form of a leopard, he transforms into a tiger; when taking the form of a tiger, he transforms into a lion; when manifesting as wearing fire, he transforms it into rain; and when manifesting as rain, he transforms it into a parasol.
The Bodhisattva himself manifested a lapis lazuli pedestal and sat upon it in the full lotus posture—this being a transformation that obscures the physical form but does not obstruct the eyes.
Having completed this manifestation, the Bodhisattva thought:
"If my various transformations were to be disturbed when I practice the Dharma for the sake of others, then Māra Pāpīyān would surely be able to disturb me."
If I do not cause disturbance when others practice the Dharma, then Māra Pāpīyān will ultimately be unable to disturb me.

Having thus brought to witness the supernormal power of recollecting past lives through this matter, the Bodhisattva, having resolved it, observes hundreds and thousands of sentient beings practicing the Dharma and provides them with whatever is required to the utmost degree.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

"Just as my various transformations are based on the causes of wholesome deeds performed in previous lives, so that even hundreds of thousands of billions of Māras like these who have come here could never disturb me, how much less could a single Māra?"
The Bodhisattva established himself in this mental abiding.

Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyān and eighteen billion Māras assumed hideous faces and teeth, produced terrifying sounds and most foul voices, and brandishing various spears and halberds, they proceeded to the site of the Bodhi tree, filling an area of thirty-six yojanas.
Having arrived, he said to the Bodhisattva:
"Siddhārtha Ānanda!
Do you see this wicked assembly?"
"Arise quickly; do not undergo immeasurable suffering within this place.
The Bodhisattva said: "Pāpīyān!"
"Your words are like those of a child.
It was due to the power of cause and effect from a single offering of a meal you made in the past that you have now attained such sovereignty. Māra said:
"I have given one offering of a meal; how many meals have you given?
The Bodhisattva replied, "I have given immeasurable hundreds of thousands of meals."
Māra said: "My offering of almsgiving has you as its witness;
who, then, is your witness?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva, adorned with a hundred thousand marks and signs of merit and possessing the color of purple-polished gold, pressed his joined palms against the earth; the earth immediately shook violently, serving as a witness to this.
At that time, this earth produced a sound like that of a vessel made of the seven treasures.
Having heard it, the hosts of Māra were struck with terror; they scattered and fled, looking back over their shoulders, emitting evil cries as they returned by the way they had come.
The eye born of the Bodhisattva’s birth does not see the hosts of Māra beyond one yojana.
Having realized and manifested this supernormal power of the divine eye, the Bodhisattva sees them but does not hear them.
Once the Bodhisattva has realized and manifested this supernormal power of the divine ear, he is able to hear [them], yet he does not know with what intention they have come.

Once the Bodhisattva has realized and manifested this supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, he observes that the assembly of Śakras has come with sublime intentions, while the assembly of Māras has come with evil intentions.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"For what reason has Māra Pāpīyān come here?
He has come because he observes and guards his own domain."
For what reason does one guard the boundaries?
One then reflects: "It is because of the fetters."

Thereupon, having severed all fetters, the Bodhisattva attains the path of unsurpassed, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment within thirty-four moments of mind. Regarding these thirty-four moments of mind:

there are fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the sixteenth is the knowledge of the path’s unknown (*mārgānvayajñāna*), which is termed the knowledge of the path already known (*mārgajñāna*).

When this bodhisattva eliminates desire from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this constitutes the path of means (*upāyamārga*). The severing of the nine grades of fetters within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consists of nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*); this is what is meant by "within the duration of thirty-four moments of mind."

This means that all Samyaksaṃbuddhas rely upon this to subdue Māra and his retinue and to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment; it is said to be one and not two. Having alone, by the power of merit, subdued Māra and his retinue and achieved the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, they are unlike any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Some say: it refers to the fulfillment of the knowledge of what is already known, the practice of the path of awakening, the conditions for practice, the roots of those conditions, and the meaning of those roots. Others say:
This refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*).
Alternatively, it is said:
it refers to being free from the eight worldly dharmas, possessing the boundless merit that cannot be grasped, and acting as a refuge for those in peril and distress.
Some say: It is said that Great Compassion has long since come forth, subtly entering and universally pervading all sentient beings, evolving and proceeding in such a manner.
"Having come from afar" means it has traveled a great distance through the complete cultivation of practices over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
"Subtle entry" refers to the subtle entry into the three types of suffering: first, the suffering of suffering; second, the suffering of conditioned existence; and third, the suffering of change.
"Universal arrival" refers to the universal entry into the conditions of the three realms.

Regarding the "equal turning of practice toward all sentient beings": because one maintains an impartial mind toward enemies, kin, and those who stand between them, one practices the equal turning toward all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is said that great compassion has long since subtly entered and universally pervaded this equal turning of practice toward all sentient beings.
For this reason, the three [teachings] equally speak of one Buddha, not of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Question:

For what reason are the eye faculty, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties established as "faculties" (indriya) within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), while visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects are not so established?
The answer is:
It is said that those established as faculties (*indriya*) are internal, while external things are not established as faculties.
Furthermore, it is said that those belonging to the category of sentient beings at the present time are established as faculties, whereas indeterminate things are not established as faculties.
That is to say, those who accept [the classification] are established as faculties (*indriya*), while those who do not accept it are not so established.

That is to say, at the time of abandonment, those for whom painful sensations (*vedanā*) constitute a heavy burden are established as faculties, while those who are indeterminate are not so established.
That is to say, a faculty is established as a faculty because it possesses the meaning of a faculty; that which does not possess the meaning of a faculty is not established as a faculty.
For this reason. Question:
Why is this? Within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), pleasant sensations establish two faculties: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*);
likewise, painful sensations establish two faculties: the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Why is it that neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is established as a single faculty, the faculty of equanimity?
The answer is: It should be explained.

If it were not explained, one should know that the Blessed One’s words would be incomplete; they would merely manifest the meaning, manifest the gateway to the meaning, manifest the summary of the meaning, and manifest the transition to the meaning.
Some say: Two gates, two summaries, two crossings, two torches, two illuminations, and two lights are manifested; two locations are manifested.

Just as pleasure and pain are established as two faculties (*indriya*), so too should neither-pain-nor-pleasure be established as two faculties. There is a distinction here, namely that in that case, two faculties can arise.

Just as neither-pain-nor-pleasure is established as a single faculty (*indriya*), so too should pleasure and pain each be established as a single faculty; since such modes of activity exist, one faculty arises for each.
This explains the manifestation of two gates, two summaries, two measures, two torches, two clarities, and two lights, manifesting the number two.
Alternatively, it is said:
because they are free from contradiction.
Pleasurable feeling is contrary to painful feeling, and painful feeling is also contrary to pleasurable feeling.
That neither-painful-nor-pleasurable feeling has no other feeling as its contrary; this is because it is free from contrariety, and for that reason it is so.
Some say: Because it functions as something else.
This pleasant sensation differs from the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and its functioning differs from the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
Painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*) is distinct from the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), and the transformation of activity (*pariṇati*) is distinct from the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
All other transformations of that neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*) are likewise so; for this reason it is thus.
Or, as some say:
Pleasurable sensation may be beneficial or non-beneficial, deranged or undeluded, stable or unstable, and concentrated or unconcentrated.
That which is non-beneficial, deluded, unstable, and unconcentrated is established as a single faculty.
This faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is sharp, causing madness, and being unstable and unfixed, they establish it as the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
The same applies to painful sensation.

That sensation which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant is entirely dull, does not cause madness, and is fixed; for this reason, two faculties are established for pleasant sensation: the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
Painful sensation is also established as two faculties: the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation is established as one faculty: the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). Question:
Question: For what reason is perception (*saṃjñā*) not established as a faculty (*indriya*)? Answer:
There are many factors that are not established among the faculties; why then do you ask specifically about perception?

Question: The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is sometimes established as a faculty (indriya) and sometimes not; likewise, the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is sometimes established as a faculty and sometimes not.

The aggregates of feeling (vedanāskandha) and consciousness (vijñānaskandha) are entirely established as faculties. For what reason is this aggregate of perception (saṃjñāskandha) not entirely established as a faculty?
Answer: It refers to the characteristic of being without faculties; because it lacks the characteristic of faculties, it is not established as a faculty.
Alternatively, it is said:
The faculties function through their own power, whereas this perception functions through the power of another.
It is like a disciple or a laborer who follows instructions: when told to take something, they take it; when told to discard it, they discard it.
Such is perception: whatever is felt as sensation, that is perception; whatever is thought as volition, that is perception; whatever is cognized as consciousness, that is perception.
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
For what reason is perception (*saṃjñā*) not established as a faculty (*indriya*)? The meaning of "faculty" is the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*), and perception is not predominant. He asked:
Just as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) mutually increase one another, so too do unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) increase conditioned phenomena.
Why is it that perception (*saṃjñā*) is not predominant?
The answer is:
This means that those dharmas which can increase the fetters (saṃyojana) are established as faculties (indriya), whereas perception (saṃjñā) can destroy the fetters. Question:
Perception can also destroy the fetters.
The Blessed One has said:

"By cultivating and repeatedly practicing the perception of impermanence, one destroys all craving for sense-desires, craving for form, and craving for the formless; one destroys all ignorance and conceit."
For what reason is it said that perception cannot destroy the fetters?
The Venerable Dharmatrāta replied:
"O Venerable Ones!"

Perception arises dependent on another's feeling and perception; it originates from that other [mind] as the basis for feeling, just as other mental factors act as conditions before feeling and perception arise.
Therefore it is said: "O Venerable Ones!
Perception arises dependent on another's perception; it originates from that other and relies upon what is perceived. For this reason, perception is not established as a faculty."
Question: For what reason are the fetters (*saṃyojana*) not established as faculties (*indriya*)? Answer:

The meaning of "predominance" (*adhipati*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*). The fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not predominant, because feeling (*vedanā*) is predominant over the fetters. Question:

Since the fetters are predominant in causing one to fall back from liberation and to remain far removed from the wholesome within saṃsāra, for what reason is it said that the fetters are not predominant?
The answer is:
It is not superior in this way.
For instance, to fall back from liberation and to remain within saṃsāra, far removed from the wholesome—this is described as base, inferior, and evil; it is not superior.
Question: Since this suffering arises with the fetters as its predominant condition, why is suffering established as a faculty (*indriya*) while the fetters are not? Answer:
Although suffering arises because of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and increases by means of the fetters, the fetters themselves are base.

It is like a wealthy and noble lord in a city who appoints a gatekeeper; although that gatekeeper may be extremely wicked, he is not the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the lord’s status.
In this way, although such pain arises because of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and gains its predominance (*adhipati*) through them, the fetters are inferior;
for this reason, pain is established as a faculty (*indriya*), whereas the fetters are not.
Question: For what reason are all feelings— whether wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral— established as faculties (*indriya*),
while wisdom (*prajñā*) is established as a faculty only when it is wholesome, but not when it is defiled or non-obscured neutral?

Answer: Feeling (*vedanā*) is the primary basis for the fetters (*saṃyojana*); therefore, it is established as a faculty (*indriya*) in its entirety—whether wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral.
Wisdom (*prajñā*), on the other hand, is the primary basis for wholesome phenomena; that is to say, it is wholesome, and thus it belongs to wholesome phenomena.
That which is defiled (kliṣṭa) severs the wholesome dharmas;
that which is non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) cannot be employed for such purposes.

For this reason, among sensations (vedanā), only those that are wholesome, defiled, or obscured-neutral are established as faculties (indriya). The wise maintain that only the wholesome among them are established as faculties, while the defiled and the non-obscured neutral are not.
Question: If "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*), then since *nirvāṇa* is the most subtle among all phenomena, why is it not established as a faculty? Answer:
That nirvāṇa destroys the faculties and the non-faculties.

As for the non-faculties, it is like a chariot that, when destroyed, is no longer a chariot; a jar that, when destroyed, is no longer a jar; or wealth and goods that, when destroyed, are no longer wealth and goods. In this same way, in nirvāṇa, the faculties are destroyed and thus become non-faculties.
Some say: "The faculties fall into birth, old age, and impermanence; nirvāṇa does not fall into birth, old age, and impermanence.
Others say:

The faculties (indriya) are attained through causes and possess the characteristics of the conditioned (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa); nirvāṇa is attained without cause and possesses the characteristics of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa). Some say:

the faculties involve transmigrating through worlds, performing formations (saṃskāra), receiving fruits, and being able to know conditions; nirvāṇa does not involve transmigrating through worlds, does not perform formations, does not receive fruits, and does not know conditions.
Some say: "The faculties (indriya) can be perceived as having a sequence of before and after, whereas nirvana has no such sequence. Others say:
The faculties (indriya) are obtainable as weak, middling, or superior; nirvāṇa is free from being weak, middling, or superior. Some say:
the faculties fall within the world, while nirvāṇa is beyond the world.
Some say: "The faculties (indriya) are the aggregates (skandha), while nirvana is the departure from the aggregates. Others say:
The "roots" (*mūla*) bind one to suffering, while *nirvāṇa* is the departure from suffering.

Some say: because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise through causal activity, they are described by the meanings of "wonderful" (*praṇīta*) and "root" (*mūla*); however, among all conditioned phenomena, *nirvāṇa* alone is the most wonderful.
The detailed exposition concludes in the section on the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśatīndriya*).
*Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll Four; *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll Five.

Compiled by the Arhat Śītabhāṇi; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty. 17. The Seventeenth [Chapter]: The Eighteen Bases and Elements (*Aṣṭādaśadhātusthāna*).

Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*): the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tactile element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
It is said:
This realm is both a brief exposition and a detailed exposition.
The brief exposition is based on extensive scriptures, such as the *Mahāvadāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The "extensive explanation" is so called because it enters [into the details].
This "entry" is both a brief explanation and an extensive explanation.
It is a brief explanation by way of the *dhātus* (elements), and an extensive explanation by way of the *skandhas* (aggregates).
The "aggregates" (skandhas) are both a brief exposition and a detailed exposition.
They are a brief exposition because they are [the objects of] entry; they are a detailed exposition as it has been said:
"All conditioned things are the cause of suffering, because they are such."
Furthermore, there are those who say that the "elements" (*dhātu*) constitute both a brief exposition and an extensive exposition, because they are precisely these elements.
Within this exposition of the elements, matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are explained extensively, while mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are explained briefly.

The "entrances" (*āyatana*) are both a brief exposition and an extensive exposition; because they are these very entrances, within them form (*rūpa*) is explained extensively while the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) are explained briefly.

The "aggregates" (*skandha*) are also both a brief exposition and an extensive exposition; because they are these very aggregates, within them mental factors are explained extensively while form and mind are explained briefly.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "dhātu" (element) invariably signifies "extensiveness. Question:
For what reason does "dhātu" invariably signify extensiveness?
Answer: Because it encompasses all dharmas.
Although the *Mahāvadāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* speak extensively, they do not encompass all dharmas.
Although the *Madhyamaka-avatāra* includes all phenomena, it does not explain them extensively;

the *skandhas* do not include all phenomena, for while the *skandhas* include conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they do not include unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), nor are they explained extensively;
this *dhātu*, however, exclusively explains them extensively and includes all phenomena.

This is the brief and detailed exposition of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; it is not the extensive exposition as you have provided, such as the *Mahāvadāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, nor is it the concise exposition as you have provided, such as the two kinds of giving:
the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth.
Question: If it is not so, then how is it? Answer:
If a phenomenon was explained extensively previously and concisely later— namely, the eighteen *dhātus* being subsumed therein—
or was established among the twelve *āyatanas*, namely, the twelve *āyatanas* being subsumed therein.
Established within the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), excluding unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), these five aggregate dharmas are what is grasped.
It is said:
"All conditioned things (saṃskṛta) sought after are suffering."
"Those who seek among all conditioned phenomena"—this is what the Blessed One has briefly stated in a single direction.
This is the Buddha’s brief exposition and detailed exposition.
On this account, the Blessed One addressed Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra! I am able to provide both brief and detailed explanations of the Dharma for my disciples, yet it is difficult for them to understand.
Because of these brief and detailed explanations, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:"
"O World-Honored One!
Please provide both a brief and an extensive explanation of the Dharma, so that there may be those capable of understanding it.
For the sake of this brief and extensive explanation, I shall employ a simile."

It is like a great dragon in the ocean; having fully nourished its body within the sea, it ascends into the void, covers the sky with clouds, emits flashes of lightning, and thunders with a great sound, saying:
"I shall let fall the rain."
At that time, the tree spirits of the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and trees were terrified and thought:
"The sea dragon has a massive body; if it rains, there will surely be destruction.
At that time, this earth was not afraid, being able to endure the dragon's rain for a hundred years or a thousand years, as I am capable of receiving the great sea dragon in its entirety.

In this way, World-Honored One, following the Tathāgatas Dhvajāgra, Dīpaṃkara, Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa, you have nurtured the Dharma-body; by means of the vehicle of great compassion, you traverse the void, and with the cloud of great kindness, you cover and shelter the world, emitting the lightning-flash of wisdom and thundering the sound of the Great Dharma:
"Śāriputra!..."
I am able to provide both brief and detailed explanations of the Dharma for my disciples, yet those who can truly understand it are rare.
Just as the spirits of the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, trees, and forests are terrified, so too are all these śrāvakas struck with fear and think to themselves:

"The World-Honored One is able to express the Dharma through different names, different phrases, different flavors, different teachings, and different meanings; if he were to preach the Dharma [in such a manner], we fear we would not be able to comprehend it."

Just as the earth is fearless and capable of receiving the rain from the dragon, so too has the Venerable Śāriputra cultivated wisdom and vision for sixty eons, such that he is capable of receiving the Blessed One’s brief and detailed teachings;
he is one who can truly know the Dharma.
Therefore, this is a brief explanation of what was extensively taught. Question:
Suppose there is a phenomenon such that even for Śāriputra, with his hundreds of thousands of koṭis of calculations, it would not fall within the range of his knowledge.
For what reason? Śāriputra is capable of receiving [the teaching] within the domain of a śrāvaka, not the domain of a Buddha;
he is capable of receiving the wisdom of a śrāvaka, not the wisdom of a Buddha; he is capable of receiving the practice of a śrāvaka, not the practice of a Buddha.
Someone said:
"He is capable of relying upon the Buddha.
The Venerable Śāriputra then had this thought:
The Blessed One and others speak for the benefit of beings; they do not preach the Dharma in vain, but always teach the Dharma in its full perfection according to the capacity of the vessel.
For this reason, the Venerable Śāriputra is worthy to receive the teaching from the Blessed One.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), they are the eye element up to and including the mind element. Question:
What are the categories of these eighteen elements?
Answer: They are called the eighteen *dhātus* by name, but as for their actual types (*jāti*), there are either seventeen or twelve.
If one includes the six consciousnesses while excluding the mind-element (*manodhātu*), then they are called eighteen by name, but there are seventeen types.
If one takes the mind-element (manodhātu) as the basis, the six consciousnesses are subsumed within it; thus, these eighteen types are [reduced to] twelve.
These are called the eighteen elements (dhātus); alternatively, they may be categorized as seventeen or twelve types.

Just as it is with names and seeds, so too should one fully understand name-sets and seed-sets, name-characteristics and seed-characteristics, name-differences and seed-differences, name-distinctions and seed-distinctions, and name-awakenings and seed-awakenings.
Question: If the seeds of the eighteen elements are sometimes seventeen or sometimes twelve, why are they established as eighteen elements? Answer:
By way of three factors—body, basis, and object—the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) consist of six bodies, six bases, and six objects.
As for the six bodies, they are the six internal elements: the eye element, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind elements.
The six bases (*āśraya*) are the six consciousness elements: the eye-consciousness element, the ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness elements.
The six objects (*ālambana*) are the six external elements: the form, sound, odor, taste, tangible, and mental-object elements.
It is said that for three reasons—body (*āśraya*), basis (*āśraya*), and object (*ālambana*)—the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are established.
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:
"The sixty-two elements are all included therein" because of these three reasons: body, basis, and object.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One teach the sixty-two elements? Answer:
Because it severs the intentions of those of other teachings,
this view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of the sixty-two views.
Because it severs the view of a self, the Buddha’s sūtras speak of the sixty-two realms (dhātu).
As it is said in that Buddha’s sūtra: "Kauśika!
These various realms and immeasurable realms in this world—this is what is meant by 'knowing the realms'."
Regarding those various realms, it is taught that they are definitively included within [the eighteen] by means of forceful appropriation.
This sūtra of the Buddha designates the realms by way of their "seeing.
All these are included within the eighteen realms due to three factors: the body, the support, and the object-condition.
In the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, a great tree is used as a metaphor to explain:
"O bhikṣus! Just as there are leaves on a great tree, so too is the number of elements."
In this Buddha’s sutra, the elements (dhātu) are explained by way of their names as they are perceived.
These [bases] are also fully included within the eighteen elements (aṣṭādaśadhātu) due to these three factors: the body, the support, and the object-condition.
This is what is called the establishment of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
This is the inherent nature of the body of characteristics already sown within the elements.
Having explained their nature, one should now explain their activity.
For what reason is "element" (dhātu) taught?
What is the meaning of "element"?
The answer is:
The meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*) is the meaning of "element.
It signifies a portion, a division, a subtle particle, a distinct characteristic, a dissimilarity, and a separation.
The various phenomena are the phenomena of the elements.
Śāṭīputra said: "The 'realms' (dhātu) are the various destinies; the realms are that which sustain and nourish.
If the meaning of 'realm' is the meaning of 'nature' (svabhāva), then within a single body and a single mind there are eighteen natures."

It is like a mountain that contains many natures: the nature of iron, the nature of copper, the nature of white tin, the nature of lead and tin, the nature of gold, the nature of silver, the nature of lapis lazuli, and the nature of crystal.
In this way, a single body and a single mind possess eighteen natures; this meaning of "nature" (dhātu) is the meaning of "element" (dhātu).
As for the meaning of "element" being the meaning of "division" (skandha), when the flesh is sequentially laid out, there are then counted males and females.

Just as bamboo strips woven together in succession are designated as a mat or a fan, and as pieces of wood are designated as a chariot, a palace, a hall, or a tower, so too are successive portions of flesh designated as "man" or "woman. This meaning of "portion" (khaṇḍa) is the meaning of "element" (dhātu).
The meaning of "division" (*bhāga*) is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*): there are eighteen divisions for women and eighteen divisions for men;

this meaning of division is the meaning of element. The meaning of "subtle" (*aṇu*) is the meaning of "element": there are eighteen subtle particles for women and eighteen subtle particles for men; this meaning of subtle is the meaning of element.

The meaning of "distinct characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*): from the distinct characteristic of the eye up to the distinct characteristic of the mind, this meaning of distinct characteristics is the meaning of element.

The meaning of "dissimilarity" (*asādharmya*) is the meaning of element: from the dissimilarity of the eye-element up to the dissimilarity of the mind-element, this meaning of dissimilarity is the meaning of element.

Regarding the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) as the meaning of "severance": from the eye-element severing the three realms up to the mind-element severing the three realms—this severance is the meaning of "element.

Regarding the meaning of "element" as the meaning of "diverse entities": this refers to the entity of the eye-element not being the entity of the mind-element, and the entity of the mind-element not being the entity of the eye-element; these diverse entities are the meaning of "element."
Śāntideva said: "The 'going' (gati) is the realm (dhātu); the 'sustaining and nourishing' is the realm.
As for 'the going is the realm,' it means going to various realms, various destinies, and various births; going through the cycle of birth and death."
That which is held is one's own nature (*svabhāva*); that which nurtures is the nature of another (*parabhāva*).

This is called the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*), which is the meaning of "element. Furthermore, the meanings of "portion," "division," "subtlety," "distinct characteristic," "dissimilarity," "severance," and "various phenomena" are the meanings of "element."
Śāṭhā said: "This is the realm of proceeding; this is the realm of maintaining and nourishing.
Having thus explained their common practice, he shall now explain their distinct practices.
What is the eye-element?
The answer is:
that which sees forms by means of the eye—whether it has already seen, will see, or is seeing them now—as well as all other things belonging thereto.
That which has already been seen belongs to the past; that which is yet to be seen belongs to the future; and that which is being seen now belongs to the present.
Furthermore, whatever else exists therein refers to that eye-consciousness as being either empty or non-empty.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "That my eye sees forms is what belongs to me; all other sentient beings have other [eyes] as their own.
That my eye does not see forms is what belongs to others; all other sentient beings likewise have [their eyes] as their own."
Furthermore, there are those who say: "That my eye sees forms is what belongs to me; that all other sentient beings [see forms] is also what belongs to them.
That my eye does not see forms is what belongs to others; that others do not see forms is also what belongs to others."
Question: If this were not the case, then two people would see a form with a single eye, let alone many.
Why, then, do you say that "I see forms with my eyes" and that these are "mine," while they are also possessed by all other sentient beings?
Answer: Is it possible for one to see forms with another's eye?
It is simply that the function of the eye consists in seeing forms; once that seeing has occurred, the function ceases—meaning that as soon as its function has been performed, it ceases.
For this reason it is said: "When I see forms with my eye, they are mine; they are also the property of all other sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "When I see forms with my eye, they are mine; they are neither the property of all other sentient beings, nor the property of anyone else."
That is to say: "My eye does not see forms; this is mine, and belongs to no others. All other sentient beings do not possess them, nor do they belong to others.
This is not to be discussed.
How is it that this eye is neither "belonging to anything" nor "belonging to anything else"?
Question: If it is not discussed [in those terms], how is it so?
The answer is:
It is so, it is good.
As previously stated, one thinks: "I see forms with my eyes; these are mine; all other sentient beings have their own [forms]."
That is to say: "My eye does not see forms; they are mine, yet they belong to others, and all other sentient beings likewise possess them as others. Question:
Just as one eye can see forms, two eyes do not see forms.
What is meant by "seeing as the cause of non-seeing" and "non-seeing as the cause of seeing"?
The answer is:
because seeing arises from non-seeing, and non-seeing arises from seeing; since these arise reciprocally, they are called causes.
Seeing while not seeing is sustained by [the state of] not seeing while seeing; these are mutually sustained, and therefore they are called causes.
Seeing while not seeing is sustained equally by [the state of] not seeing while seeing; these are mutually sustained in equal measure, and therefore they are called causes.
Seeing arises because of not-seeing, and not-seeing arises because of seeing; as they arise in mutual dependence on one another, they are called "causes.
Seeing nourishes not-seeing, and not-seeing nourishes seeing; as they nourish one another in mutual dependence, they are called "causes."
The seeing does not lengthen the non-seeing, and the non-seeing does not lengthen the seeing; because they mutually augment one another, it is called a "cause" (*hetu*). Some say:

regarding both the eye's seeing and its non-seeing, these two are identical in terms of being one element (*dhātu*), one sense-base (*āyatana*), and one faculty (*indriya*), and constitute a single act of seeing.
The one element is the eye-element; the one base is the eye-base; the one faculty is the eye-faculty; the one seeing is the seeing of the eye.
As it is with the eye-element, so it is with the elements of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Question: What is the realm of form (rūpadhātu)? Answer:
This refers to form (*rūpa*): that which has been seen by the eye, that which will be seen, and that which is being seen now, as well as all other such forms.
"That which has been seen" refers to past form; "that which will be seen" refers to future form; and "that which is being seen now" refers to present form.
Regarding "and whatever else exists," the Kaśmīrīs explain that there are four kinds of other matter:
there is past matter, which refers to that which has already ceased and is no longer seen by the eye;
and there is future matter, which refers to that which will cease and is not yet seen by the eye.
There is present form, which means that which ceases without being seen by the eye;
furthermore, there is future form, which refers to those dharmas that are not destined to arise.
This is what the Kaśmīrīs say; all other forms are of four kinds.
The external [teacher] explains that all other forms are of five kinds:
there is past form, which refers to that which has already ceased and is no longer seen by the eye;
There is future form, which means that which is not seen by the eye and will cease;
there is present form, which means that which is not seen by the eye and ceases;
and furthermore, there is future form that is of a nature not to arise.
Regarding the non-arising dharma of form (*rūpa*), there are two types: either the eye-consciousness is empty or it is not empty.
This refers to the external; all other forms are said to be of five kinds. It is said:
Furthermore, there is all that exists as form, whether it be the domain of one sentient being, or two, or up to a hundred thousand—
meaning that what one sentient being sees extends up to a hundred thousand. How is this so?

For example, when a Dharma teacher ascends the high seat, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, upon seeing him, give rise to the corresponding consciousness; that which does not arise for them is something else entirely.
Just as when the new moon first appears, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, having seen it, give rise to a consciousness conditioned by that [moon], while other things do not arise for them;

or just as when a single female performer is adorned at a great assembly, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, having seen her, give rise to a consciousness conditioned by that [performer], while other things do not arise for them.
It is said:
Furthermore, there is other form that may not be seen by one sentient being, or by two, or even up to a hundred thousand.

Just as within mountain roots, valleys, ridges, and interiors, or within this great earth, the great ocean, and Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains—though these fall within the range of the divine eye, they are not seen because it does not employ them.
Question: Is this not the domain of the Buddha-eye? Answer:
Is there a Buddha for whom the divine eye is constantly present?
As it is with the realm of forms, so it is with the realms of sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. Question:
What is the eye-consciousness element?
The answer is:
conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises.
Question: If,
excluding its own nature, all other phenomena serve as conditions for the arising of visual consciousness,
why is it said that "the eye conditions the arising of visual consciousness"?
The answer is:
It refers to its being an immediate and predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

When that eye and visible form give rise to visual consciousness, they act as an immediate and predominant condition in an extremely proximate manner, unlike [the conditions] such as birth, aging, and impermanence which have already arisen.
Some say: it refers to that basis and its object; the basis is the eye, and the object is form. Others say:
This refers to the internal and the external; the internal is the eye, and the external is form.
Alternatively, it is said:
this refers to the faculty and the object of the faculty; the faculty is the eye, and the object of the faculty is form.
This explains that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms. Question:
Just as consciousness arises conditioned by visible forms, why is it called "eye-consciousness" and not "form-consciousness"?
Answer: It should be explained.
As it is stated in the *Bāhyārtha-sūtra*:
Consciousness arises conditioned by form and contact.

If this were not stated, it would mean that the Blessed One’s teaching is incomplete; one should understand the meaning through these presented gateways to the meaning, these presented summaries of the meaning, and these presented transitions of the meaning.
Some say: It is because it is a subtle teaching and a subtle meaning.
Although consciousness arises conditioned by form, when that eye gives rise to consciousness, there is a subtle meaning, as in the cases of a musician, a dyer, or a scribe.

As it has been said: when one says that a performance is being held in a certain place, it is not that there are no female performers, nor no lute players, nor no singers, nor no instructors, nor no guards; rather, it is because the master of the performance is exceptionally excellent that one says a performance is being held in that place.

As it is said, "a person dyes their clothes," it is not that the person dyes the clothes; rather, it is the color that dyes the clothes. However, because that person is the primary agent in the act of dyeing, one says, "the person dyes their clothes."

It is as when it is said that one writes characters with a brush; it is not that there is no ink, nor no paper, nor no human skillful means, yet because that brush is exceedingly excellent for producing the characters, it is called "the excellence of the brush."

Thus, although consciousness arises conditioned by form, it is specifically when the eye gives rise to consciousness that it is a sublime matter; because this is a sublime teaching and a sublime meaning, it is like a performance, dyeing, or writing.
Some say: "The eye and eye-consciousness can each have a single basis and a single object, whereas visible form is not so fixed. Others say:
Within the eye, forms are not fixed.
Some say: "The eye resides within oneself; 'intention' (yi) refers to the spirit (shen), while forms are not fixed."
The Venerable Vasumitra said:
"If consciousness arises conditioned by form, why is it called 'eye-consciousness' and not 'form-consciousness'?
He replied:
Based on the eye, it is not form.
To state it again:
the eye is sublime, not form.
It is stated again:
"The eye, the self, and the mind are obtainable, but not form.
It is stated again:
The eye is proximate, while visible forms are indeterminate.
To state it again:
the eye is a faculty, not a form.
It is stated again:
"When the eye increases or decreases, consciousness also increases or decreases, but not form.
It is stated again:
The eye is the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), not the object (*rūpa*). The Venerable Dharmatrāta said:
"If there were no eye, consciousness would certainly not arise."
Question: If that which is formless does not give rise to consciousness either, how is this so? Answer:
If there were not even a single form, let alone two or even hundreds of thousands of forms;
and if there were no eye, then even with millions of forms appearing before one, consciousness could not arise based upon them. For this reason, the various factors are enumerated.
"Reliance and excellence, / One’s own mind and proximity to reception, / Increase and superior objects,
/ With the perception of the teacher following after.
This refers to the eye cognizing forms.
Question: Just as consciousness cognizes form, it is not the eye that cognizes form.
For what reason is it said that "the eye cognizes form"?
Answer: This explanation should be so.
It is appropriate that the eye reaches the object and the visual consciousness performs the function of seeing; this is how it ought to be.
Question: If it is not so, what is the intention? Answer:

Because it is possessed [of the requisite]. It is like a merchant’s guide: he is not himself a merchant, yet he travels by foot; however, because that merchant relies on him for his journey, he is called the merchant’s guide.
Thus, although one cognizes form (*rūpa*), it is the eye that possesses the capacity to see form; therefore, it is said that "the eye knows form.
Alternatively, it may be said:
to avoid the fault of redundancy, as will be explained later, "the eye knows form" refers to the mind, mentation, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).
Question: What is the difference between *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*?
One school of thought says there is no difference between them.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are one in meaning; they do not have different meanings.
Just as these ten names are recited, so it is said that fire has ten names:
fire, flame, burning, blazing, consuming fuel, black evil, smoke-dweller, light, radiance, and enemy of snow.
These are the ten names of fire; they are all one and the same.
Thus, regarding those who recite the "colors of fire," it is said that the colors of fire have ten names:
"Fire is red when there is much pestilence and death; Yellow gives rise to weapons and war."
A red flame portends famine; a variegated color is auspicious for the five grains;
a green color brings abundance and joy; a white color signifies the flourishing of the nation;
a black color indicates the decline of the realm. These are called the ten colors of fire.
Thus other sūtras state: namely, feeling (vedanā), feeling that is equal, distinct feeling, and feeling as the fruit of cognition; although these have many names, they are one and the same feeling.
Thus, another sūtra states in verse:
“Śakra, the Greatly Meritorious; The Thousand-Eyed Kauśika; The Heavenly King Āditya;
Indra follows behind.”
"Although these are ten names, they are nonetheless one.
Thus it is said that *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* have the same meaning and are not distinct.
Or it is said:"
There is a distinction:
"mind" (*citta*) refers to the past, "intellect" (*manas*) refers to the future, and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the present.
Alternatively, it is said:

The designation of the elements (*dhātu*) is mind (*citta*); the designation of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is intellect (*manas*); the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Alternatively, it is said: the meaning of "nature" (*gotra*) is the meaning of mind; the meaning of "gate of entry" (*āya-dvāra*) is the meaning of intellect; the meaning of "accumulation" (*rāśi*) is the meaning of consciousness.

Some say: "The nature of arrogance and indulgence regarding speech is explained as *citta*; the meaning of 'nature' (*dhātu*) is the meaning of 'element' (*dhātu*). Arrogance and indulgence based on wealth are explained as *manas*; the meaning of 'conveying the gateway' (*āyadvāra*) is the meaning of 'entrance' (*āyatana*). Arrogance and indulgence based on life-force are explained as *vijñāna*. As for the aggregates (*skandha*), they are like enemies."
Some say: "Thinking is the mind (citta), awareness is the intellect (manas), and cognition is consciousness (vijñāna).
The Venerable Pavaraka said:

That which is capable of thinking and capable of cutting is the mind (*citta*); that which is capable of awakening and capable of feeling sympathy is the intellect (*manas*); that which is capable of knowing and capable of discriminating is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

That which is capable of thinking is with outflows (*sāsrava*); that which is capable of cutting is without outflows (*anāsrava*). That which is capable of awakening is with outflows; that which is capable of feeling sympathy is without outflows. That which is capable of knowing is with outflows; that which is capable of discriminating is without outflows.
Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these are the distinctions.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness. Question:
What is the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
The answer is:
it refers to that which has known, will know, or is currently knowing mental objects (*dharma*), as well as all other [factors] associated with it.
That which has already been known is the past; that which is yet to be known is the future; and that which is being known now is the present.
Furthermore, whatever else exists therein refers to the mind, whether it be empty or non-empty.
Question: What is the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu)? Answer:
This refers to the mental cognition of phenomena that has been known, will be known, and is being known now.
That which has been known is the past; that which will be known is the future; and that which is being known now is the present. Question:
Why are the six consciousnesses not established as including all other [factors]?
The answer is:
they are established as the six consciousnesses because they involve active engagement (*abhisamskāra*); that past mind does not engage in such activity.
Someone says:
"The six consciousnesses are established because they are produced; that past mind, however, is a non-produced phenomenon (*anutpattidharma*).
For this reason, the six consciousnesses do not include anything else."
Question: For what reason is nothing else established as the dharma-dhātu? Answer:

Having already discussed the mind, one should know that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) has been explained in brief. That is to say, what was not mentioned there is what is explained here; what was explained there as being with remainder (*śeṣa*) is explained here as being without remainder (*niḥśeṣa*). Therefore, no other entities are established apart from the dharma-realm.
Someone said:
"It is not because of the *dharmadhātu* that 'existence' and 'other-existence' are established.

If it were because of the *dharmadhātu* that 'existence' and 'other-existence' were established, then all twelve bases (*āyatana*) would also have to be established as 'existence' and 'other-existence'."
However, because it is not the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), one establishes "that which exists" and "other than that which exists.
For this reason, the following treatise is composed:
Is there, among the dharmas of the form realm (rūpadhātu), anything that exists or anything other than that which exists?

Answer: There are ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) that constitute "this possession"; as for the remaining possessions, they refer to the birth, aging, and impermanence of those [ten bases]. Question:
Why is this? The answer is:
it is because they have entered into the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and within the dharma-realm there is nothing else that exists.
For this reason it is so.
Is there anything else that exists within the formless dharmas?
Answer: Yes.
There are seven mental-object elements (dharmadhātu) that belong to all [beings]; as for the rest, they belong to those who have undergone birth, aging, and impermanence.
Question: Why is this so?
The answer is:
It refers to his entry into the dharma-realm; for the dharma-realm is that which possesses nothing else. Therefore it is so.
Is there a location where [the eye] is bound, such that at that location the eye is also bound, visible forms are also bound, and visual consciousness can arise?
The answer is:
either in that very location or in another location.
Question: What is this "proper place"? Answer:
When one is born in the desire realm and sees forms of the desire realm, those eyes of the desire realm and those forms of the desire realm can produce eye-consciousness of the desire realm.

When one is born within the first dhyāna and sees forms of the first dhyāna with eyes of the first dhyāna level, those eyes of the first dhyāna level and those forms of the first dhyāna level can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna level.
This is called "the proper place. Question:
What is meant by "other places"?

Answer: One born in the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna; those forms of the desire realm can produce an eye-consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna by means of that eye belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, when one is reborn in the desire realm and sees forms of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the second dhyāna level, those forms of the desire realm can produce eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna level by means of that eye of the second dhyāna level.

When the eye of the second dhyāna stage sees forms of the first dhyāna stage, that eye of the second dhyāna stage and those forms of the first dhyāna stage can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the second dhyāna stage sees forms of the second dhyāna stage, that eye of the second dhyāna stage and those forms of the second dhyāna stage can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when one is born in the desire realm, the eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the desire realm; those forms of the desire realm can produce eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage by means of that eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the first dhyāna stage, that eye of the third dhyāna stage and those forms of the first dhyāna stage can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the second dhyāna stage, that eye of the third dhyāna stage and those forms of the second dhyāna stage can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the third dhyāna stage, that eye of the third dhyāna stage and those forms of the third dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the desire realm, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the desire realm can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the first dhyāna stage, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the first dhyāna stage can give rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the second dhyāna stage, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the second dhyāna stage can give rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the third dhyāna stage, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the third dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the fourth dhyāna stage, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the fourth dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.
This is called being born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As it is for birth in the desire realm, so it is for birth in the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; these are called "other places."
Is there another location where [the eye] is bound, another location where form is bound, such that they can produce visual consciousness? Answer: There is.

When one is born in the desire realm and sees forms of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the second dhyāna stage, those forms of the desire realm can produce an eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage through that eye of the second dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when one is born in the desire realm and sees forms of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage, those forms of the desire realm can produce an eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage through that eye of the third dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the second dhyāna stage, that eye of the third dhyāna stage and those forms of the second dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the desire realm, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the desire realm can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the second dhyāna stage, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the second dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the third dhyāna stage, that eye of the fourth dhyāna stage and those forms of the third dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.
This is called being born in the desire realm.
As it is for birth in the desire realm, so it is for birth in the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
This is called the eye being bound to another place, the form being bound to another place, and the ability to produce visual consciousness.
Is there a location where one is bound, such that one is bound at that location, the eye is also bound there, and visible forms are also bound there, yet visual consciousness can arise?
The answer is:
either in that same location or in another location.
Question: What is this "place"? Answer:

When one is born in the desire realm, if one sees a form of the desire realm with an eye of the desire realm, then that body of the desire realm, that eye of the desire realm, and that form of the desire realm can produce an eye-consciousness of the desire realm.

When one is born in the first dhyāna, if one sees a form of the first dhyāna stage with an eye of the first dhyāna stage, then that body of the first dhyāna stage, that eye of the first dhyāna stage, and that form of the first dhyāna stage can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.
This is called "the locus. Question:
What is meant by "bondage to other loci"?

Answer: One born in the desire realm sees forms of the desire realm with an eye belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna; in that case, the body of the desire realm, the eye of the first dhyāna stage, and the forms of the desire realm can give rise to an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna sees forms belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, that body belonging to the desire realm, the eye belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, and the forms belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna can give rise to an eye-consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, when one is born again in the desire realm, the eye belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna sees forms of the desire realm; that body of the desire realm, with the eye of the second dhyāna stage, can produce an eye-consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna in relation to those forms of the desire realm.

When the eye of the second dhyāna stage sees forms of the first dhyāna stage, those forms of the first dhyāna stage—perceived by the eye of the second dhyāna stage belonging to a body in the desire realm—are able to produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the second dhyāna stage sees forms of the second dhyāna stage, that body of the desire realm, the eye of the second dhyāna stage, and the forms of the second dhyāna stage can give rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when one is born again in the desire realm, the eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the desire realm; that body of the desire realm, with the eye of the third dhyāna stage, can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage in relation to those forms of the desire realm.

When one with an eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage sees a form belonging to the first dhyāna stage, that body belonging to the desire realm, the eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage, and the form belonging to the first dhyāna stage can give rise to an eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the third dhyāna stage sees the forms of the second dhyāna stage, that body of the desire realm, the eye of the third dhyāna stage, and the forms of the third dhyāna stage can give rise to the eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the third dhyāna stage sees forms of the third dhyāna stage, that body of the desire realm, the eye of the third dhyāna stage, and the forms of the third dhyāna stage can give rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when one is born again in the desire realm, the eye belonging to the stage of the four dhyānas sees forms of the desire realm; that body of the desire realm, with the eye of the four dhyāna stage, can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage in relation to those forms of the desire realm.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the first dhyāna stage, that body belonging to the desire realm, with its eye of the fourth dhyāna stage, can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage in relation to those forms of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna sees forms belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna, with that body of the desire realm, the eye of the fourth dhyāna, and the forms of the second dhyāna, the visual consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna can arise.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the third dhyāna stage, those forms of the third dhyāna stage—perceived by the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage belonging to a body of the desire realm—can give rise to eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna sees forms belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna, that body belonging to the desire realm, the eye belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna, and the forms belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna can give rise to eye-consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
This is called being born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As it is for birth in the desire realm, so it is for birth in the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; these are called other places.

Is there any other place where [the person] is bound, such that the body is bound in that other place, the eye is bound in that other place, and visible forms are bound in that other place, yet visual consciousness is produced?
Answer: There is.

When one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the eye belonging to the third dhyāna stage sees forms belonging to the second dhyāna stage; in that case, the body of the desire realm, the eye of the third dhyāna stage, and the forms of the second dhyāna stage can give rise to an eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) belonging to the first dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when one is reborn in the desire realm, the eye belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna sees forms belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna; that body of the desire realm, the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage, and the forms of the second dhyāna stage can give rise to an eye-consciousness belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the third dhyāna stage, those forms of the third dhyāna stage can produce eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage, based on a body of the desire realm and an eye of the fourth dhyāna stage.
This is called being born in the desire realm.

When one is born in the second dhyāna or the third dhyāna stage and sees forms of the desire realm with the eye, those forms of the desire realm can produce eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage, based on the body of the second dhyāna stage and the eye of the third dhyāna stage.

Furthermore, when one is born in the second dhyāna, the eye belonging to the fourth dhyāna stage sees forms of the desire realm; there, the body belongs to the second dhyāna stage, the eye belongs to the fourth dhyāna stage, and the forms of the desire realm can give rise to eye-consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage.

When the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage sees the forms of the third dhyāna stage, those forms of the third dhyāna stage can produce an eye-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage, based on the body of the second dhyāna stage and the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage.
This is called being born in the second dhyāna.
As it is for being born in the second dhyāna, so it is for the third dhyāna; this is called "other places.
Just as the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element have been explained, so too are the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element.
Is there a location where the nose is bound, and that same location where the odor is also bound, such that olfactory consciousness can arise?
Answer: Yes, there is.
The nose of the desire realm and the odors of the desire realm can give rise to the nose-consciousness of the desire realm.
As has been explained regarding the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element, so it is for the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element.
Is there a location where the body is bound, and that same location is also where the subtle and smooth [tangible object] is bound, such that body-consciousness can arise?
Answer: It may be in that very location, or it may be in another location.
Question: What is this "place"? Answer:

One born in the desire realm who perceives the fine and smooth [tangibles] of the desire realm: that body of the desire realm and those fine and smooth tangibles of the desire realm can produce a body-consciousness of the desire realm.

One born in the first dhyāna who perceives the fine and smooth tangibles of the stage of the first dhyāna: that body of the first dhyāna stage and those fine and smooth tangibles of the first dhyāna stage can produce a body-consciousness of the first dhyāna stage.
This is called "this place. Question:
What is meant by "other places"?

Answer: When one is born in the second dhyāna and experiences the tactile sensations (*spraṣṭavya*) of the second dhyāna level, those tactile sensations of the second dhyāna level can produce body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) belonging to the first dhyāna level.

When one is born in the third dhyāna and perceives the tactile objects of the third dhyāna level, those tactile objects of the third dhyāna level can produce body-consciousness in a body belonging to the first dhyāna level.

When one is born in the fourth dhyāna and perceives the tactile objects of the fourth dhyāna level, those tactile objects of the fourth dhyāna level can produce body-consciousness in a body belonging to the first dhyāna level.
That is to say, the subtle and smooth [tangible object] can be perceived by its own level, but not by another level;

this is what is meant by "other places. Is there any place where the mind is bound, and that same place to which the mental object (dharma) is also bound, such that it can give rise to a mental consciousness?
Answer: Either in this place or in another place. Question:
What is this "proper basis"?
The answer is:

being born within the desire realm and knowing the phenomena of the desire realm; that mental faculty of the desire realm and those phenomena of the desire realm can give rise to the mental consciousness of the desire realm.

In this way, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one knows the phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and those phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception can give rise to the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called "the proper place. Question:
What is meant by "other places"?

Answer: One born within the desire realm who knows the dharmas of the first dhyāna stage—those dharmas of the mental consciousness of that person’s desire-realm mind belonging to the first dhyāna stage—are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

One sequentially knows the phenomena of the desire realm following the first dhyāna; that mental consciousness of the first dhyāna stage [knows] the phenomena of the desire realm, whether they belong to the first dhyāna stage or extend up to the sphere of perception or the sphere of non-perception.

One born within the desire realm who knows the dharmas of the second dhyāna stage possesses a mental faculty of the desire realm and a mental consciousness of the second dhyāna stage; these dharmas are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

In the sequence following the second dhyāna, one knows the dharmas of the desire realm; that mental consciousness of the second dhyāna stage takes as its object the dharmas of the desire realm, whether they pertain to the second dhyāna stage itself or extend up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born within the desire realm who knows the phenomena of the third dhyāna stage possesses a mental faculty of the desire realm and a mental consciousness of the third dhyāna stage; these phenomena are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

Successively knowing the dharmas of the desire realm from the third dhyāna: the mental consciousness of that third-dhyāna stage takes the dharmas of the desire realm as its object, whether they belong to the third-dhyāna stage itself or extend up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born within the desire realm knows the dharmas of the four dhyāna stages; that mental consciousness of the desire realm regarding the dharmas of the mental consciousness of the four dhyāna stages is either bound to the three realms or unbound.

One sequentially knows the dharmas of the desire realm through the four dhyānas; the mental consciousness of that stage of the four dhyānas takes the dharmas of the desire realm as its object, whether it pertains to the stage of the four dhyānas or extends up to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born within the desire realm cognizes the phenomena of space and earth; that mental consciousness of the desire realm cognizes the phenomena of space and earth, which may be bound to the three realms or unbound.

One sequentially knows the phenomena of the desire realm within the sphere of infinite space; that sphere of infinite space and the mental consciousness of the desire realm may pertain to the sphere of infinite space itself, or extend as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born in the desire realm cognizes the mental states belonging to the level of the desire realm; those mental states of the consciousness-level consciousness of the desire realm are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

One cognizes the states of the desire realm in successive stages of consciousness; those mental states of the consciousness-level consciousness of the desire realm belong either to the level of that consciousness or extend up to the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born within the desire realm who knows the dharmas of the sphere of non-perception possesses a mental consciousness of the desire realm that takes those sphere-of-non-perception dharmas as its object; these dharmas are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

One sequentially knows the phenomena of the desire realm by means of the sphere of nothingness; that sphere of nothingness takes as its object the mental consciousness phenomena of the desire realm, whether they belong to the sphere of nothingness itself or to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born within the desire realm cognizes the dharmas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that mental faculty of the desire realm and the mental consciousness-dharmas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

Successively knowing the phenomena of the desire realm within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one understands that the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes the phenomena of the desire realm as its object. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception [is thus established].

This is called being born within the desire realm and, while born in the first dhyāna, knowing the dharmas of the second dhyāna stage. Therein, the mind of the first dhyāna stage and the mental consciousness-dharmas of the second dhyāna stage are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

Through the sequence of the second dhyāna, one knows the factors of the first dhyāna stage; that mental faculty of the second dhyāna stage cognizes the factors of the first dhyāna consciousness, whether they pertain to the first dhyāna stage or extend as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born in the first dhyāna knows the dharmas of the third dhyāna stage; the mental faculty of that first dhyāna stage and the mental consciousness-dharmas of the third dhyāna stage are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

Through the sequence of the third dhyāna, one knows the dharmas of the first dhyāna stage; the mental faculty of that third dhyāna stage cognizes the dharmas of the consciousness of the first dhyāna stage, whether they belong to the first dhyāna stage or extend as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born in the first dhyāna knows the dharmas of the fourth dhyāna stage; the mental faculty of that first dhyāna stage and the mental consciousness-faculty dharmas of the fourth dhyāna stage are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

Through the sequence of the four dhyānas, one knows the dharmas of the stage of the first dhyāna; the mental faculty of that fourth dhyāna stage cognizes the dharmas of the consciousness of the first dhyāna, whether they belong to the stage of the first dhyāna or extend as far as the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One born in the first dhyāna knows the dharmas of the stages of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the mental consciousness of that stage of the first dhyāna pertains to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and its dharmas are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

One sequentially knows the factors of the first dhyāna stage from the perspective of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that is, the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes the mental factors of the first dhyāna stage as its object, whether those factors belong to the first dhyāna stage or extend up to the stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called being born in the first dhyāna.
As it is for being born in the first dhyāna, so it is for being born up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is what is meant by "birth. Question:
What is right attainment (*samyaksamādhi*)?
The answer is:

following a wholesome mind of the desire realm, there is the right attainment of the first dhyāna. The mental faculty (*manas*) of that desire realm and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the first dhyāna take as their objects phenomena (*dharma*) that are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

From the first dhyāna one enters the second dhyāna absorption; the mental states of that first dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the second dhyāna are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

From the second dhyāna one enters the first dhyāna absorption; the mental states of that second dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the first dhyāna belong either to the level of the first dhyāna or extend up to the level of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

From the first dhyāna, one enters the third dhyāna in direct order; the mental states of the first dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the third dhyāna that arise accordingly are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

From the third dhyāna, one emerges into the first dhyāna in reverse order; the mental states of the third dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the first dhyāna that are thus transcended belong either to the level of the first dhyāna or extend as far as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

From the second dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the third dhyāna; this accords with the mental states of the second dhyāna and the mental consciousness-factors (*manovijñāna-dharma*) of the third dhyāna, which may be bound to the three realms or unbound.

Rising from the third dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment of the second dhyāna; this is contrary to the mental states of the third dhyāna and the mental consciousness-factors of the second dhyāna, which may belong to the level of the second dhyāna or extend as far as the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

From the second dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the fourth dhyāna by ascending; this transcends the mental states of the second dhyāna and the mental consciousness-states of the fourth dhyāna, which may be bound to the three realms or unbound.

Rising from the fourth dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment of the second dhyāna by descending; this transcends the mental states of the fourth dhyāna and the mental consciousness-states of the second dhyāna, reaching either the second dhyāna or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

From the third dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the fourth dhyāna; the mental states of that third dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the fourth dhyāna are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

Arising from the fourth dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment of the third dhyāna; the mental states of that fourth dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the third dhyāna belong either to the level of the third dhyāna or extend as far as the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
