Following the third dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). In accordance with that, the mental states of the third dhyāna and the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space—whether pertaining to the three realms or being unconditioned—are objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Arising from the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the third dhyāna within the sphere of infinite space, one transcends in reverse the mental consciousness and mental factors of that third dhyāna belonging to the sphere of infinite space, whether they pertain to the level of the third dhyāna or up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Following the sequence of the four dhyānas, one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space; the mental states of that fourth dhyāna and the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

Emerging from the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna based on the sphere of infinite space, one reverses the mental intention directed toward that sphere of infinite space; the consciousness of the fourth dhyāna then engages with its own objects, whether within the stage of the fourth dhyāna itself or extending up to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

From the fourth dhyāna, one enters the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). This involves transcending the mental consciousness and its objects of the four dhyānas in forward order; these objects may be bound to the three realms or unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Rising from the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna. This involves transcending the mental consciousness and its objects of the sphere of infinite consciousness in reverse order; these objects may belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna or extend up to the level of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Following the sequence from the sphere of infinite space to the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the mental consciousness and its mental objects pertaining to that sphere of infinite consciousness are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

Emerging from the meditative attainment of the sphere of consciousness, one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space; reversing the mental states of that sphere of consciousness toward the sphere of infinite space—namely, the mental consciousness and its objects—one dwells either in the sphere of infinite space or proceeds to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Following the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana). In accordance with that transcending of the sphere of infinite space, the mental states of the sphere of nothingness consist of mind-consciousness and mental objects (dharmas) which are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

Emerging from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, one transcends it in reverse order, directing the mental consciousness of the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of infinite space, or toward the sphere of infinite consciousness, or even up to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Following the base of consciousness (vijñānāyatana) in sequence is the meditative attainment of the base of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana-samāpatti). The mental states associated with that base of consciousness and the mental consciousness of the base of nothingness are either bound to the three realms or are unbound.

Emerging from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, one proceeds in reverse order through the consciousness-sphere mind and the mental phenomena of that consciousness-sphere, either entering the sphere of infinite consciousness or reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Following the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), one enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). In accordance with this transcendence of that sphere of infinite consciousness, the mental consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes as its object mental phenomena (dharmas) that are either bound to the three realms or unbound.

From the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one transcends it in reverse; regarding the consciousness-sphere and the mental phenomena of that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one either enters the sphere of consciousness or reaches the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

From the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), one successively attains the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Corresponding to that sphere of nothingness, there is the mental faculty (*manas*), the consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*vijñāna*), and mental objects (*dharma*), which may be bound to the three realms (*tridhātupratisaṃyukta*) or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).

Emerging from the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the meditative attainment of the sphere of nothingness; in this process, the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the consciousness and mental factors of the sphere of nothingness—whether belonging to the sphere of nothingness or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—are reversed.
This is called right attainment (*samyaksamādhi*). Question:
What are the other forms of right attainment?

This establishes the four kinds of transformative minds of the desire realm: first, the fruit of the first dhyāna; second, the fruit of the second dhyāna; third, the fruit of the third dhyāna; and fourth, the fruit of the fourth dhyāna.

When the mundane first dhyāna manifests in immediate succession to the transformation-mind (nirmāṇa-citta) that is the fruit of the first dhyāna, regarding those mental factors of the desire realm mind and the first dhyāna consciousness: those transformations consist of either six bases (āyatana) or four. The "six" refers to those abiding in one's own mind; the "four" refers to those not abiding in one's own mind.

In the worldly first dhyāna, following the sequence of the first dhyāna fruit, there is the transformation of the desire realm. Regarding that mental consciousness of the first dhyāna stage which takes the phenomena of the desire realm as its object, this transformation consists either of six bases (āyatana) or four bases.
Question: There should be six; why are there only four? Answer:
Because it does not transform odors or tastes. Question:
Why does it not transform odors or tastes?
Answer: It is so that they do not achieve [the result]; therefore, they do not transform it.
Furthermore, some say that although those transformed [beings] possess fragrance and taste, these are merely not achieved [by them].
Just as a woman possesses the female faculty and a man possesses the male faculty, yet they do not possess them [in that specific sense],
so too those transformed [beings] manifest fragrances and tastes, yet they do not possess them.
One who speaks thus must necessarily manifest fragrances and tastes.

When the mundane second-dhyāna transformation-mind (nirmāṇa-citta) arises in succession to the two fruits of the desire realm, the mental faculty of that desire realm and the mental-consciousness-element of the second dhyāna consist of either six bases or four.

Regarding the mundane second dhyāna and its successive fruit—the transformation-body of the desire realm—if the mind of that second dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the desire realm engage with dharmas, these constitute the six bases of transformation.

When the mundane (laukika) minds of the three dhyānas manifest in succession following the transformative mind (nirmāṇacitta) that is the fruit of the three dhyānas of the desire realm, those mental objects (dharma) of the mental consciousness belonging to the mental faculty of the desire realm consist of either six bases (āyatana) or four.

Regarding the transformation of the desire realm resulting from the sequential third dhyāna of the mundane level: when the mind of that third dhyāna and the mental consciousness of the desire realm engage with phenomena, these constitute the six sense bases of transformation.

When the mundane (laukika) four dhyānas manifest in succession as the result of the four dhyānas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those mental factors of the desire-realm mind and the consciousness-factors of the four dhyānas consist of either six or four transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*).

Regarding the sequential four dhyānas of the mundane world, the fruit of the fourth dhyāna is the transformation-body of the desire realm; as for that mind of the fourth dhyāna which takes the mental consciousness and dharmas of the desire realm as its object, it is the six sense-bases of transformation.
This refers to the remaining meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Question:
If one accomplishes the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), does one also accomplish the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the eye-element, one also accomplishes the form-element.
Is it possible to possess the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) while not possessing the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*)? Answer: Yes.
One born in the desire realm may not obtain the eye element; even if obtained, it is immediately lost.
Those who do not obtain it include those born blind and those dwelling within the mother’s womb or the thickening layers of the egg-membrane.

Those who obtain it and then lose it include cases where the eye element is detached, putrefied, broken, fallen away, plucked out, sunken, blurred, obscured by smoke, or covered in dust—such being the various afflictions that ruin the eye.
Question: If one is endowed with the eye element, is one also endowed with the visual consciousness element? Answer:
Or, one may accomplish the eye-element but not the eye-consciousness-element.
How does one accomplish the eye-element but not the eye-consciousness-element?
The answer is:

When one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, the visual consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) does not manifest before one; this is called "accomplishing the eye element but not the visual consciousness element.
How is it that one accomplishes the visual consciousness element but not the eye element?

Answer: When one is in the womb, within the egg, or within the fetal membranes and gradually thickening; or if, having been born in the desire realm, one has not yet obtained the eye faculty, or if having obtained it, one subsequently loses it—this is called "accomplishing the element of eye-consciousness but not the element of the eye."
How is it that one who accomplishes the eye-element also accomplishes the eye-consciousness-element? Answer:

One born in the desire realm who possesses all faculties, or one born in the first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, or fourth dhyāna, at the time when eye-consciousness is present before them—this is called accomplishing both the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element.
What is it that neither accomplishes the eye-element nor accomplishes the eye-consciousness-element?
The answer is:
one born in the formless realm; this is called neither accomplishing the eye-element nor accomplishing the eye-consciousness-element.
Question: If one accomplishes the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), does one also accomplish the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? Answer:
Or, one may accomplish the form element (*rūpa-dhātu*) but not accomplish the visual consciousness element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*).
How does one accomplish the form element but not the visual consciousness element?
The answer is:

When one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, and the eye-consciousness element is not present before them, this is called "accomplishing the form element but not the eye-consciousness element.
How is it that one accomplishes the eye-consciousness element but not the form element?
Answer: This does not exist.
How could one be accomplished in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and also be accomplished in the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?

Answer: One born in the desire realm who possesses all faculties, as well as one born in the first dhyāna, second dhyāna, third dhyāna, or fourth dhyāna, when the visual consciousness element is present before them—this is called being accomplished in the form realm and also accomplished in the visual consciousness element.
What is meant by not accomplishing the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and also not accomplishing the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
The answer is:
one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); this is called not accomplishing the form realm and also not accomplishing the eye-consciousness realm.
Question: If one does not possess the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), does one also not possess the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*)? Answer:
It is so. If one does not possess the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one also does not possess the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
Is there anyone who does not possess the eye element, yet it is not the case that they do not possess the form realm?
Answer: There are.
For example, one born in the desire realm who does not obtain the eye-faculty, or who obtains it but then loses it.
Question: If one does not possess the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), does one also not possess the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? Answer:
Or, one may not possess the eye-element but not the eye-consciousness-element.
How is it that one does not possess the eye-element but not the eye-consciousness-element?
The answer is:

While dwelling in the womb or within the egg and membrane as they gradually thicken, or if one is born in the desire realm and does not obtain the eye-faculty, or if having obtained it one then loses it—this is called not accomplishing the eye-element but not the eye-consciousness-element.
What is meant by not accomplishing the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) while not failing to accomplish the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
The answer is:

for one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, the eye-consciousness element does not manifest before them; this is called not accomplishing the eye-consciousness element while not failing to accomplish the eye element.
What is it to not possess the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element?
The answer is:
one who is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu); this is called not possessing the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element.
What is meant by "neither non-attainment of the eye-element nor non-attainment of the eye-consciousness-element"?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who possesses the faculty of sight, or one born in the first dhyāna, or likewise in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, when the eye-consciousness-element is present before them—this is called neither non-attainment of the eye-element nor non-attainment of the eye-consciousness-element.
Question: If one does not possess the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), does one also not possess the eye-consciousness realm (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? Answer:
It is so. If one does not possess the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one also does not possess the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
Is there anyone who does not possess the eye-consciousness element but is not without the form realm?
Answer: There is.
When one is born into the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, the visual consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) does not manifest before one.
Question: If one achieves or fails to achieve the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), does one also achieve or fail to achieve the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)? Answer:
It is thus:
if one achieves or fails to achieve the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one also achieves or fails to achieve the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
Is there any case where one achieves or fails to achieve the eye element, yet does not [achieve or fail to achieve] the form realm?
Answer: There is.
For example, one born in the desire realm who acquires the eye-faculty and then immediately loses it.
Question: If one achieves or fails to achieve the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), does one also achieve or fail to achieve the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*)? Answer:
Or, one may achieve or fail to achieve the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), but not the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
How is it that one achieves or fails to achieve the eye-element, but not the eye-consciousness-element?

Answer: One born in the desire realm who acquires the eye faculty and then loses it is said to have the accomplishment of the eye element but not its non-accomplishment; this is not the case for the eye-consciousness element.
What is the accomplishment of the eye-consciousness element but not its non-accomplishment, while there is no accomplishment of the eye element?

Answer: When one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and arises from the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), this is called the accomplishment of the visual consciousness element and its non-accomplishment, but not of the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
What is it that constitutes the attainment of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and the non-attainment [of its opposite], as well as the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
The answer is:

when one passes away from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called the attainment of the eye-element and the non-attainment [of its opposite], as well as the eye-consciousness-element.
What is it that one neither possesses nor fails to possess the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), yet also does not possess the visual-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
The answer is:

one who is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is fully endowed with the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), or one who is born in the first dhyāna, or likewise in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, when the visual-consciousness-element is present before them—this is called neither possessing nor failing to possess the eye-element, yet also [not possessing] the visual-consciousness-element.
Question: If one achieves or fails to achieve the form element (rūpadhātu), does one also achieve or fail to achieve the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)? Answer:
It is so. If one achieves or fails to achieve the form element (*rūpadhātu*), one also achieves or fails to achieve the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
Is there any case where one achieves or fails to achieve the eye-consciousness element, yet does not [achieve or fail to achieve] the form element?
Answer: There is.
When one is born into the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, it arises from the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).

Question: If one who was not previously accomplished in the eye-element attains accomplishment in it, is that person also not previously accomplished in the form-element and then attains accomplishment in it? Answer:
It is so. If one who was not previously endowed with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) attains such endowment, they likewise attain endowment with the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
Is there any case where one attains endowment with the eye element without having been previously endowed with the form realm?
Answer: There is.
One born in the desire realm who does not possess the eye faculty may acquire the eye faculty.

Question: If one who was not previously accomplished in the eye-element attains accomplishment in it, is that person also not previously accomplished in the eye-consciousness-element and then attains accomplishment in it? Answer:
Or, there is the case where the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is not accomplished and then becomes accomplished, while the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) is not.
What is the case where the eye-element is not accomplished and then becomes accomplished, but the eye-consciousness-element is not?

Answer: One born in the desire realm who lacks the eye faculty but subsequently acquires it—this is called the non-accomplishment of the eye element followed by its accomplishment, without the accomplishment of the eye-consciousness element.
What is it that constitutes the non-attainment and subsequent attainment of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), but not the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
The answer is:

when one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and the visual consciousness element manifests before one, this is called the non-attainment and subsequent attainment of the visual consciousness element, but not the eye element.
How is it that the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is not attained and then becomes attained, and likewise the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
The answer is:

when one dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this is called the case where the eye-element is not attained and then becomes attained, and likewise the eye-consciousness-element.
What is it that is not unaccomplished but becomes accomplished with respect to the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), and likewise with respect to the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
The answer is:

one born in the desire realm who possesses the faculty of the eye, or one born in the first dhyāna, or the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, when the eye-consciousness-element is present before them; this is called being not unaccomplished but becoming accomplished with respect to both the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element.

Question: If one who was not previously accomplished in the form realm (rūpadhātu) attains accomplishment therein, does that person also attain accomplishment in the eye-consciousness element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu)?
Answer: No.

It is so. If one who was not previously accomplished in the form realm attains accomplishment therein, they likewise attain accomplishment in the eye-consciousness element while being previously unaccomplished in it.
Is there any case where one attains accomplishment in the eye-consciousness element without having attained accomplishment in the form realm?
Answer: There is.
When one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, the visual consciousness element manifests before one.
As it is with the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element, so it is with the remaining elements.
This is explained in detail for all eighteen elements and bases.

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kapiśa during the Fu Qin dynasty.

18. The Twelve Bases (Āyatana), Chapter Eighteen. Regarding the twelve bases: the eye-base and the form-base; the ear-base and the sound-base; the nose-base and the odor-base; the tongue-base and the taste-base; the body-base and the tangible-base; the mind-base and the mental-object-base.
Question: For what reason did those who composed this treatise base their discourse upon the twelve bases (āyatana)? Answer:
The intention of the author of that treatise was indeed such.
Acting according to his intent, he composed the treatise in this manner so that it does not contradict the Dharma.
For this reason, the discussion is based upon the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Someone said:
"The author of that scripture has no purpose.
He asked: "Why?"
Why is this? Because there is no basis for those who composed the sūtras.
The answer is:
This is the Buddha’s own sūtra.

In that sutra, there was a brahmin named Jātiśroṇa; after his midday meal, he wandered about and went to where the Blessed One was staying. Upon arrival, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Once he was seated, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Gautama! I wish to ask you a few questions."
"Listen to my question, and I shall explain it for you.
The World-Honored One replied: "Brahmin!"
"Ask whatever you wish," [the Buddha said].
The brahmin replied, "Gautama!"
"Everything, O Gautama, means everything. How many things are there that constitute 'everything'?"
"How is it, Gautama? Is everything designated as 'everything' by means of a designation?
The Blessed One replied:
"O Brahmin! There are twelve bases (āyatana), from the eye-base to the mental-object-base.
This, O Brahmin!"
There are all those things;
it is in this way that the Tathāgata designates all designations, O brahmin!
If one were to speak thus: "This is not all.
I reject all that has been designated by the śramaṇa Gautama, and I shall designate another 'all'."
They have nothing but words; though they ask repeatedly, they do not understand, and their delusion only increases.
Why is this? Because it is not within their sphere of experience.

Question: If there were someone who made such a statement: "All that exists consists of the eighteen elements (dhātus); all that exists consists of the five aggregates (skandhas) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta); all that exists consists of the four noble truths and space and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha); all that exists consists of name (nāma) and form (rūpa)."
This too is merely words; having questioned repeatedly, one still does not know, which only increases delusion as if it were not one's proper domain.
He replied: "This is not so."
Question: If it is not so, then what is it? Answer:
This explains the removal of the object (*artha*), not the removal of the flavor (*rasa*).

This explains the removal of the object of designation (*prajñapti-artha*), not the removal of the flavor of designation; that is to say, the nature of all phenomena (*sarva-dharma-svabhāva*) is entirely subsumed within the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
If someone were to say, "I shall set aside the meaning of the twelve bases (āyatana) and establish another meaning," they would ultimately be unable to establish it.
Therefore, this statement speaks of setting aside the meaning, not the flavor; it speaks of setting aside the established meaning, not the established flavor.
"Expounding" means that these twelve bases (āyatana) are excellently expounded, joyfully expounded, most excellently expounded, and supremely expounded. Question:
Why are these twelve bases (āyatana) called well-spoken, excellently spoken, most excellent, and supreme?
The answer is:
because these bases are taught without confusion and encompass the entire realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Although it encompasses all phenomena, this is merely a confused exposition, in that one mind is established as seven mind-elements and aggregates.
Although it is not a confused exposition, it nonetheless does not encompass all phenomena, in that it includes the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) but excludes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This entrance is not a confused explanation, yet it encompasses all dharmas.
Some say: "Within this entrance, it is taught that all dharma-realms are encompassed."
Although [the other systems] encompass all dharmas, they do so by way of extensive exposition; the aggregates (skandhas) do not encompass all dharmas, nor is it a medium-length exposition.
This entrance (āyatana), however, is a medium-length exposition and does encompass all dharmas.
For this reason, it is said:
"The twelve bases are well-spoken, excellently spoken, supreme, and sublime.
It is for this purpose that this treatise is composed.
One who wishes to contemplate all phenomena should rely on the twelve bases (āyatana) for contemplation.
Having relied on the twelve bases for contemplation, there arises the illumination of the phenomena of the twelve bases and the manifestation of the images of the twelve meanings.
Just as when a person polishes twelve mirrors and observes their own reflection, they see that reflection within all twelve mirrors;
likewise, one who wishes to observe all phenomena should rely upon the twelve bases (*āyatana*) for observation.
Having contemplated based on the twelve bases (*āyatana*), there arise twelve illuminations of the Dharma and the manifestation of the images of the twelve meanings.
These bases can be apprehended within a single body and a single mind; there is only a difference in their various modes of activity.
Just as twelve people may belong to a single household yet each performs different tasks, so too,
although the twelve bases (*āyatana*) may be found within a single body and a single mind, they differ only in their various functions and degrees of distinction.
This is the spontaneous nature of the body that has already entered the stage of the seeds of the [Buddha] nature.
Having explained the nature, one should now explain the practice.
For what reason is "entry" taught?
What is the meaning of "entry" (*āyatana*)?
The answer is:

the meaning of a gateway is the meaning of entry; the meanings of a path of arrival, a storehouse, a granary, a signpost, a mechanism, a field, a spring, a stream, an ocean, whiteness, and purity are the meanings of entry.

The meaning of "conveyance-gate" (*āyadvāra*) is the meaning of "entry. Just as the conveyance of goods from villages, cities, and kingdoms can be obtained, thereby enriching the king and his officials;

so too, by means of the bases (*āśraya*) and conditions (*pratyaya*), the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) can be obtained, which is to say they nourish sentient beings. This is what is meant by the meaning of "conveyance-gate" being the meaning of "entry."
The meaning of "conveying" (*āya*) is likewise.

As for the meaning of "storehouse" (*ālaya*) being the meaning of "entry" (*praveśa*): just as gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and mani jewels can be obtained within a storehouse, which is said to benefit sentient beings;

so too, this basis (*āśraya*) and its conditions—the mind and mental factors—can be obtained, which is said to nurture sentient beings. This is what is meant by the meaning of "storehouse" being the meaning of "entry."
That the meaning of "storehouse" (kośa) is the meaning of "entrance" (āyatana) is as follows: just as food and drink can be obtained within a storehouse, which is said to nourish sentient beings;

so too, based upon the [internal] bases and conditions, the mind and mental factors can be obtained, which is said to nourish sentient beings. This is what is meant by the meaning of "storehouse" being the meaning of "entrance."
That the meaning of "marking" (*paccuṭṭhāna*) is the meaning of "entering" (*okāsa*) is as follows:

just as one marks out [a space] below which hundreds of thousands of beings are to have their lives cut off, so too, within this basis (*ārammaṇa*) and condition (*paccaya*), beings are extinguished by impermanence; this is called the meaning of marking being the meaning of entering.
The meaning of "mechanism" (yukti) is the meaning of "entry" (praveśa):

just as a loom weaves by applying warp and woof according to its mechanism, so too, based on these bases and conditions, the mind and mental factors are established; this is called the meaning of mechanism being the meaning of entry.
The meaning of "field" (*kṣetra*) is the meaning of "entrance" (*āyatana*). Just as various grains grow within a field, thereby nourishing sentient beings;

so too, based upon these [bases] and conditions, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) can arise, thereby nourishing sentient beings. This is what is meant by the meaning of "field" being the meaning of "entrance."
That "spring" (*utsa*) has the meaning of "entry" (*praveśa*) is as stated in that sutra:
A certain deva approached the World-Honored One and asked in verse:
"From where does the spring turn?"
"What is it that turns and does not turn?
What is it that, being subject to suffering and pleasure, is extinguished without remainder?
The World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The eye, ear, and nose, the tongue, body, and mind—these are the springs from which [the stream] flows.
When this flowing ceases and does not turn back, this suffering and pleasure are extinguished without remainder."
This meaning of "source" (āya) is the meaning of "entry" (āyana).
Regarding the meaning of "flow" (āya) as the meaning of "entry," it is as stated in that sutra:
A certain deva approached the Blessed One and asked him in verse:
"All flows flow; by what are they restrained?
It is said that flows are guarded against; by what are they blocked?
The Blessed One replied in verse:
"It is said: 'Regarding the various floods of the world, the mindful one restrains the floods;
I say that one wards off the floods and blocks the floods with wisdom.
This is the meaning of 'floods' (ogha) and the meaning of 'entrance' (āyatana)."
The meaning of "ocean" (*sāgara*) is the meaning of "entering. As it is said in that sutra:
"Bhikṣus, what is called an 'ocean' is something unheard of by the foolish and the ordinary;
it is merely a verbal expression used by common people. It is not the ocean within this Dharma of the Noble Ones; it is merely a numerical designation for a vast accumulation of water."
"The eye is an entrance into the great ocean; those forms are its waves.
If one cannot endure the waves of form, one does not cross the ocean of the eye;
tossed about by the waves, one is seized by malevolent rākṣasas."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
"The mind enters the great ocean; those phenomena are its waves.
If one does not endure the waves of phenomena, one does not cross the ocean of the mind."
"Whirled about by waves and tides, / Held fast by malevolent spirits and rākṣasas.
This is called the meaning of "ocean" as the meaning of "entry.
Regarding the meaning of "purity and clarity" as the meaning of "entry," the explanation of "white and clear" is likewise so.
Because it is light, that which is spoken of in external scriptures is called both "earth" and "activity.
As stated in that sūtra,
the heterodox teacher Makkhali Gosāla said:
"O Śramaṇa Gautama! When the earth is destroyed and the earth has been destroyed, what remains to be done?

This is called the meaning of 'entrance' (sotā), which is the meaning of 'entry. It is the meaning of 'channel,' the meaning of 'repository,' the meaning of 'granary,' the meaning of 'sign,' the meaning of 'mechanism,' the meaning of 'field,' the meaning of 'spring,' the meaning of 'stream,' the meaning of 'ocean,' the meaning of 'purity,' and the meaning of 'clarity'—these are the meanings of 'entry.'"
Having explained the common practice, one should now explain the distinct practice.
What is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*)?
The answer is:
This refers to the eye and forms that have been seen, will be seen, and are being seen now, as well as all other such things.
"Have been seen" refers to the past; "will be seen" refers to the future; and "are being seen now" refers to the present.
And as for whatever else exists therein, it refers to that eye-consciousness being either empty or non-empty.
As it is with the sense-base of the eye, so it is with the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Question: What is the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana)? Answer:
That is to say, visible forms already seen, yet to be seen, and currently being seen by the eye, as well as all others besides these;
those already seen in the past, those yet to be seen in the future, those currently being seen in the present, and all others besides these.
As it is with the sense-base of form, so it is with sound, odor, taste, and tangibles. Question:
For what reason is the sense-base of form mentioned?
Regarding the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), for what reason is only one called the "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*)?
The answer is:
the term "base of form" is a singular designation, whereas the others have dual designations.

The sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is designated by a common name, whereas the other spheres are designated by names that are both common and uncommon; thus, it is said they are not designated by a common name.
Alternatively, it is said:
the two eyes are the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), and this is what is called the sphere of form.
Someone says:
The sense-base of form consists of the three types of eye-faculties—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble wisdom-eye—and these are said to be the sense-base of form;
the remaining sense-bases do not consist of these three eye-faculties, and for this reason they are not called the sense-base of form.
Someone says:
"The sense-field of form (rūpāyatana) is that which is the object of both the eye-faculty and eye-consciousness; this is what is called the sense-field of form.
As for the remaining sense-fields, they are neither the objects of the two eye-faculties nor the objects of eye-consciousness; therefore, they are not called the sense-field of form."
The Venerable Ghoṣaka also says the same:
because of the two eye-elements (*cakṣurdhātu*) and because of the object-condition for eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), one speaks of a single "form-base" (*rūpāyatana*). Others say:
That which is called the "sphere of form" (rūpāyatana) is that which can be cut and destroyed;
this is what is designated as the sphere of form. As for the other spheres, they cannot be cut and destroyed; therefore, they are not so designated.
Alternatively, it is said:
The sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is characterized by great obstruction and can be relinquished; therefore, it is called the "sense-base of form.
The remaining sense-bases are neither characterized by great obstruction nor can they be relinquished; for this reason, they are not called the "sense-base of form."
Some say: "The sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) possesses spatial extension and is designated as having spatial extension; it possesses length and is designated as having length.
As for 'possessing spatial extension,' spatial extension is what belongs to the sense-sphere of form."
Regarding the designation of "direction": direction is designated based on form (*rūpa*).
Regarding the possession of "extension" (*dīrghatva*): extension is that which belongs to the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
Regarding the designation of "extension": extension is designated based on form.

That which is called the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) possesses spatial extension and is designated as having spatial extension; it possesses linear extension and is designated as having linear extension—this is what is called the sense-base of form.

As for the other sense-bases, they do not possess spatial extension nor are they designated as having spatial extension, and they do not possess linear extension nor are they designated as having linear extension; therefore, they are not called the sense-base of form.
Someone says:
That which is called the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) consists of twenty or twenty-one types; this is what is described as the sphere of form.
As for the remaining spheres, they consist of neither twenty nor twenty-one types; therefore, they are not described as the sphere of form.
Some say: The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) can be designated as abiding here or abiding there; this is what is called the sense-base of form.
The other sense-bases cannot be so designated as abiding here or abiding there; therefore, they are not called the sense-base of form.
Some say: "The sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) refers to that which is designated by the name 'form' and that which belongs to form; this is what is called the sense-base of form.
As for the remaining sense-bases, although they belong to form, they are not designated by the name 'form'; therefore, they are not called the sense-base of form."
There are phenomena that do not belong to form, yet are subsumed under the designation "form. As it is said:
"That liberation through the cessation [of perception], which transcends form and is without the formless, is such a form-attainment that one realizes with one's own body and dwells therein."
These are said to be the eleven types of the tangible base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). What are they?
The four great elements, softness, roughness, lightness, heaviness, cold, heat, food, and thirst.
These are called the eleven types of the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). Question:
For what reason is the sphere of tangibles taught?
Is it that which is touched that constitutes the sphere of the smooth and soft?
Is it that whose nature is smooth and soft that constitutes the sphere of the smooth and soft?
Or is it that which has the smooth and soft as its object-condition that constitutes the sphere of the smooth and soft?
If that which is touched were the base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), then an atom should not touch another atom.

If it is by its very nature smooth that it constitutes the base of tangibles, then mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caittadharma*) would also be smooth by nature, yet they are not smooth as tangibles.

If the object of touch (spraṣṭavya) were itself the sphere of touch (spraṣṭavyāyatana), then the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) taking touch as their object would be taking the sphere of touch as their object, rather than taking touch as their object while not being the sphere of touch.
Having raised this argument, he replied:
"That which is touched is what is called the sphere of touch."
Question: It should not be that an atom touches an atom. Answer:
It is impossible to designate a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
If one were to designate it, it is only after many have been combined and aggregated that it is designated.
Or, as some say:
That is to say, it is caused by bodily contact.
To say "caused by bodily contact" is a definition of contact.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
Should it be said that an atom (paramāṇu) is tangible,
or should it be said that it is not tangible?
The answer is:
It should be said that there is no contact;
however, because the elements are exchanged in equal measure, the notion of contact arises.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta said:
Venerable sirs!
One should say that atoms do not touch; it is only because matter is joined together without any interval between them.
If there were contact, there would be perception, as in the case of exchanging things according to their true nature.
Question: Are reflections in water and images in a mirror real,
or are they unreal?
If it were real, the face would not enter into the mirror, nor would the mirror enter into the face.
Apart from these, what further form could there be?
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"It is not real. He asked:
"For what reason is it not real?"
The answer is:
It is said that the face does not enter into the mirror, nor does the mirror enter into the face; apart from these, what further form (rūpa) could there be?
The Abhidharmikas say:
The actual characteristic of the seed is that which belongs to the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and is known by visual consciousness. Question:
Just as a face does not enter into a mirror, nor does the mirror enter into the face, apart from these, how can there be any further form?
The answer is:
My manifestation of form is of immeasurable kinds, not of a single kind.
For example, by relying on the moon and a sun-crystal lens, one obtains water from a vessel; this is the actual functioning of water.
Just as fire is obtained through the conditions of the sun and a magnifying crystal, or through cow dung and human effort, and this is the actual application of fire;

so too, it is said that the reflections in water and images in mirrors truly possess specific characteristics, and are thus objects of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and cognizable by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Question: Just as an echo responds to a call, is that [the echo] real, or is it unreal?
If it were real, this sound would perish as soon as it is produced; once this has ceased, how could there be any further sound?
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
It is not real.
Question: For what reason is it not real? Answer:
A sound produced here perishes immediately; apart from this, how could there be any further sound?
The Abhidharmikas say: There truly exists a characteristic of the seed (bīja-lakṣaṇa), which is known by the sphere of sound (śabda-āyatana) and by the auditory consciousness (śrotra-vijñāna).
Question: Since this sound arises and immediately perishes, apart from this, how could there be any further sound? Answer:
My voice is produced through immeasurable varieties rather than a single kind; that is to say, sound is emitted through the mutual conditioning of the cheeks, jaws, gums, throat, tongue, and teeth.
Question: What is the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?
The answer is:
It refers to the mental consciousness of phenomena that has known, will know, or is currently knowing.
That which has been known belongs to the past; that which is to be known belongs to the future; and that which is currently being known belongs to the present.
Question: If all twelve bases (āyatana) are entirely the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), for what reason is only one base called the "base of phenomena" (dharmāyatana)? Answer:
Thus, although all twelve bases (*āyatana*) are the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is but one location for the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Likewise, although the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are the nature of phenomena, there is but one location for the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Although the ten knowledges are the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they have but one locus, which is the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna).
Although the seven factors of enlightenment are the nature of phenomena, they have but one locus, which is the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Although the six recollections are the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), they have but a single locus within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Although the four foundations of mindfulness are the nature of phenomena, they have but a single locus within the foundation of mindfulness regarding phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
Although the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) are the dharma-nature, there is but one place where the analytical knowledge of phenomena resides.
Although the four faiths (śraddhā) are the dharma-nature, there is but one place where the faith in the dharma resides.
Although the Three Jewels and the three refuges are the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is only one Jewel of Dharma and one locus for refuge in the Dharma.
Likewise, although the twelve bases (āyatana) are the nature of phenomena, there is only one base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Some say: The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) has one name, while the remaining spheres have two names.
The sphere of mental objects shares a common name, whereas the remaining spheres share both common and distinct names; thus, they are said to have distinct names.
Some say: That which is called the constant entry into those phenomena—neither different from birth and aging, nor subject to impermanence or destruction—is termed the extinction of nirvana.
Because that enters into the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it is therefore called the "one sphere of phenomena."
Some say: It refers to the perception of the seal of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), namely the three characteristics of the conditioned.
Since these enter into the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), it is therefore called the single sphere of phenomena.

Some say: that which refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)—namely, their manifestation, recitation, and study—is called "name" (*nāman*); since these are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is therefore said that there is one sphere of mental objects.
Some say: To regard the dharma of awakening as "dharma" and non-awakening as "self" is called the samādhi of emptiness.
Because one enters therein into the sphere of dharmas (dharmāyatana), it is therefore called the single sphere of dharmas.

Question: Since the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) also enters into the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)—insofar as one perceives a phenomenon as the self—why is the sphere of mental objects not established on the basis of the view of a self? Answer:
This is not the awakening to suchness that perceives the view of a self-body; rather, it is the awakening to suchness through the samādhi of emptiness.
This is called entering the Dharma by means of the samādhi of emptiness, not by means of the view of a self-body.
Some say: "This dharma can be apprehended, just as the place from which the wind comes is called 'wind-entry' (vāyu-āyatana).
In this same way, dharmas can be apprehended within the dharma-entry; therefore, it is called the 'dharma-entry'."
Some say: Because many dharmas can be apprehended, one speaks of a single *dharmāyatana*.

Within the *dharmāyatana*, there are many constituent dharmas, namely: material dharmas and non-material dharmas; visible dharmas and invisible dharmas; resistant dharmas and non-resistant dharmas; associated dharmas and dissociated dharmas; dharmas based on [the body] and dharmas not based on [the body]; active dharmas and inactive dharmas; bodily dharmas and non-bodily dharmas; dharmas with common objects and dharmas without common objects. This is what is meant by saying that because many dharmas can be apprehended, it is called a single *dharmāyatana*.
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, regarding the six internal bases (*āyatana*), the eye-base is mentioned first, followed by the others up to the mind-base.
Regarding the six external bases, the form-base is mentioned first, followed by the others up to the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*).
Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One, regarding the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), first speak of the eye base and lastly of the mind base;
and regarding the six external sense bases, first speak of the form base and lastly of the phenomena base?
Answer: Because his teaching is conformable.
Just as his teaching is conformable, so too should one savor the sequence accordingly.

Some say: Because the World-Honored One speaks in accordance with reality, and others likewise receive it in accordance with reality, the Buddha’s teaching is thus concordant, and their reception is likewise concordant. Others say:
Because of their relative coarseness and subtlety:
among the six internal bases (āyatana), which is the coarsest?
It is the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana).
Therefore, it was said before the Buddha:
"What is the most subtle?
It is the sense-base of mind (manāyatana)."
Therefore, the Buddha spoke of it last.
Among the six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*), which is the coarsest? It is the sense base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
Therefore, it was said before the Buddha:
"What is the most subtle?
It is the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana)."
For this reason, the Buddha spoke of them last.

Because they range from coarse to subtle, within his sūtras the Buddha first speaks of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) among the six bases, and subsequently speaks of them up to the mind-base (*mano-āyatana*).
Regarding the six external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), the *rūpāyatana* was explained first, followed by the others up to the *dharmāyatana*.
As the Buddha stated in his sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus!"
"Monks, this shore consists of the six internal sense bases. Monks,
the further shore consists of the six external sense bases."
Question: For what reason does the Buddha’s sūtra describe the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*) as this shore and the six external sense bases as the other shore? Answer:
Because of the principle of proximity and distance. Just as in a river, that which is near is this bank and that which is distant is the opposite bank, so it is with the mind:
the basis of the mental river is near, while the object-condition is distant; this is what is meant by the principle of proximity and distance.
Someone said: It is because of the principle of "downward" and "upward.
For example, regarding a river, the place where one descends is called this shore, and the place where one ascends is called the other shore.
In this way, the mind is the basis for mental factors, being "lower" in its support and "higher" in its object; thus it is called the "lower-and-higher dharma.
Alternatively, it is said:
"The other shore" refers to the ultimate truth of cessation, which is nirvāṇa.

Those comprise the external sense bases; for this reason, within the Buddha’s sūtras, the six internal sense bases are called "this shore" and the six external sense bases are called "the other shore. Question:
What is the river?
Answer: It refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Just as the number of sentient and non-sentient beings supported by the two banks of a river are carried away and flow into the great ocean.
In this way, sentient beings, carried away by the river of mind and mental factors—which flows along the banks of the internal and external sense bases—enter the ocean of birth and death.
Question: What is the boat?
Answer: It is the Noble Path.
Just as by relying on a boat or raft, immeasurable sentient beings are able to cross the river.
In this way, relying upon the raft of the Noble Path, immeasurable sentient beings cross over the river of birth and death.
As the Buddha’s sūtra says:
"One should know that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are internal; one should know that the six spheres of contact (ṣaṭsparśāyatana) are internal."
Question: One should also understand these external factors in this way.
For what reason did the Blessed One say that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) should be understood as internal, and that the six contacts (*ṣaṭsparśa*) should be understood as internal?
The answer is:
In the sūtras, the Blessed One taught internal contemplation.
The Blessed One said:

Regarding the internal sense bases and faculties, let the mind not turn outward; first, internally, one contemplates the body within the body, and subsequently, externally and both internally and externally.
This is because it is the preliminary internal contemplation.
Someone said:
"Because the World-Honored One teaches his disciples to contemplate without inversion.
The World-Honored One said:
Do not view things through the inversion of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self;
rather, you should contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as causes, accumulations, roots, and conditions, and destroy existence by means of the Noble Eightfold Path.
This is called observing without inversion.
Alternatively, it is said:
because the World-Honored One teaches his disciples a unique method of observation.
The World-Honored One said:
"Do not contemplate [the aggregates] as coarse or harsh.
You should contemplate them as a disease, an ulcer, an arrow, and a snake; as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; and as the burning fire of the six internal sense-bases."
This is because it is not a shared contemplation.
Alternatively, it is said:
the Buddha’s sūtras speak of internal *smṛtyupasthāna*.
Question: For what reason does the Buddha teach internal mindfulness of the mind (adhyātma-cittasmṛtyupasthāna)? Answer:
For the sake of the self, one conceives of a self, thinking, "This is mine," "I am this," and "I act.
Once there is attachment to the self, there are the requisites for attachment; because one seeks to nourish the internal [self], one seeks external requisites.
For this reason, the Buddha’s sūtra says:
"The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) should be known as internal; the six bases of contact (ṣaṭ sparśāyatanāni) should be known as internal. Question:
What is the distinction between the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*)?
One explanation is that there is no distinction.

The six bases are the eye base, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases; the six bases of contact are likewise the eye base, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. Therefore, there is no distinction.
Furthermore, there are those who say there is a distinction:
that which is "near" refers to the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), while that which is "far" refers to the six spheres of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*). Question:
As you have stated, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are present, while the six contacts (*ṣaṭsparśa*) pertain to the past and future.
Furthermore, there are others who say that what is proximate refers to the six contacts, while what is remote refers to the six sense bases.
Question: As you have stated, the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatana*) are present, whereas the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) are past and future.
Or it is said:
This means that when one practices, these become the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatana*), while the remainder are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Alternatively, it is said:
practicing in dependence upon the six sense bases constitutes the six sense bases; practicing in dependence upon the six bases of contact constitutes the six bases of contact.
Some say: "That which exists is the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatana*); that which remains is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
As it is said:
The bowl of a bhikṣu is by its very nature a bowl; just as it is used for the affairs of a bhikṣu, it is therefore called "the bhikṣu’s bowl.
In the same way, whatever constitutes the six bases of contact (ṣaḍ-āyatana), that which remains is the six sense-bases (ṣaḍ-āyatana).
The Venerable Dharanandin said:
"The 'entry of nature' refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the 'entry of activity' refers to the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*).
It is like the expression 'iron-butter bowl': the nature is the iron bowl, yet because it is used for butter, it is called an 'iron-butter bowl.'"
In this way, the "entrance of nature" refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and the "entrance of activity" refers to the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭsparśāyatana*).
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:
there are two entrances—the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Question: For what reason does the Buddha’s sūtra speak of two bases:
the non-percipient beings and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
The answer is:
The other stages have two types of names: first, "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*), and second, "dwellings of sentient beings" (*sattvāvāsa*).

One intends to apply these two names to the [first] two [stages]; that is to say, although these possess the name "dwellings of sentient beings," they lack the name "abodes of consciousness. These are what are called the two names.
Therefore, the Buddha’s sūtra says:
"There are two [realms of] entry: the non-percipient beings and the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Someone says:

After the Buddha has established the designations of the "abodes of beings" (*sattvāvāsa*) and the "stations of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*) in his sūtras, there are those abodes of beings that are not included among the stations of consciousness; these he establishes as two bases (*āyatana*): the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Some say: It is because of their long life span.

Among all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there is no place where the life span is as long as that of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*); among all places, there is none where the life span is as long as that of the Heaven of Neither-Conception-nor-Non-conception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). This is what is meant by "long life."
Therefore, the Buddha’s sūtra states:
"There are two [realms of] entry: the non-percipient beings and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Someone says:
In order to sever the intention of those of other schools—
who conceive the notion of liberation within the two bases—
the Blessed One said:
This is an entry into birth and death, not liberation.
This is called severing the intentions of those of other schools.
Therefore, the Buddha’s sūtra says:
The two entrances:
the non-percipient beings and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Some say:
Because of practicing the Dharma,
the heterodox teachers conceive that within the two bases, the mind is liberated through non-practice.
The Blessed One said:
Furthermore, within this, one proceeds through the various elements, destinies, and births, revolving in the cycle of birth and death;
this is called the dharma of formations.
Therefore, the Buddha’s sūtra says:
The two entrances are the non-percipient beings and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Some say: because they are subject to the dharma of regression.
The heterodox teachers reckon that within the two bases, the mind does not regress from liberation.
The World-Honored One said:
"In this regard, one may still regress through the various realms, destinies, and births, revolving within the cycle of birth and death."
This is called the dharma of retrogression.
Therefore, the Buddha’s sūtra says:
"The non-percipient beings and the gods of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
In this sutra of the Buddha,
the Venerable Śāriputra, having approached the World-Honored One, spoke as follows:
"World-Honored One!"
This is the unsurpassed matter, namely, the entry established by the Blessed One.

For that, O Blessed One, there is no further knowledge and no further discrimination; there is no other unsurpassed knowledge, namely any other knowledge of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or those who have attained equal enlightenment.
Question: "All that" refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Since the Venerable Śāriputra was not omniscient nor possessed of all-seeing vision, how did he know that "all that" refers to the twelve bases?
Answer: It is known from the teaching of the "without remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa).

As the Buddha’s sūtra states, after explaining the eleven bases (āyatana), he then explains the base of phenomena (dharmāyatana). The Venerable Śāriputra understood with certainty that regarding all dharmas not yet explained or manifested, they should all be known to be included within the bases.
Some say: "It is already known through observation by means of the wisdom of sublime vows. Others say:
They are known by their characteristics.
As the Buddha stated in a sutra:
"All those things refer to the twelve bases (āyatana)."
The Venerable Śāriputra has attained indestructible faith; he possesses even greater faith in what the Blessed One has taught, and for this reason, he knows all those twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This is called knowing through signs. Question:
Why is it that the Venerable Śāriputra’s knowledge through signs is not considered direct perception?
Answer: He knows through direct perception and he also knows through inference.
Venerable Śāriputra also knows all dharmas by means of the twelve bases (āyatana).
Question: If the Venerable Śāriputra also knows all dharmas by means of the twelve bases (āyatana), what is the difference between the Buddha and Śāriputra?
The answer is:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows all and knows everything; although the Venerable Śāriputra knows all, he cannot know everything.
Or it is said:
The Venerable Śāriputra knows all phenomena by means of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as a whole, rather than through their individual characteristics.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and also knows the infinite internal bases within each individual characteristic.
This refers to how the Venerable Śāriputra received this sūtra from another, as spoken by the Blessed One.
With what words did Śāriputra proclaim this excellence?
He uttered a resolute lion’s roar, saying: "There is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in the world who is equal to the Blessed One, the Fully Awakened One, let alone one who surpasses him."
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received and upheld it exactly as the Tathāgata has spoken it, Ānanda!"
It is impossible; it cannot be that two Tathāgatas appear in the world simultaneously, one after the other—there is no such possibility.
[The interlocutor] asks:
How does the World-Honored One, for the sake of those to be transformed, speak of the elements (dhātu)?
What is entry (*āyatana*)?
The answer is:

In the teaching of the World-Honored One, "lack of wisdom regarding all phenomena" or "lack of wisdom regarding some phenomena" refers to the teaching of the elements (*dhātu*). "Lack of wisdom regarding some phenomena" refers to the teaching of the bases (*āyatana*).

Some say: In the World-Honored One’s teaching and transformation, there are those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties; for those of sharp faculties he teaches the *āyatana*, while for those of dull faculties he teaches the *dhātu*.

Some say: In the World-Honored One’s teaching and transformation, there is either the power of great causes or the power of manifold conditions. For those with the power of great causes, he teaches the "entrances" (*āyatana*); for those with the power of manifold conditions, he teaches the "elements" (*dhātu*).

Some say: In the World-Honored One’s teaching, there are cases where internal power predominates and cases where external power predominates; for those in whom internal power predominates, he teaches the *āyatana* (entrances), and for those in whom external power predominates, he teaches the *dhātu* (elements).

Some say: When the World-Honored One teaches, for those who internally contemplate the nourishment of the body, he explains "entry" (āyatana); for those who have heard it from another, he explains "elements" (dhātu).

Some say: In the World-Honored One’s teaching, there are those who understand through initial opening and those who understand through analytical discernment; for those who understand through initial opening, he teaches the *āyatana* (entrances), and for those who understand through analytical discernment, he teaches the *dhātu* (elements).
Some say: "For those who are deluded regarding the *dhātus*, one teaches the *dhātus*; for those who are deluded regarding the *āyatanas*, one teaches the *āyatanas*. Others say:
For those who are attached to their own nature (*dhātu*), the Blessed One teaches the *dhātus*; the meaning of "nature" is the meaning of *dhātu*.
For those who are attached to material wealth, he teaches the *āyatanas*; the meaning of "gate of entry" (*āya-mukha*) is the meaning of *āyatana*.
Thus, the Blessed One teaches the *dhātus* for the sake of such training, and likewise teaches the *āyatanas* for the sake of such training.
The detailed exposition of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is complete. 19.

The Vibhāṣā on the Section on the Five Aggregates (*skandha*). The nineteenth section on the five aggregates consists of: the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Question: What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)? Answer:
The Buddha’s sūtra says:
"What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever forms there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all of them are not-self, I am not they, and they are not mine."
Thus, observing with wisdom according to reality, this is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"What is the aggregate of form?"
Whatever forms there are, all of them consist of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
As it is said in the Abhidharma:
"What is the aggregate of form?"
The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and all forms contained within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Question:
What is the distinction between these three types of explanations?
Answer: In each of the three types of proclamations, the intention is severed individually. Question:
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever forms there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all those are not-self, I am not they, and they are not mine."
Thus, one observes according to reality with wisdom.
What is it that is abandoned therein?
The answer is:
At that time, the heterodox teacher Lohitya Śikhin wished to render the past and future non-existent.
To sever his intention, the Sūtra says:
"What is the aggregate of form?"
Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; whether internal or external—one contemplates it with wisdom according to reality in this manner.
Question: As it has been said:
What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever forms there are, all of them consist of the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
In this regard, what is the intended meaning of "abandoning"?
Answer: Because one contemplates the future.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke this sūtra:
The Omniscient One, who has well awakened to and clearly seen the past, future, and present, declared:

"After my parinirvāṇa, in a future age, there will certainly be those who claim that apart from the four great elements, there is no such thing as derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) which should be produced."
In order to sever that misconception, the Sūtra says:
"What is the aggregate of form?
Whatever forms there are, all of them are the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements."
Question: As it has been stated:
"What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)?"
The ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*) and all other forms (*rūpa*) are contained within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding this, what is the intended meaning of the term "cessation" (*prahāṇa*)? The answer is:
At that time, there was the Venerable Dharmatrāta, who maintained that among the dharmāyatana, one should not allow the existence of matter (rūpa).
He was asked:
"For what reason, Venerable Dharmatrāta, do you maintain that among the dharmāyatana, one should not allow the existence of matter?"
The answer is:

That which is spoken of as "form" refers to that which is the cause of the five groups of consciousness and that which is the object-condition for the five groups of consciousness; this is called form.

That which exists within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is not the cause of the five groups of consciousness, nor is it the object-condition for the five groups of consciousness; therefore, it is not form.
In order to sever that [wrong] view, he speaks of enumeration.
What is the aggregate of form?
It consists of the ten bases of form and all forms contained within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Question: If that is so, how are the words spoken by the Venerable Dharmatrāta to be reconciled? He said:
That is to say, form is that which has the five groups of consciousness as its cause and the five groups of consciousness as its condition; this is called form.

That form which exists within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) does not have the five groups of consciousness as its cause, nor does it have the five groups of consciousness as its condition.
Answer: It can be said that it is not the cause of the five groups of consciousness, but is the object-condition for the six groups of consciousness.

That which is form within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), although not the cause of the five groups of consciousness, is also not the object-condition for the five groups of consciousness; it is only the cause of the group of mental consciousness and the object-condition for the group of mental consciousness.

Some say: Although that [object] is a form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is neither the cause of the fivefold body of consciousness nor the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for the fivefold body of consciousness; rather, it is merely its causal support and its objective support.
Question: What is that basis? Answer:
These are the four great elements. Question:
What is the aggregate of sensation?
Answer: The Buddha’s sūtra asks:
"What is the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha)?"
Sixth, bodily pain.
This is as taught in the Sūtras, and the Abhidharma is likewise. Question:
What is the aggregate of perception?
The answer is:
as stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:
What is the aggregate of perception?
It is the six groups of perception.
This is as stated in the Sūtras, and so it is in the Abhidharma as well.
Question: What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)? Answer:
The Buddha’s sūtra states:
"What is the aggregate of formations?
It is the six groups of volition."
The Abhidharma says:
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)? It replies:

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is of two kinds: first, those associated with the mind (*citta-saṃprayukta*), and second, those dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta*). Question:
What are the formations associated with the mind?

Answer: Feeling, perception, volition, contact, mindfulness, desire, liberation, attention, concentration, wisdom, wholesome roots, unwholesome roots, indeterminate roots, fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, afflictions, entanglements, the known, the seen, and the observed—all such mental concomitants associated with the mind are called the aggregate of formations associated with the mind.
Question: What is the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*)? Answer:

Acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), genus (*nikāyasabhāga*), acquisition of a location (*sthānaprāpti*), acquisition of a lineage (*gotraprāpti*), acquisition of an entrance (*āyatanaprāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), death (*maraṇa*), impermanence (*anityatā*), and the group of names (*nāmakāya*), the group of phrases (*padakāya*), and the group of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*): all such formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) are called the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*).

Question: Why does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, establish the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) based on a single volition (*cetanā*) among all the formations that are associated or dissociated [with consciousness]? Answer:

This volition (cetanā) gathers the seeds at the time of the manifestation of formations (saṃskāra); therefore, among all the conditioned factors (saṃskāraskandha), whether associated or dissociated, the Buddha established a single volition as the saṃskāraskandha.

Just as craving (tṛṣṇā) gathers the seeds at the time of the manifestation of accumulation (upādāna), the Buddha established a single craving among all contaminated seeds as the truth of accumulation (samudayasatya).

Thus, when this volition (cetanā) manifests as formations (saṃskāra), it encompasses all seeds; for this reason, among all the associated and dissociated aggregates of formations (saṃskāraskandha), the Buddha established volition alone as the aggregate of formations.
Question: What is the aggregate of consciousness? Answer:
The Buddha’s sūtra states:
"What is the aggregate of consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness."
This is as stated in the Sūtras; the Abhidharma is likewise.
This is the inherent nature of the body characterized by the seeds already planted within the aggregates (*skandha*).
Having explained nature (*svabhāva*), one should now explain activity (*saṃskāra*).
For what reason are the aggregates (skandha) taught?
What is the meaning of "aggregate"?
The answer is:

The meaning of "aggregation" (*rāśi*) is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*); it means a "mass," an "accumulation," a "collection," and a "conglomeration. It is the conventional designation of an aggregate and the conventional designation of a heap;

the meaning of "multitude" is the meaning of "aggregate. Regarding the statement that the meaning of aggregation is the meaning of aggregate: whatever form (*rūpa*) there is—whether past, future, or present—all of it, having been unified as one, is established as the "form aggregate" (*rūpaskandha*). This continues in the same way up to the "consciousness aggregate" (*vijñānaskandha*). This is called the meaning of aggregation being the meaning of aggregate.

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'mass' (*rāśi*) is the meaning of 'aggregate' (*skandha*"): when immeasurable conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) varieties have been gathered together, they are established as the five aggregates; this is what is meant by "the meaning of mass is the meaning of aggregate.

Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'accumulation' (*caya*) is the meaning of 'aggregate': just as there is an accumulation of dung or various kinds of accumulations, so too the aggregates are various kinds of accumulations."

Regarding the meaning of "investigation" as the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*): whatever form (*rūpa*) there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all of that, having been investigated as a single unit, is established as the aggregate of form. This applies likewise up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is called the meaning of investigation being the meaning of an aggregate.

Regarding the designation of the world (*loka-prajñapti*) and the designation of the aggregates (*skandha-prajñapti*): it means that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) belongs to the three times, and likewise the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) also belongs to the three times; this is the designation of the world and the designation of the aggregates.
As for the meaning of "multitude" (*bahutva*) being the sense of "aggregate": it means that the aggregate of form is a multitude, and likewise the aggregate of consciousness is also a multitude.
Question: As you have stated, a single atom (paramāṇu) should not possess the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), because it lacks plurality.
Answer: [As follows:]
It cannot be designated by means of a single atom;
if it were so designated, it would be designated as a manifold accumulation.

As for the Abhidharma, if one maintains the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*), they say that an atom is subsumed under one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and a portion of one aggregate.
If one does not maintain [the conventional], they speak of the atom as a single element (*dhātu*), a single base (*āyatana*), and a single aggregate (*skandha*).
It is like a person who takes a single grain from a great heap of grain; if someone asks, "What has this person taken? [one would say, "A grain," though it is part of a larger whole].
