It is like two people standing on a riverbank when someone is being swept away and drowned in the river.
Although that first person intended to rescue him, he lacked the strength and could only grasp his hand and stand there.
That second person, however, possessed both the intention and the strength to rescue that man and place him in a state of safety.
Just as that first person who, having seen [the suffering], stands with palms joined yet lacks the power [to help], so too is compassion (*karuṇā*).
Just as that second person who possesses both the intention and the power to rescue that person and establish them in a state of security, so too is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The Venerable Dharmatrāta said: "Venerable ones! The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses great compassion;

from time immemorial, he has encompassed all through the *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality spheres), beginning with the most subtle. How could any sentient beings, whether ordinary people or *śrāvakas*, be able to extend their compassion as far as the sentient beings of the form and formless realms?"
Question: For what reason is great compassion (mahākaruṇā) taught? Answer:
Because one attains this through great sacrifice, it is called "Great Compassion.

It is not like the path of the Śrāvaka, which relies on a single act of giving for the sake of a single person, nor is it like the path of the Pratyekabuddha, which relies on the gift of a single willow twig or a handful of offerings; rather, it is attained only after one has given away all things that are most exquisite and most beloved, setting aside nothing that is not one's own.
This is called "Great Compassion" because the great merchant has attained [this name].
Alternatively, it is said that he is called "Great Compassion" because he has produced a great body.
It is not like the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, where the body cannot be fully attained.

Rather, that Great Being’s body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his skin is the color of purple-polished gold, and he has a halo extending one fathom. His Brahma-voice is as exquisite as that of the kalaviṅka bird, and one never tires of beholding him. Because he thus gives birth to a "Great Body," he is called "Great Compassion."
Some say: It is called "Great Compassion" because it is attained through great skillful means.

It is not like the path of the Śrāvakas, which consists of one type, two maturations, and three liberations; nor is it like the Venerable Śāriputra, who increased his wisdom over sixty kalpas; nor is it like the Pratyekabuddhas, who increased their wisdom over a hundred kalpas. Rather, it can only be attained after fulfilling three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas of practicing immeasurable asceticism. Because it is attainable by seeking through such great skillful means, it is called Great Compassion.
Some say: It is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā) because it brings about the utmost benefit for sentient beings.

Thus, whether sentient beings aspire to seek the path of a Buddha, the path of a Pratyekabuddha, or the path of a Śrāvaka; or wish to attain great wealth, be born into a noble and wealthy family with handsome features, or be reborn among gods and humans—all of these arise from great compassion.
This is called "great compassion" because it concerns a vast multitude of sentient beings.
Alternatively, it is said that it is called "great compassion" because it is able to rescue and deliver those sentient beings who have fallen into the great pit.

Just as the Buddha perceives sentient beings fallen into the five destinies and delivers them, establishing them securely in the fruits of the Path—all of this is due to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Because he is able to pull out and rescue those sentient beings who have fallen into the great ditch, it is called "great compassion."
Some say: It is called "Great Compassion" because it can move Mount Mahāpālaka.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not share the same dwelling place as those in the four dhyāna stages; this is called Mahāpālaka.

This means that when the Buddha’s protection is present before them, at that time all sentient beings in the hells, the hungry ghost realm, and the animal realm are ablaze, like a grove of burning sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, hemp, and forests.

The Buddha’s mind was unshakable in that state; yet, once Great Compassion manifested before him, the power of the Buddha’s body—though extremely firm and solid—was moved by Great Compassion, like a wind blowing through a plantain tree. This is what is meant by "that which can move" the Great Protection Mountain, namely, Great Compassion.
Some say: Because a Great Being is able to enter into the midst of interrogation and flogging, he is called "Great Compassion.

For example, the Buddha manifested in the form of a Malla wrestler, or the form of a potter, or the form of a beggar, or the form of a courtesan, and with his own hand led Nanda into the five realms of existence.
For the sake of Aṅgulimāla, he turned the ground in front wide and turned the ground behind wide.
The Buddha remained constantly in meditative concentration without distraction; from his mouth he extended a broad and long tongue, covering his own face.
Perfectly accomplished in a sense of shame and remorse, he manifested the male organ concealed within a sheath for the sake of women.

Renouncing the bliss of sublime dhyāna and forsaking the most excellent Buddha-dharma, he traversed hundreds of thousands of billions of Iron Ring Mountains and Great Iron Ring Mountains to reach lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; all this was due solely to his great compassion.
This is called the Great Being’s ability to enter into great torment, which is termed "Great Compassion.
As stated in the Vinaya of the World-Honored One:
the World-Honored One, having fulfilled his compassion for sentient beings, then preached the Dharma.
Question: It is said that the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma for the sake of fulfilling his compassion toward sentient beings.
Do those sentient beings obtain happiness?
"Is it not possible to bring happiness?

If sentient beings can obtain happiness, why do you not use your loving-kindness to fill all the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and humans, and thereby preach the Dharma for them?"
If those sentient beings do not obtain pleasure, how is this verse to be reconciled?
"Just as when a hungry ghost harbors evil thoughts in its mind, And approaches a person,
though it neither touches nor harms them, It can cause them to experience pain and fear."
"If even that ghost, when it conceives an evil thought, can bring about an evil result, how much more so for the Buddha, who, when he conceives a virtuous thought,
cannot fail to bring about a virtuous result? Having made this argument, he said:
The World-Honored One, with a mind of compassion fulfilled for sentient beings, preaches the Dharma for them, and those sentient beings obtain happiness.
A question is asked:
"If they obtain happiness, why does he not preach the Dharma by filling all the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and humans with compassion?"
The answer is:
The World-Honored One observes whether the conduct of sentient beings is evolving or not.
Seeing that sentient beings engage in evolving conduct, he preaches the Dharma for them so that their compassion may be fulfilled.
This means that sentient beings engage in non-turning conduct and do not listen to the Dharma for the sake of fulfilling loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Furthermore, it is said that if the World-Honored One were to teach the Dharma to sentient beings solely for the sake of fulfilling loving-kindness, those sentient beings would not attain happiness.
Question: If sentient beings do not obtain happiness, how can this verse be reconciled?
"Just as when a hungry ghost harbors evil thoughts in its mind, If it goes and possesses a human being..."
"Without touching and without harming, it can cause pain and fear to arise. He replied:

"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is filled with immeasurable kinds of loving-kindness; he does so either through supernormal power, or by manifesting objects of affection, or by knowing [their] pleasure, or through excellent smoothness, or through his cool shadow."
Regarding those who possess supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), it is as has been said:

The World-Honored One, during his final journey through the world, arrived at the Jambū Grove Monastery in the country of Pāvā. When the people of Pāvā heard that the World-Honored One was traveling through the world and had reached this Jambū Grove Monastery in Pāvā, they [responded].
When the people of Pāvā heard this, they gathered in one place and established a covenant together:
"We shall all go to see the World-Honored One.
If anyone does not go, they shall be fined five hundred old gold coins."
Having made such a resolution, they all went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the minister Lūśa, who harbored no faith or reverence toward the World-Honored One, also went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, Ānanda saw the minister Liuzhi approaching from afar; having seen him, he said:
"Welcome! Excellent, excellent!"
"Levaka! You have been able to come and see the World-Honored One.
This World-Honored One is endowed with the unsurpassed field of merit; before long, he will be destroyed by impermanence."
The minister Lohicca said:
"Ānanda! It was not for the purpose of seeing the śramaṇa Gautama that I came; it was only because I did not wish to violate my promise to my kinsmen."
The Venerable Ānanda said to Liuzhi:
"What essential command did your kinsmen not violate?
The minister Liuzhi replied:
"Venerable Ānanda!
Our kinsmen have gathered in one place and made a solemn agreement:
'We shall all go together to see the World-Honored One.'"
"If you do not go, you shall be fined five hundred old gold coins.
Venerable Ānanda!
I would rather pay five hundred old gold coins than come to see the śramaṇa Gautama."
However, I thought to myself:
"Let there be no dispute among my kinsmen.
Thereupon, Venerable Ānanda took hold of the arm of the minister Lohitaka and led him to where the Blessed One was; having arrived, he addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"O World-Honored One!
This minister, Liuzhi, was formerly a close relative of mine;

however, he has no faith or reverence for the World-Honored One. I only pray that the World-Honored One will skillfully preach the Dharma for him, so that he may develop faith and reverence toward the World-Honored One and give rise to joy."
The mind and conduct of that Vatsa were attached and his will was distracted and unstable; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, never preach the Dharma for those whose minds are distracted.
At that time, not far from his dwelling place, the World-Honored One manifested the Hell of Boiling Excrement, immeasurable in depth and breadth, and caused [Vatsa] to cry out:
"There is a great minister named Vatsa who lacks faith and reverence toward the World-Honored One; after his life ends, he shall be reborn within this [hell]."
When the minister Liuzhi saw the great hells and heard their sounds, he was struck with fear and developed a sense of revulsion.
Knowing that he had become fearful and disillusioned, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught him the most sublime Dharma in accordance with his disposition.
Having heard the Dharma, the minister Liuzhi attained the Dharma-eye, which is free from dust and devoid of defilement regarding all phenomena.
This Buddha, with great compassion, fulfilled the minister Liuzhi.
He then asked:
How is it said that loving-kindness is fulfilled?
The answer is:
it is those supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda).
Furthermore, there was also the case of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), as it has been told:
Devadatta incited King Ajātaśatru, saying, "There is an elephant named Dhanapālaka; intoxicate him with clear liquor and release him to charge at and harm the World-Honored One."
At that time, the elephant saw the World-Honored One from afar and rushed toward him.

When the World-Honored One saw the elephant approaching from a distance, he manifested an exceedingly high wall on his left and right sides; behind him, he manifested a vast chasm hundreds of thousands of *zhang* deep; above, he manifested a massive mountain descending with the roar of thunder; and in front, he manifested five great lions.

When that elephant saw the five great lions, it was seized with extreme terror. Looking to its left and right, it saw immense walls; looking back, it saw a vast chasm hundreds of thousands of fathoms deep; and looking upward, it saw a great mountain of fire descending with the sound of thunder. Having seen this, it conceived the thought that all the fires of the world were burning.
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, saw that the elephant was greatly terrified, he withdrew the five great lions.
Having withdrawn the five great lions, he saw only the cool and refreshing radiance beneath the Buddha’s feet.
Having seen him, he went to where the World-Honored One was; upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, pressing his trunk against the World-Honored One’s feet.

At that time, the World-Honored One was adorned with all the marks [of a Great Man], his purple-golden complexion perfected by five thousand merits. The World-Honored One stroked the elephant’s head with his right hand; once the elephant’s head had been stroked, its intoxication was immediately dispelled.
Once his intoxication had subsided, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for him:
"Do not harm the Great Naga; The appearance of a Naga in the world is rare.
Do not harm the Great Naga; Otherwise, you shall never be born in a good realm."
One who strikes those who should not be struck, and gives rise to anger where there was no anger,
shall receive a tenfold retribution and swiftly be reborn there;
they shall endure extreme suffering and their bodies shall likewise be destroyed.
When one encounters severe illness, the mind becomes disordered and the will distressed by evil;
or when beset by calamities and misfortunes, one is slandered by others;
or when separated from kinsmen, wealth and property are utterly lost.
"All that belongs to one's dwelling shall be consumed by fire;
when the body perishes without wisdom, one shall be born in the midst of hell.
Having heard this verse, tears fell from the elephant’s eyes.
The Buddha manifested the voice of an elephant and preached the Dharma; having heard the Buddha’s teaching, that elephant’s life ended and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thus, for the sake of the elephant, the Buddha’s compassion was fulfilled.
Question: How is loving-kindness fulfilled in this context? Answer:
That very supernormal power (ṛddhi) is what is called "supernormal power.
Regarding the manifestation of conditions through craving, it is as has been said:
A brahmin had a son who was guarding a rice field when a great torrential rain fell, and he was killed by hailstones, while the rice field was also destroyed.
Because he had lost both [his wealth and his son], that brahmin’s mind became deranged and he went mad, running about naked as far as the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden in Śrāvastī.
That brahmin was one who should have been converted by the Buddha; however, when the World-Honored One saw the brahmin approaching from afar, he perceived this thought:
"At this time, even if Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to preach the Dharma for him, they could not cause him to cross over."
At that time, not far from him, the World-Honored One manifested a rice field and a son.
Upon seeing these two, the brahmin regained his original state of mind and thought to himself:
"These are my son and my rice field, which have caused me constant grief and anxiety."
Having seen him, he went to where the World-Honored One was; upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit to one side.
Possessing faith and reverence for the World-Honored One and harboring joy within, the World-Honored One, in accordance with his disposition, preached the sublime Dharma to him.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, that brahmin was freed from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him.
This Buddha brought fulfillment through his compassion for the brahmin. He asked:
In this context, what is the fulfillment of loving-kindness?
The answer is:
it consists precisely in that present condition of affection.
Furthermore, regarding the condition of craving for what is presently manifest, it is as described:
the brahmin Vāseṭṭha had six sons who died; grieving for his children, his mind became deranged and he went mad, running about naked until he reached the Anāthapiṇḍika Park in Śrāvastī.
That female brahmin was destined to be converted by the Buddha. Seeing the female brahmin approaching from afar, the World-Honored One perceived her and thought:
"At this moment, even if Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to preach the Dharma for her, they would not be able to bring her across."
At that time, not far from him, the World-Honored One manifested six sons. When the female brahmin saw the six sons, she regained her original state of mind and thought:
"These are my sons; they have caused me constant grief and affliction."
Feeling shame and remorse, he knelt down and sat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda: "Ānanda!"
He took the *uttarāsaṅga* and gave it to that brahmin woman.
"So be it, Blessed One! [she replied].
Having received the instruction of the Blessed One, the Venerable Ānanda took his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) and gave it to the female brahmin.
The female brahmin took the Venerable Ānanda’s upper robe, put it on, and went to where the Blessed One was.
Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One; having prostrated, he withdrew to stand to one side.
Possessing faith and reverence for the World-Honored One and harboring joy within, the World-Honored One, in accordance with his disposition, preached the sublime Dharma to him.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the female brahmin attained the Dharma-eye, which is free from dust and stainless.
Because the Buddha had thus fulfilled his compassion for this female brahmin,
it was asked:
In this context, what is the fulfillment of loving-kindness?
The answer is:
it is precisely that which manifests as the object of affection.
This is called the present condition of craving.
As for the medicine of present knowledge, it is as described:
the laywoman Mahāprajāpatī invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide them with medical supplies.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who had fallen ill and was taking medicine; the physician instructed him that he should take meat broth.
That sick bhikṣu said to his attendant:
"Venerable one!"
"Tell the upāsikā Mahāśāla:
'A certain bhikṣu is ill and is taking medicine; he requires meat broth.
Then the attendant bhikṣu went to where the upāsikā Mahāśāla was, and having arrived, he said to the upāsikā Mahāśāla:"
"Sister, you should know that a certain bhikṣu has fallen ill and is taking medicine; he requires meat broth.
That upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī said to her messenger:
'Take these goods and go buy some meat to give to that bhikṣu.'"
The man sent with goods went and searched throughout the city of Vārāṇasī for meat, but was unable to obtain any.
It is said that King Brahmadatta had given birth to a son, and he had issued a decree throughout the city that no living beings were to be killed.
That messenger returned to Mahāprajāpatī Upāsikā, and upon arrival, he said to her:
"Madam, you should know that although we have searched throughout the entire city, meat cannot be found."
The upāsikā Mahāśī gave rise to this thought:
"This is a calamity.
If the bhikṣu falls ill and takes medicine, yet fails to obtain meat, he may well pass away."
He then took a sharp knife, entered the house, cut the soft flesh from his own body, and gave it to the servant, saying:
"You, servant, cook this yourself and give it to that bhikṣu.
The servant, as instructed, took it and gave it to the bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu did not know [what it was], yet he took it and gave it to the sick bhikṣu.
That sick bhikṣu also did not know [what it was], yet he consumed it, and his illness was cured.
The upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī suffered from bodily pain.
At that time, the husband of the upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī had gone out on some business and was away.
When the husband of the upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī returned, he asked his wife:
"Where is Mahāprajāpatī now?"
The palace attendants replied,
"O Great Lady!
Mahākāla has been suffering from extreme pain within his chamber."
At that time, having heard this, Mahāsenapati became extremely incensed and devoid of any sense of respect, saying:
"If the giver does not know [the recipient], does the recipient also not know?"
"I shall go before the Buddha and debate with him.
Thereupon, Mahāśāṭha went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands who were listening to his teaching; having seen this, Mahāśāṭha thought to himself:
"I shall not discuss this now.
Tomorrow, when I have requested the World-Honored One to assemble the community, then we shall discuss it.
Having formed this thought, he proceeded to where the World-Honored One was.
Having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One; having prostrated, they withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the Blessed One, for the sake of Mahāsenāpati, taught the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting him, inspiring him, and gladdening him.
He taught the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting them with equal exhortation and gladdening them with equal gladdening, and then remained silent.
At that time, Mahāsenāpati rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the World-Honored One, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O World-Honored One!"
He prepared a modest assembly and requested, "May the World-Honored One and the Saṃgha, out of compassion, accept this.
The World-Honored One accepted Mahāsena’s invitation by remaining silent.
Thereupon, Mahāsenapati, knowing that the World-Honored One had consented by remaining silent, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him, and returned to his own quarters.
Having arrived, he prepared various delicacies that very night, arranging many kinds of pure and exquisite offerings; when they were ready, he announced that the time had come.
At that time, the World-Honored One dressed in the morning and, surrounded by the bhikṣus who followed before and behind him, went to the house of Mahāprajāpatī.
Having arrived, he took his seat; knowing [the situation], the World-Honored One asked the women of the household:
"Where is the upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī now?"
The palace attendants said, "Indeed, World-Honored One!
Mahāprajāpatī the Upāsikā has ceased coming and going; she is suffering from extreme pain within her chamber."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, understood internal dependent origination, and he understood external dependent origination in the same way.

Thereupon, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, the World-Honored One arrived at Mount Himavat, took the medicinal herbs, and returned; having brought them, he applied them to the wound.
Having applied it to the wound, he said to the husband of the upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī:
"Call the upāsikā Mahāprajāpatī; the World-Honored One calls for you.
"Very well, World-Honored One," [he replied].
Having received the instruction from the World-Honored One, Mahākaśyapa went to where Mahākaśyapa was; having arrived, he said to Mahākaśyapa, "The World-Honored One calls for you.
Upon hearing that the World-Honored One called him, his ulcer immediately healed and became the same color as the rest of his skin.

Having heard this, his faith and reverence for the Blessed One increased manifold; filled with inner joy, he went to where the Blessed One was, and upon arrival, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

The World-Honored One, in accordance with their needs, preached the sublime Dharma; having heard this teaching, the laywoman Mahāprajāpatī and her retinue attained the Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena.
The Blessed One, out of his compassion for the laywoman Mahāprajāpatī,
asked: "In this context,
what is meant by 'the fulfillment of loving-kindness'?"
The answer is:
it is that very medicine of wisdom.
Furthermore, as for the medicine of wisdom, it is as has been said:
At that time, the foolish King Virūḍhaka destroyed the city of Kapilavastu and took six of the most exquisite Śākya maidens; standing upon the upper terrace, he boasted to himself:
"I have been able to destroy your kinsmen, leaving none remaining."
The Śākya woman replied:
"The King possesses the merit of past lives.
My kinsmen have realized the Truth and are all noble ones (ārya), yet the King should not have come here with his life intact."
That king thought to himself:
"It is precisely because of this that she dares to speak out against me.
Having abandoned all compassion for the future life, the king cut off the hands and feet of that Śākya woman and cast her into a ditch.

All those women of the Śākya clan were destined for the Buddha’s transformation; thus, for the sake of teaching and transforming them, the World-Honored One went to that place and saw that they were beset by immeasurable suffering and affliction.
Having seen this, he thought:

"If these six Śākya daughters were to have the Dharma preached to them by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges at this very time, they would still be unable to undergo transformation because of their current suffering."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, understood internal dependent origination, and he likewise understood external dependent origination.

Thereupon, in the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm, the World-Honored One arrived at Mount Himavat, took the medicinal herbs, and returned; having brought them back, he applied them to the wound.
Once they had applied it to their sores, the suffering was immediately relieved and a pleasant sensation arose.
When the pleasant sensation had arisen, the World-Honored One, in accordance with their needs, preached the sublime Dharma to them.
Having heard this teaching, those six Śākya women distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement; the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
In this world, the Blessed One asked the six Śākya women, headed by Mṛgajā: "In this context,
what is meant by 'fulfillment through loving-kindness' (maitrī-pūrṇā)?"
The answer is:
It is precisely that medicinal wisdom.
This is what is called the medicinal wisdom.
Regarding "or by means of contact," it is as described:
The Blessed One was wandering through various rooms and arrived at one dwelling.
There, the Blessed One saw a bhikṣu in that room who was afflicted by illness and suffering, lying alone without a companion amidst excrement and urine, unable to rise or move about.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the reason], asked the bhikṣu:
"For what reason have you encountered this affliction alone, without a companion?
The sick bhikṣu, being straightforward, replied to the World-Honored One:
"O World-Honored One!
I am indolent and unable to look after others, nor do others look after me.
O World-Honored One!"
I have no refuge, O Sugata! I have no protector.
The World-Honored One said:
"Bhikṣu! Did you not leave the household life to study the Way and become a śramaṇa for my sake?"
The bhikṣu said:
"So be it, World-Honored One!
So be it, Sugata!"
The Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus! I am your refuge, as well as that of the world of devas."
At that time, the World-Honored One gently raised him from his place of rest and led him outside to lie down again at ease.
Then the World-Honored One returned to the room, removed the straw mats, cleared away the excrement and urine, plastered the sleeping quarters, and spread new mats once more.

After bathing the sick bhikṣu and having him put on new clothes, they washed his old garments, brought him back into his room, and gently laid him upon a fresh bed and mattress, where he rubbed his body with his hands.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks! If you do not increase your diligent practice so as to reach what has not yet been reached, to attain what has not yet been attained, and to realize what has not yet been realized, then, monks!"
However, he again encountered a grave illness even more severe than this.
Just as when the World-Honored One stroked a sick bhikṣu with his hand, the suffering was immediately removed and he attained ease from his pain.
Once he had attained this pleasant sensation, the World-Honored One, in accordance with his needs, taught him the sublime Dharma.
Having heard this teaching, the bhikṣu became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him.
The Blessed One, out of compassion for that bhikṣu,
asked: "In this context,
what is meant by the fulfillment of loving-kindness?"
The answer is:
that contact is it.
Furthermore, as for "contact," it is as has been said:
The World-Honored One was staying on one side of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, while Devadatta was also on another side.
At that time, Devadatta suffered from a severe headache that was unbearable.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with his hand—endowed with the primary and secondary marks, the color of purple-polished gold, and filled with hundreds of thousands of merits—pierced the head of Devadatta on Mount Maṇi; he removed all his suffering and pain, whereby Devadatta immediately attained pleasant sensation.
Having obtained this pleasant sensation, Devadatta thought to himself:
"Whose grace is this?
He looked back and saw that it was the hand of the World-Honored One.
Having seen this, he said:
"Excellent, Siddhārtha!
You have studied this medicine well; with such medical formulas, you will surely be able to make a living."
The World-Honored One’s compassion is fulfilled for the sake of Devadatta.
Question: In this context, what is meant by “compassion being fulfilled”?
Answer: It is precisely contact (*sparśa*).
This is what is called contact.
Regarding "or by means of cool shadows," it is as described:
the World-Honored One and the Venerable Śāriputra were traveling together in one place, while the Venerable Ānanda stood behind the Buddha holding a fly-whisk to fan him.
At that time, there was a bird pursued by a hawk; terrified, it flew into the shadow of the Venerable Śāriputra and stayed there, its body trembling like a solitary swaying tree.
When that bird left the shadow of Śāriputra and flew into the shadow of the Buddha, it became free from fear.
Having seen this, Ānanda joined his palms and said to the Buddha:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
When these birds were within the shadow of Venerable Śāriputra, their bodies trembled like a single swaying tree."
Having left the shadow of Śāriputra and reached the shadow of the World-Honored One, he was then free from fear.
The World-Honored One said:
"It is so, Ānanda!"
Thus it is, Ānanda!
Although the bhikṣu Śāriputra has abstained from killing, he is not yet utterly pure; therefore, when the bird stays within his shadow, its body trembles like a solitary swaying tree.
Ānanda! For three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have abstained from taking life and have fully perfected pure conduct; therefore, when birds dwell within my shadow, they are free from fear.
The Blessed One has fulfilled loving-kindness for the sake of those birds.
Question: In this context, how is loving-kindness fulfilled?
Answer: It is precisely this cool and refreshing shadow.
Furthermore, as for "cool and refreshing shadow," it is as has been said:
There was a thief whose hands and feet had been severed and who had been cast into a ditch.
That thief was one for whom the World-Honored One should manifest transformation; the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"If at this time the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to preach the Dharma for a single thief, they would not be able to deliver him."

Then the World-Honored One went to where the bandits were; having arrived, those bandits came within the shadow of the World-Honored One, and immediately their painful sensations ceased and they experienced pleasant sensations.
Having attained these pleasant sensations, the World-Honored One, in accordance with their needs, preached the sublime Dharma to them.
Having heard the Dharma, the thieves were distanced from dust and free from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
Thus, the World-Honored One’s compassion was fulfilled for the sake of these thieves.
It is asked:
In this context, what is the fulfillment of loving-kindness?
The answer is:
it is precisely the cool shade.
This is called the cool shade.
Just as the World-Honored One’s immeasurable kinds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) are not of a single type, for this reason the Vinaya states:
"The World-Honored One, having suffused all sentient beings with loving-kindness, teaches the Dharma."
As the Blessed One stated in a sutra:

"There are four kinds of persons who receive Brahma-merit. First, when a person establishes a stūpa for the relics of the Tathāgata in a place where none had previously been established, this is called the first person receiving Brahma-merit."

Furthermore, it is said that when a person builds a dwelling in a place where none has previously been established and dedicates it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, this is called the second person who receives Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, it is said that if a person reconciles a schism within the Saṃgha, this is called the third person who receives Brahma-merit.

Furthermore, it is said that when a person’s mind, accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), has filled one direction and dwells having accomplished it, and likewise fills the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—filling all directions—and dwells having accomplished it;

so too, when the mind, accompanied by compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), has filled one direction and dwells having accomplished it, and likewise fills the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—filling all directions—and dwells having accomplished it.
These are called the four persons who receive Brahma-merit.
The Parables (Avadānavādins) say:
"This was not spoken in the Buddha’s sūtras, nor is it Brahma-merit."
The Buddha’s sūtras state that "immeasurability" and so forth constitute Brahma-merit. Why is this?
That is to say, through acts such as the immeasurables and the giving of fruits, one thus receives Brahma-merit.

Is it the case that by erecting a small stūpa at such places as the Vajrāsana, the place where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, or the place where [the Buddha] descended from heaven, one obtains Brahma-merit equal to those [great stūpas]?
If one receives such Brahma-merit from [building] the Bamboo Grove, the Jeta’s Grove, or a deep forest of standing trees as a great monastic complex,
would one receive an equal amount of Brahma-merit by building a small hut in such a place?
In this way one receives Brahma-merit, namely by reconciling a schism caused by Devadatta’s incitement to strife.
Is it the same as receiving Brahma-merit by reconciling the minor disputes of the bhikṣus at Kauśāmbī?
Therefore, it is neither a Buddhist sūtra nor is it "Brahma-merit.
A Buddhist sūtra states that immeasurable [merits] and so forth are also Brahma-merit.
That which is spoken in this manner is the teaching of the Buddha’s sūtras, and it is also Brahma-merit. Question:
Such a fruit is not equal [to others].
Answer: Because they benefit others, these are the marks of worldly merit.
For example, "immeasurable" refers to benefiting others immeasurably, such as when one cultivates the immeasurables (apramāṇa) and so forth.
In this way, there is also immeasurable benefit for others: namely, at a place where none had previously been established, one establishes a *stūpa* with the relics of the Tathāgata.

Because of that site, hundreds of thousands of sentient beings cultivate wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; they make offerings to the World-Honored One with silken banners, flower canopies, flags, pennants, music, powdered incense, and ointments; and they aspire to the path of the Buddha, the path of the Śrāvaka, or the path of the Pratyekabuddha. They attain great wealth, are born into noble families, possess handsome features, and are reborn among gods and humans. Observing this, it is seen to be exceedingly beneficial.
In this way, there is immeasurable and supreme benefit for others, namely, the generation of immeasurable [roots of goodness] and so forth.
This too is likewise immeasurable benefit for others, namely, having constructed a dwelling in a place where none had previously been established and then offering it to the *caitya* Sangha.

That is to say, because hundreds of thousands of sentient beings in that place cultivate wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; recite, study, read, inquire, and teach; and contemplate the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma; and contemplate in silent seclusion to eliminate the fetters of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, thereby attaining the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship.

For the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one assists in various affairs; aspiring for the path of the Buddha, the Śrāvaka, or the Pratyekabuddha, one attains great wealth, is born into a noble and wealthy family, possesses a handsome appearance, and is reborn among gods and humans.
Contemplating this, one sees it is exceedingly beneficial.
Just as such immeasurable acts bring immense benefit to others— namely, the arousal of immeasurable [virtues] and so forth—
so too does this bring immeasurable benefit to others, namely, reconciling those who have caused schisms and discord within the Saṃgha.

Just as when the Saṃgha is divided, in turmoil, and ruined, at that time one has not yet attained realization and does not attain it; one has not yet obtained the fruits and does not obtain them; one cannot eliminate the fetters and does not achieve the exhaustion of outflows; nor does one recite or study the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma, nor contemplate the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma, nor contemplate silent stillness; one does not eliminate the fetters of the desire realm, nor the fetters of the form and formless realms, and one does not obtain the fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat.
In this trichiliocosm, from the turning of the Wheel of Dharma up to the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, the minds of beings were distracted.

Having brought about discord and strife within the Saṃgha, they claimed to have attained what they had not yet attained, and to have realized the fruits they had not yet realized; they claimed to have eliminated the fetters and attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). They recited and studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, contemplated the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and also practiced silent meditation. Yet they merely removed the fetters of the desire realm and the fetters of the form and formless realms, and [falsely] claimed to have attained the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*.
While turning the wheel of Dharma throughout the trichiliocosm, his mind remained undisturbed even as far as the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
To observe this is truly of great benefit.
Someone said:

That is to say, where no shrine has previously been established, one establishes a *stūpa* with the relics of the Tathāgata; since the Tathāgata is the cause of the sublime (*brahman*), one receives sublime merit at that place.

That is to say, where no dwelling has previously been established, one constructs a hall and offers it to the *saṃgha of the four quarters*; because it is a place for those who practice the sublime way, one receives sublime merit.
This refers to those who reconcile a divided and discordant Saṃgha; it is said that this is a cause for the Noble Path, and one receives Brahma-merit in that state.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated:
"One receives Brahma-merit by establishing a *stūpa* with the relics of the Tathāgata at a site where none had previously been established, due to four reasons."
What are the four? They are:
opening up an exceedingly sublime site, extensively bestowing wealth and goods, establishing relics, and completing the construction.
That is to say, when one builds a dwelling at a site where none has previously been established and offers it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, one receives Brahma-merit due to these four factors.

Having opened up the most wondrous intent and extensively bestowed material wealth, and having completed what was to be done, one recites, practices, and contemplates until attaining concentration where it had not yet been attained.
This refers to reconciling those who have caused strife within the Saṃgha; by means of four matters, one receives Brahma-merit:
eliminating the four verbal transgressions, practicing the four purities of speech, removing all that is unrighteous, and abiding in the dharma of giving.
That is to say, by practicing the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth, one receives "Brahma-merit" (*brahmapuṇya*) due to four reasons:
being free from strife, not engaging in strife, removing the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and having the fruit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as its reward within the form realm.
Question: What is the measure of the merit of Brahma-merit?
One school of thought says that the amount of merit by which one attains the status of a Wheel-turning King (cakravartin) through its causal practice constitutes the measure of Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the practice by which one attains the status of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, constitutes a unit of Brahma-merit.
Still others say that the practice by which one attains the status of a son of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven constitutes a unit of Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the practice by which one attains the state of Mahābrahmā constitutes a unit of Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Still others say that when the world is destroyed and begins to form again, the practice by which all sentient beings establish this great earth constitutes a unit of Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, there are those who say that when Brahmā requested the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma,
the merit received by the noble Great Brahmā for the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the Buddha constitutes the measure of Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Question: Since Mahābrahmā invited the Blessed One with a mind that is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), how can he receive the merit of Brahmā (*brahmapuṇya*)?
One explanation states that as soon as Mahābrahmā first resolved, "I shall go and invite the Blessed One," at that very moment Mahābrahmā received the merit of Brahmā.
This shall not be discussed.
Why? Because according to what you have said, one would receive retribution without having performed any action.
Question: If it is not so, then how is this? Answer:
The Great Brahmā requested the World-Honored One to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Having heard this, the Great Brahmā thought to himself:
"It is because I made the request that the Buddha has turned the wheel of Dharma."
With a heart full of joy, he makes an exceedingly sublime and virtuous vow; at that time, he receives Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Furthermore, others say that the merit received by all sentient beings, with the exception of those who have already become Bodhisattvas, constitutes the measure of Brahma-merit.
Regarding the statement that "thus speaking is called Brahma-merit," this is a term of praise and commendation.
Indeed, Brahma-merit is immeasurable, incalculable, asaṃkhyeya, and beyond counting.
As the Blessed One stated in the Sūtras:

"By cultivating and frequently practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one is reborn in the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*); by cultivating and frequently practicing compassion (*karuṇā*), one is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); by cultivating and frequently practicing sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); and by cultivating and frequently practicing equanimity (*upekṣā*), one is reborn in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)."

Question: If it is said that by practicing and repeatedly cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one is reborn in the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), this should indeed be so—that is, the retributive fruit of loving-kindness resides in the Heaven of Universal Purity.

However, as for the claim that by practicing and repeatedly cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) one is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), by practicing and repeatedly cultivating sympathetic joy (*muditā*) one is reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and by practicing and repeatedly cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*) one is reborn in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), this should not be so.
Why is this? These are the wholesome roots of merit belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and they should not receive retribution in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Why, then, is it said that through the repeated cultivation and frequent practice of compassion one is born in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), through the repeated cultivation and frequent practice of sympathetic joy one is born in the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and through the repeated cultivation and frequent practice of equanimity one is born in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
There is one who says that once Maitreya has descended, he shall explain it, for others are unable to do so.
Or it is said: "He speaks because [the teaching] is similar [to his own]."

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is a pleasant practice and a faculty of happiness; it is the most sublime among all states of birth and death, and it can be attained within the third dhyāna. Therefore, the Buddha taught that by cultivating loving-kindness, one is reborn in the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*).

The one who practices compassion (*karuṇā*) can censure the discoloration [of the body], and the sphere of emptiness (*ākāśāyatana*) likewise censures discoloration; therefore, the Buddha taught that by cultivating compassion, one gives rise to the sphere of emptiness.

The one who practices sympathetic joy (*muditā*) acts with delight, and the mind in the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) also acts with delight; therefore, the Buddha taught that by cultivating sympathetic joy, one gives rise to the sphere of consciousness.

The protector is able to relinquish; the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is also called relinquishment. For this reason, the Buddha taught the cultivation of the sphere of nothingness as the protection of life. Others say:
it is because that practitioner causes the mind to be joyful and contented.
There may be a practitioner who desires to attain the third dhyāna, or who desires to attain the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness.

Regarding one who desires to attain the third dhyāna: having abandoned the fetters of the desire realm, they experience neither pleasure nor joy; having abandoned the desire for the first dhyāna, they experience neither pleasure nor joy; and when abandoning the desire for the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna manifests before them, and their mind experiences rapturous joy.

This means that one who wishes to attain the sphere of infinite space eliminates desire for the realm of desire; the mind is neither delighted nor pleased. This continues until, having eliminated desire up to the third dhyāna, the mind is neither delighted nor pleased. At the moment of eliminating desire for the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space manifests before them, and the mind experiences joy and pleasure.

This means that one who seeks to attain the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana) eliminates desire for the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), such that the mind is neither delighted nor pleased; and so on, up to eliminating desire for the fourth dhyāna, such that the mind is neither delighted nor pleased. When desire for the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) is eliminated, the sphere of infinite consciousness manifests before the mind, and the mind is then delighted and pleased.

This means that one who seeks to attain the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) eliminates desire for the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), and the mind is neither delighted nor pleased; reaching the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), it eliminates desire there, and the mind is neither delighted nor pleased; when eliminating desire in the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), the sphere of nothingness manifests before the mind, and the mind is delighted and pleased.
This is said because it causes the practitioner’s mind to be joyful; for this reason, it is so.
Alternatively, it is said:
herein the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are explained.
That is to say, the factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path eliminate the second dhyāna; there, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is designated as their name.
That is to say, the factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path eliminate the fourth dhyāna; there, compassion (*karuṇā*) is designated as their name.
Regarding the factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path, excluding the sphere of infinite space, they designate "joy" as their name.
Regarding the factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path, excluding the sphere of infinite consciousness, they designate "equanimity" as their name.
This is called explaining the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) and the factors of the path (mārgāṅga); it is for this reason.
Some say: it is because of the severing of the intentions of those of other teachings (tīrthika).
The heterodox teachers conceive the notion of liberation within the formless realms, and they proclaim the notion of the path regarding the immeasurables and so forth.
As for those heterodox teachers who conceive the notion of liberation within the formless realms, the Blessed One declares that these are neither equal nor comparable.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka also says this:
"The heterodox practitioners are deluded regarding that which is free from [defilements], and they conceive the notion of liberation regarding that which is not free from them.
As for those who conceive the notion of liberation, the Blessed One has stated that they share in common [the attainment of] the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) and so forth."
The detailed exposition concludes in the section on the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
*Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 11; *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 12.
Compiled by the Arhat Śītabhāṇi;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kaśmīra during the Fu Qin dynasty.

35. The Four Formless Spheres (Ārūpya-āyatana). Chapter Thirty-Five: The Four Formless Spheres. Regarding the four formless spheres: they are the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Question: For what purpose is this treatise composed? Answer:
This treatise was composed in order to refute the views of others.

Some maintain that there is form within the formless realm (*ārūpya*), while others maintain that there is no form within the formless realm. The Vāibhāṣikas maintain that there is form within the formless realm, whereas the Aśmāparāntakas maintain that there is no form within the formless realm.
Question: With what intention does the Vībhajyavādin wish to maintain that there is form within the formless realm? Answer:
He [bases his position] on a sūtra of the Buddha concerning the existence of form within the formless realms.
He says: "The World-Honored One stated in a sūtra:"
Name-and-form conditions consciousness, and consciousness conditions name-and-form; yet there is consciousness within the formless realm.
If there is consciousness within the formless realm, there should likewise be form.
Furthermore, other sūtras state:
"Life-force (āyus), warmth (uṣman), and consciousness (vijñāna)—these three factors are always conjoined and never separate; these three factors cannot be established as distinct entities."
If these three dharmas cannot be established as distinct from one another, then there must be consciousness within formlessness (*ārūpya*).
If there is consciousness within formlessness, there should likewise be warmth; and warmth is precisely form (*rūpa*).
In another sutra, the Blessed One said: "If one were to say:
'Apart from form, apart from feeling, perception, and formations, I designate consciousness alone as coming, staying, being born, or passing away.'"
This should not be stated: that there is consciousness within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If there were consciousness within the formless realm, there would likewise have to be four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Furthermore, another point of censure is stated:

If there is no form within the formless realm, it means that when one passes away from the desire realm or the form realm to be born in the formless realm, for eighty thousand kalpas, form is permanently severed.
If one passes away from there to be born in the desire realm or the form realm, those eighty thousand kalpas of permanent severance of form are resumed once again.

If form were to arise again after being permanently severed for eighty thousand kalpas, then an Arhat who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder and has permanently severed all conditioned formations (saṃskāra) would likewise have to be reborn hereafter.

If an Arhat who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder were to be reborn again after all conditioned formations have been permanently severed, then there would be no liberation, no deliverance, no transcendence, and no essential way of escape.
Do not say there is fault; therefore, there is form within the formless.
Since this sūtra serves as proof, the Vāibhāṣikas maintain that there is form within the formless.
Question: With what intention does the Vaitulika (Yùduōbótí) wish to maintain that there is no form within the formless realm? Answer:
Starting from the Buddha’s sūtras, he wishes to establish that there is no form within the formless realm.
He says: "The World-Honored One stated in a sūtra:"
That liberation through cessation transcends form and reaches the formless; such a meditative attainment (samāpatti) he realizes within his own body and dwells having accomplished it.
Since he has transcended form and reached the formless, therefore there is no form within the formless.
Furthermore, other sūtras state:
"One departs from desire to reach the realm of form; one departs from form to reach the formless realm.
Since one departs from form to reach the formless, there is therefore no form within the formless.
Furthermore, another sutra states:

"Having transcended all perceptions of form, having extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space."
If one transcends all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), for that reason there is no form within the formless (*ārūpya*).

Furthermore, other sūtras in the *Dhyāna-pāda* state that there is attainment and what is to be attained, and existence and what exists, whether it be form, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
He contemplates these phenomena as a disease, an abscess, a thorn, an arrow, and a venomous snake; he contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.

As stated in the section on the formless (*ārūpya*), this refers to that which is attained and that which is obtainable, whether it be feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
He contemplates these phenomena as being like a disease, like an abscess, like a thorn, like an arrow, and like a venomous snake; he contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
If form is mentioned in the section on dhyāna but not mentioned in the section on the formless, one can thereby know that there is no form within the formless realm.
Furthermore, another point of censure is stated:
if there were form within the formless realm, the sequence of the abandonment of phenomena could not be known.
That is to say, regarding phenomena that exist in the desire realm and those that exist in the form and formless realms, such a sequence for abandoning phenomena would be impossible to discern.

If the sequence of the factors to be abandoned were unknowable, the ultimate abandonment of those factors would be unknowable; it is precisely because the sequence of the factors to be abandoned is known that one can arrive at the ultimate state and establish it as such.
If one were to reach the ultimate without severing [the afflictions], there would be no liberation, no release, no departure, and no essential way of transcendence.
Do not say there is fault; therefore, within the formless there is no form.
Based on the evidence of this sūtra, the Yuktavādin maintains that there is no form within the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
Such is one statement; such are two statements. Thus, it is well said that there is no form within the formless realm.
Question: If there is no form within the formless realm, how can this view of the Ayatavādin be reconciled with the scriptural evidence cited by the Vibhajyavādin?
Answer: This sūtra contains an underlying intention that can be interpreted. Question:
What is the underlying intention?
How is this reconciled?
The answer is:

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, sometimes expounds sūtras on account of the desire realm; sometimes on account of the form realm; sometimes on account of the formless realm; sometimes on account of both the desire and form realms, or the form and formless realms; sometimes on account of all three realms; and sometimes on account of that which transcends the three realms.
Regarding the statement that this refers to the desire realm and not the form or formless realms, it is as stated:
"There are three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of ill-will, and the realm of harmfulness.
This sūtra speaks of the desire realm, not the form or formless realms.

Regarding the statement that it pertains to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and not to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is as explained above in the Chapter on Dhyāna (*dhyānapaṭala*).
This sūtra speaks of the form realm, and not of the desire realm or the formless realm.
Regarding the statement that it is neither the desire realm nor the form realm because it belongs to the formless realm, this is as explained in the preceding "Chapter on the Formless.
This sūtra states that because it belongs to the formless realm, it is neither the desire realm nor the form realm.
Regarding the statement that this is taught with reference to the desire and form realms and not the formless realm:
as in this sūtra, "Name-and-form conditions consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form.
This sūtra is taught with reference to the desire and form realms, not the formless realm.
Why is this? Because within these realms of desire and form there is form, it is said that "name-and-form conditions consciousness, and consciousness conditions name-and-form.
Within the formless realm there is no form; therefore, it is said that "name conditions consciousness, and consciousness conditions name."
For this reason, this sūtra speaks in reference to the desire realm and the form realm, not the formless realm.
As for those sūtras that speak in reference to the form and formless realms rather than the desire realm, such as the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, the *Sūtra on What is Taught*, and the *Manomaya-sūtra*.
This sūtra speaks in terms of the form and formless realms, not the desire realm.
Regarding its being spoken in terms of the three realms, it is as stated:
"the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm."
This sūtra speaks from the perspective of the three realms.
As for that which speaks from the perspective of being apart from the three realms, it is as stated:
"O bhikṣus!"
I shall now speak of nirvāṇa and the path to nirvāṇa.
This sūtra is taught because it is free from the three realms.
As it has been said:

These three factors—vitality, warmth, and consciousness—are always conjoined and never separated; as for the statement that these three factors cannot be established separately, this sūtra was spoken with reference to the desire and form realms, not the formless realm.

Why is this? Because within these realms of desire and form there is matter; therefore, these three factors are always conjoined and never separated, and these three factors cannot be established as distinct entities.
In the formless realm there is no form; therefore, these two factors—vitality and consciousness—are always conjoined and never separated, and it is impossible to designate them as distinct entities.
This is what is intended by this sutra.

As you have stated—that these three dharmas are always conjoined, never separated, and cannot be designated separately—these three dharmas can indeed be designated separately, by way of the elements (*dhātu*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the aggregates (*skandha*).

Regarding the designation according to the elements (*dhātu*): life-force is subsumed under the element of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); warmth is subsumed under the element of form (*rūpadhātu*); and consciousness is subsumed under the seven elements of mind (*manodhātu*).

Regarding the designation according to the bases (*āyatana*): life-force is subsumed under the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); warmth is subsumed under the base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*); and consciousness is subsumed under the base of mind (*manāyatana*).

Regarding the designation of distinct aggregates: life-span is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), warmth is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and consciousness is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Thus, these three phenomena cannot remain eternally conjoined; they may also be designated as distinct because of their respective elements (*dhātu*), sense-bases (*āyatana*), and aggregates (*skandha*).
Do not speak thus:
"These three dharmas are eternally conjoined and never separated; these three dharmas cannot be designated separately.
As it has been said:
If one were to say:

"I designate consciousness alone as being apart from form, apart from feeling, perception, and formations—whether coming or going, or being born or passing away"—this should not be said; for this sutra also speaks of designations within the desire realm.
Why is this? Because within these realms of desire and form there is form, this consciousness is therefore designated by way of the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Within the formless realm there is no form; therefore, that consciousness is designated by way of the three stations of consciousness.
That is to say, if one were to assert:
"I exclude the four stations of consciousness and designate consciousness alone," this could never be successfully established.
This means that it is established by excluding one consciousness-abiding from the three consciousness-abidings;
it is that which can establish them,
as it has been said:

If there were no form within the formless realm, it would mean that when one passes away from the desire or form realms and is reborn in the formless realm, their form would be permanently severed for eighty thousand kalpas.
If they were then to pass away from there and be reborn in the desire or form realms, their form—which had been permanently severed for eighty thousand kalpas—would arise once again.

If form were to arise again after being permanently severed for eighty thousand kalpas, then an Arhat who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder and has permanently severed all conditioned formations would likewise have to be reborn later.

If an Arhat who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder were to be reborn again after all conditioned formations have been forever severed, then there would be no liberation, no deliverance, no transcendence, and no essential way of escape.
Do not say there is a fault, for this reason there is form within the formless.
The answer is:
this cannot be reconciled.

This is neither Sūtra, nor Vinaya, nor Abhidharma; one cannot subvert the Dharma of the noble ones by means of worldly analogies, for worldly analogies are of one nature and the Dharma of the noble ones is of another.
If this is to be understood universally, what is its intended meaning?
The answer is:

sometimes form and the formless arise from form and the formless; sometimes the formless arises from form and the formless; sometimes the formless arises from the formless; and sometimes form and the formless arise from the formless.

Regarding "arising in the form and formless realms due to the form and formless realms": this refers to those who, having passed away from the desire or form realms, are reborn again in the desire or form realms.
Regarding "arising in the formless realm due to the form and formless realms": this refers to those who, having passed away from the desire or form realms, are reborn in the formless realm.
Regarding "arising in the formless realm due to the formless": this refers to one who, upon passing away from the formless realm, is reborn in the formless realm.
Regarding "arising in both the form and formless realms due to the formless": this refers to one who, upon passing away from the formless realm, is reborn in either the desire or form realm.
There are cases where the continuity of form is severed until the very end, and cases where it is severed for a mere moment.
Regarding the severance of the continuity of form until the very end, that form does not arise again.
Regarding the severance of the continuity of form for a mere moment, that form arises once more.
When that Arhat enters the realm of Nirvana without remainder, all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) are forever severed; therefore, he is not born again.
Question: How does that Vībhajyavādin reconcile this with the scriptural evidence cited by the Pūrvavādin?
He replied: "That person says:
As it is stated in the Buddha’s sūtras:"
That liberation through cessation transcends form and reaches the formless; such a meditative attainment (samāpatti) he realizes within his own body and dwells having accomplished it.
This sutra was taught by the Buddha because he had transcended coarse form.
Within the formless realm there is still form; it is merely the subtle four great elements dispersed throughout the realm of space.
It is said: this is not being discussed here.
Why is this? For those who speak of the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of form (*rūpa*) still consider them coarser than the other four aggregates (*skandha*).
Yet, while they speak of those four aggregates, they do not speak of the aggregate of form.
Because of this lack of knowledge, there is no form within formlessness.
Question: As it has been said:
How is it that one departs from desire to reach the realm of form, and departs from form to reach the formless realm?
The answer is:
Just as that form is separated from the desire realm, yet form still exists within form;
so too, although the formless is separated from form, form should likewise exist within the formless.
It is said:
This need not be discussed. Why? Because:
If that form were separate from the form of this desire realm, it would be so.

However, while that form is separate from the desires within this desire realm, it is not separate from form; there is no desire within form itself. Likewise, that formless state is separate from the form within this form realm; for this reason, there is no form within the formless.
As for the proofs from other sūtras, they cannot be reconciled [with your position].

It is simply that those [propositions] are the fruit of lack of wisdom, the fruit of darkness, the fruit of delusion, and the fruit of a lack of diligence—namely, the desire to claim that there is form within the formless, when in fact there is no form within the formless.
This treatise is composed for the purpose of severing the intentions of others and revealing one’s own intention by teaching the Dharma as it truly is;
it is composed so that one does not sever the intentions of others nor reveal one’s own intention, but rather teaches the Dharma as it truly is.
The four formless [attainments] are the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the sphere of infinite space?
It is as described in the *Vasumitra-sūtra*:

Regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*): it refers to both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*) therein; that is to say, it consists of wholesome feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Question:

For what reason is it that, while for the dhyānas one sometimes speaks of both attainment and rebirth, or sometimes speaks of rebirth without attainment, for the formless realms (*ārūpya*) one speaks of all cases as being both attainment and rebirth?
The answer is:
Those formless states are not diverse, nor do they have various characteristics, nor are they dissimilar; therefore, all are said to be meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and births (*upapatti*).

Meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are of various kinds and possess diverse, dissimilar characteristics; for this reason, some speak of both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and birth (*upapatti*), while others speak of birth that is not meditative attainment.
Others say: "The formless realms (*ārūpya*) are not adorned with such diverse merits; therefore, all [states therein] are said to be both meditative attainment and birth."

The practitioner of dhyāna is adorned with various kinds of merit; therefore, some speak of both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and birth (*upapatti*), while others speak of birth that is not meditative attainment. Others say:
"In the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there are not many sublime dharmas; therefore, all [teachings] speak only of meditative attainment and birth."

Practitioners of dhyāna possess many subtle dharmas; for this reason, some speak of both meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and birth (*upapatti*), while others speak of birth that is not meditative attainment. Some say:
"The formless realms (*ārūpya*) are subtle, invisible, and difficult to manifest; therefore, all [masters] speak of both meditative attainment and birth."

The meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are coarse, being visible and manifest; for this reason, some speak of "correct attainment" (samāpatti) and "birth," while others speak of "birth" that is not "correct attainment.

The four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the sphere of infinite space?

In this regard, a bhikṣu, having transcended all perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, [perceives] "space is infinite," and thus dwells, having attained the sphere of infinite space.

Regarding "he transcends all perceptions of form": perceptions of form refer to the manifestations of the pervasive perceptions of form within the four dhyānas; these should be extinguished. For this reason, it is said that he transcends all perceptions of form.
Regarding "the extinction of the perception of resistance": the perception associated with the five bodies of sensory consciousness is what is meant by "perception of resistance. Question:

Just as the perception associated with the five bodies of sensory consciousness is extinguished when desire for the desire realm is eliminated, it may also be extinguished when desire for the first dhyāna is eliminated.
Why is it that when one eliminates desire in the fourth dhyāna, the "perception of resistance" (*pratighasaṃjñā*) is said to be extinguished?
The answer is:

although there are perceptions associated with the five bodies of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*), they may be extinguished either at the time of eliminating desire in the desire realm or at the time of eliminating desire in the first dhyāna; however, the locus of those perceptions has not yet been extinguished.
This refers to the four dhyānas, wherein having eliminated desire, that sphere of perception ceases; it is spoken of because perception has ceased.
Alternatively, it is said:
it is spoken of because its basis has ceased.

Although there are perceptions associated with the five groups of consciousness that may cease when desire for the desire realm is eliminated, or when desire for the first dhyāna is eliminated, they persist as long as they have not yet ceased;
however, once desire for the fourth dhyāna has been eliminated, their basis ceases. Therefore, it is said [they cease] because their basis has ceased.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the perception associated with aversion is what possesses the characteristic of being "with resistance" (*sāpatigha*).
A question is asked:
Just as the perception associated with aversion is eternally extinguished when one eliminates desire in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), [is this not the case here too?]
Why is it said that the four dhyānas eliminate desire?
The answer is:

It is said because they extinguish the causes; that is to say, hatred arises from causes and conditions, and form is its cause and condition. When one eliminates desire for that form through the four dhyānas, it is forever extinguished.
This is called "speaking because of the cessation of causes and conditions"; for this reason, it is said that the perception of resistance (pratigha-saṃjñā) ceases.
Regarding "not attending to diverse perceptions," these are the perceptions dispersed throughout the stages of the four dhyānas.
Question: For what reason does he say "not to be mindful"? Answer:
This refers to the practitioner dispersing the perceptions of the four dhyānas and withdrawing from the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite space.
The Blessed One said:
"One should not dwell upon these perceptions; rather, one cultivates the path for the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space."
For this reason, it is said that one does not attend to discursive thoughts.
Regarding the phrase "one who dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space":
a question is asked:
For what reason is the sphere of empty space taught?
Is it by way of its intrinsic nature,
or by way of its conditions?
If it were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would have to be the nature of the four aggregates (*skandha*).
If it were a condition (*pratyaya*), it would have to be conditioned by the Four Noble Truths (*catuḥsatya*).
Having formulated this argument, [he said]:
Answer: The sphere of emptiness (ākāśāyatana) is neither an intrinsic nature nor a causal condition; it is spoken of as the "sphere of emptiness" merely as a conventional designation (upāya).
As it is said in that *Prajñapti*:

What is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite space through skillful means? How is the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space accomplished through skillful means?

When first beginning this practice, one may dwell upon a mountain peak, or upon a high pavilion, or upon a lofty terrace. Thinking of this place as the highest point, one does not conceive of it as the lowest point; one contemplates it as empty, resolves it as empty in mind, observes it as empty, and discerns it as empty.
Because it is accomplished through emptiness, this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is achieved; since this concentration is established, it is called the "Sphere of Emptiness" (*ākāśāyatana*).
Alternatively, it is said:
this phenomenon must be so, for that stage is the first among the formless realms, and thus it is named the Sphere of Emptiness.
Some say: It is called the Sphere of Infinite Space because it is detached from form.

When that practitioner has already taken form as an object in the lower stages—from the removal of desire for the Desire Realm up to the Third Dhyāna—and having removed the desire for the Fourth Dhyāna, there is no further form remaining above the Fourth Dhyāna to serve as an object; at that time, he gives rise to the perception of space.
It is like a person who climbs from branch to branch until reaching the very top of a tree; since there are no further branches above for him to grasp, he then gives rise to the perception of space.

In this way, when a practitioner contemplates the forms of the lower stages, they eliminate desire for the Desire Realm; continuing thus up to the Third Dhyāna, they eliminate desire for the Fourth Dhyāna, as there are no further forms above it to serve as objects of contemplation. At that time, the perception of emptiness arises.
Because it is free from form, it is called the sphere of infinite space.
Alternatively, it is said that one gives rise to a corresponding perception based on the sphere of infinite space.
As for the speaker:
there was a bhikṣu who had attained the meditative absorption of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Upon arising from that concentration, he reached out his hand and felt about for his bed.
A fellow student asked,
"What do you seek? He replied:
I sought myself.
My fellow student said, "You are already on your bed; what more is there for you to seek?"
This refers to the perception of similarity upon arising from meditative concentration; this is called the sphere of infinite space. Therefore, it is said to be "infinite space.

As for "dwelling in the accomplishment of the sphere of infinite space," it means that the four aggregates belonging to the level of that sphere of space have been successfully attained and perfected; therefore, it is said to be "dwelling in the accomplishment of the sphere of infinite space."
